original_question: For a signed graph consisting of 2k odd cycles of pairwise equal length and opposite signs, is the signature described in Proposition 3.27 the signature that minimizes spectral radius?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. A signed graph is a pair $\Gamma=(G,\sigma)$ where $G=(V,E)$ is a finite simple graph and $\sigma:E\to\{+1,-1\}$ is a signature. The (signed) adjacency matrix $A_\sigma$ of $\Gamma$ has $(A_\sigma)_{uv}=\sigma(uv)$ if $uv\in E$ and $0$ otherwise. The spectral radius of $\Gamma$ is $\rho(\Gamma)=\max\{|\lambda|:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }A_\sigma\}$. The sign of a cycle $C$ in $\Gamma$ is $\sigma(C)=\prod_{e\in E(C)}\sigma(e)\in\{+1,-1\}$; the cycle is called positive (resp. negative) accordingly. Two signatures $\sigma,\sigma'$ on $G$ are switching-equivalent if there exists $\theta:V\to\{+1,-1\}$ such that $\sigma'(uv)=\theta(u)\sigma(uv)\theta(v)$ for every edge $uv$; switching-equivalent signatures yield similar adjacency matrices and hence the same spectrum.

Setup. Fix an integer $k\ge 1$ and an odd integer $\ell\ge 3$. Let $G$ be the graph obtained from $2k$ vertex-disjoint cycles of common length $\ell$ by identifying one vertex of each cycle to a single common vertex (so $G$ is a bouquet of $2k$ odd cycles of equal length sharing a single vertex). On $G$ consider the signature $\sigma^\star$ in which exactly $k$ of the $2k$ cycles are positive and the remaining $k$ are negative (this signature, up to switching equivalence, depends only on which cycles are positive and which are negative, and any two such signatures with the same partition of cycles into $k$ positive and $k$ negative are switching-equivalent). It is known that the resulting signed graph $\Gamma^\star=(G,\sigma^\star)$ satisfies $\rho(\Gamma^\star)<2\sqrt{4k-1}$.

Question. Among all signatures $\sigma$ on the underlying graph $G$, does $\sigma^\star$ achieve the minimum value of the spectral radius $\rho((G,\sigma))$? Equivalently, prove or disprove that $\rho((G,\sigma))\ge\rho(\Gamma^\star)$ for every signature $\sigma$ of $G$.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an explicit open problem in a 2019 survey on open problems in the spectral theory of signed graphs (Belardo–Cioabă–Koolen–Wang). Subsequent literature on extremal spectral radii of signed graphs (e.g., works on unbalanced signed graphs with extremal index, signed bipartite graphs, etc.) does not appear to address or resolve this specific minimization question for the bouquet of 2k odd cycles of equal length with opposite-sign pairing, so the problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Let N_α(d) denote the maximum number of equiangular lines in R^d with common angle α. Is it true that N_{1/5}(d) = 276 for 23 <= d <= 185, and N_{1/5}(d) = floor(3(d - 1)/2) for d >= 185?
self_contained_problem:
A set of lines through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is called equiangular with common angle $\arccos(\alpha)$ (where $0<\alpha<1$) if the angle between any two distinct lines in the set equals $\arccos(\alpha)$. For each dimension $d\ge 1$ and each $\alpha\in(0,1)$, let $N_\alpha(d)$ denote the maximum cardinality of such a set of equiangular lines in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with common angle $\arccos(\alpha)$.

Prove or disprove the following two statements about the case $\alpha=1/5$:
1. For every integer $d$ with $23 \le d \le 185$, one has $N_{1/5}(d) = 276$.
2. For every integer $d \ge 185$, one has $N_{1/5}(d) = \lfloor 3(d-1)/2 \rfloor$.
status_search_result: The Lemmens–Seidel conjecture for common angle arccos(1/5) was resolved by Cao, Koolen, Lin, and Yu (2022) using forbidden subgraphs for Seidel eigenvalue −5, confirming N_{1/5}(d)=276 for 23≤d≤185 and N_{1/5}(d)=⌊3(d−1)/2⌋ for d≥185. A new proof was given by Ge and Liu (2025).

context_brief: three-eigenvalue Seidel matrices without regular graph
original_question: Do there exist Seidel matrices of order at least 14 with exactly three distinct eigenvalues whose switching class contains no regular graph?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S$ be a symmetric $n\times n$ matrix with zero diagonal and off-diagonal entries in $\{-1,+1\}$; such a matrix is called a Seidel matrix. To every simple graph $\Gamma$ on $n$ vertices one associates the Seidel matrix $S(\Gamma)$ whose $(i,j)$-entry (for $i\neq j$) equals $-1$ if $i$ and $j$ are adjacent in $\Gamma$ and $+1$ otherwise. Two graphs $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$ on the same vertex set are called Seidel-switching equivalent if there exists a subset $U$ of the vertex set such that $\Gamma'$ is obtained from $\Gamma$ by complementing all edges between $U$ and its complement (and leaving all other adjacencies unchanged). The switching class of $\Gamma$ is the equivalence class under this relation; equivalently, it corresponds to the equivalence class of $S(\Gamma)$ under conjugation by signed diagonal $\pm 1$ matrices.

Question: Does there exist an integer $n \ge 14$ and a Seidel matrix $S$ of order $n$ such that $S$ has exactly three distinct eigenvalues and the switching class of (any graph corresponding to) $S$ contains no regular graph?
status_search_result: Known partial results: every Seidel matrix of odd order with precisely three distinct eigenvalues contains a regular (in fact strongly regular) graph in its switching class, and the same holds for all such matrices of order at most 12. Some sources indicate that examples (even an infinite family) of Seidel matrices with exactly three distinct eigenvalues whose switching class contains no regular graph have been pointed out in subsequent work (e.g. enumeration/classification work by Szöllősi and Östergård up to order 23, with a candidate at order 18), but the search did not yield a definitive, citable confirmation that the existence question for orders $\ge 14$ has been fully resolved. The status is therefore reported as unknown.

original_question: For a graph Γ on n vertices, must its Seidel energy satisfy S(Γ) >= 2(n - 1), with equality at the complete graph K_n?
self_contained_problem:
Let Γ be a simple graph on n vertices. The Seidel matrix S(Γ) of Γ is the n×n symmetric matrix with diagonal entries 0, off-diagonal entry −1 in position (i,j) if vertices i and j are adjacent, and +1 otherwise. The Seidel energy of Γ is defined as
   S(Γ) = ∑_{i=1}^n |λ_i|,
where λ_1,…,λ_n are the eigenvalues of S(Γ).

Prove or disprove: for every graph Γ on n vertices,
   S(Γ) ≥ 2(n − 1),
with equality attained at the complete graph K_n.
status_search_result: Haemers' conjecture on the Seidel energy of graphs has been proved. Ghorbani established the inequality under the additional assumption |det S(Γ)| ≥ n−1, and the general case was settled by Akbari, Einollahzadeh, Karkhaneei and Nematollahi (arXiv:1901.06692, published in European Journal of Combinatorics, 2020). A short proof was later given (Linear Algebra and its Applications, 2024).

paper_title: Free Boundary Minimal Surfaces in the Unit Ball: Recent Advances and Open Questions
context_brief: Topology of free boundary minimal submanifolds
original_question: Let Σ be a k-dimensional manifold, possibly immersed or embedded, inside the Euclidean unit ball B^n, with boundary on ∂B^n, such that Σ is minimal and meets ∂B^n orthogonally along its boundary; in other words, Σ is a free boundary minimal submanifold in B^n. What topological restrictions, if any, must Σ satisfy in order for such a free boundary minimal submanifold to exist? In particular, does the answer depend on whether one asks for immersed examples or embedded examples?
self_contained_problem:
Let $B^n = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : |x| \le 1\}$ denote the closed Euclidean unit ball, with boundary $\partial B^n = S^{n-1}$. Let $\Sigma$ be a smooth $k$-dimensional manifold with boundary $\partial\Sigma$, and let $\phi : \Sigma \to B^n$ be a smooth immersion (respectively, embedding) such that $\phi(\partial\Sigma) \subset \partial B^n$ and $\phi(\mathrm{int}\,\Sigma) \subset \mathrm{int}\,B^n$. Call $\phi$ an immersed (resp. embedded) free boundary minimal submanifold if:
(i) $\phi(\Sigma)$ is a minimal submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (its mean curvature vector vanishes identically); and
(ii) $\phi(\Sigma)$ meets $\partial B^n$ orthogonally along $\phi(\partial\Sigma)$, i.e., at each boundary point the position vector (the outward unit normal to $\partial B^n$) lies in the tangent space of $\phi(\Sigma)$.

Determine all topological restrictions (if any) that the underlying manifold $\Sigma$ must satisfy in order for such an immersion (resp. embedding) into $B^n$ to exist. In particular, decide whether the set of admissible topological types of $\Sigma$ depends on whether one requires $\phi$ to be merely immersed or to be embedded.
status_search_result: The general question of which topological types of $k$-manifolds admit free boundary minimal immersions/embeddings into $B^n$ remains open. Recent work (e.g., min-max constructions yielding free boundary minimal surfaces with prescribed genus and number of boundary components, and existence of new families in $B^3$) has produced many new examples but no general topological obstruction theorem, and the immersed-versus-embedded distinction has not been resolved.

paper_title: Free Boundary Minimal Surfaces in the Unit Ball: Recent Advances and Open Questions
original_question: For each positive integer p, let ω_p(B^n) denote the p-width of the unit ball and let Σ_p be a smooth embedded free boundary minimal hypersurface in B^n, with multiplicity n_p, such that ω_p(B^n) = n_p|Σ_p|. Must the family {Σ_p}_{p∈N} contain infinitely many distinct hypersurfaces? If it does, must their areas satisfy |Σ_p| → +∞ as p → ∞?
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \geq 3$ and let $B^n \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ denote the closed Euclidean unit ball. A smooth properly embedded hypersurface $\Sigma \subset B^n$ is called a free boundary minimal hypersurface if it has zero mean curvature and meets $\partial B^n$ orthogonally along $\partial \Sigma$. For each positive integer $p$, the $p$-width $\omega_p(B^n)$ is defined via Almgren–Pitts min–max theory as
$$\omega_p(B^n) = \inf_{\Phi} \sup_{x \in \mathrm{dmn}(\Phi)} \mathbf{M}(\Phi(x)),$$
where the infimum is taken over all $p$-sweepouts $\Phi$ (continuous maps from a simplicial complex into the space of mod-$2$ flat $(n-1)$-cycles in $B^n$ with boundary in $\partial B^n$, having $p$-nontrivial cohomology class), and $\mathbf{M}$ denotes mass.

It is known that for each $p \in \mathbb{N}$ there exist a smooth embedded free boundary minimal hypersurface $\Sigma_p \subset B^n$ and a positive integer $n_p$ such that
$$\omega_p(B^n) = n_p \, |\Sigma_p|,$$
where $|\Sigma_p|$ denotes the $(n-1)$-dimensional Hausdorff measure of $\Sigma_p$.

Prove or disprove:
(a) The collection $\{\Sigma_p\}_{p \in \mathbb{N}}$ contains infinitely many pairwise non-congruent (or otherwise geometrically distinct) hypersurfaces.
(b) If (a) holds, then $|\Sigma_p| \to +\infty$ as $p \to \infty$.
category_tag: Free boundary minimal hypersurfaces and min-max widths
status_search_result: A literature search did not turn up a resolution of this question. Related work establishes the existence of infinite families of free boundary minimal hypersurfaces in the unit ball (e.g., O(m)×O(n)-invariant families for m+n<8) and computes the first n widths of B^n as the area of an equatorial (n−1)-ball, but does not determine whether the min-max realizing surfaces {Σ_p} form an infinite set with areas tending to infinity. The question appears to remain open.

paper_title: Free Boundary Minimal Surfaces in the Unit Ball: Recent Advances and Open Questions
original_question: In the three-dimensional unit ball B^3, is every embedded free boundary minimal annulus congruent, up to rigid motions of B^3, to the critical catenoid? Equivalently, is the critical catenoid the unique embedded free boundary minimal annulus in B^3?
self_contained_problem:
Let $B^3 = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 : |x| < 1\}$ denote the open unit ball with boundary $S^2 = \partial B^3$. A properly immersed surface $\Sigma \subset \overline{B^3}$ with $\partial \Sigma \subset S^2$ is called a free boundary minimal surface in $B^3$ if it has zero mean curvature in its interior and meets $S^2$ orthogonally along $\partial \Sigma$. The critical catenoid is the unique (up to rigid motions of $B^3$) piece of a suitably rescaled catenoid $\{(x,y,z) : \sqrt{x^2+y^2} = c\cosh(z/c)\}$ that defines a free boundary minimal annulus in $B^3$.

Prove or disprove: Every embedded free boundary minimal surface in $B^3$ that is topologically an annulus is congruent, via a rigid motion of $B^3$, to the critical catenoid.
status_search_result: The problem is the well-known critical catenoid conjecture (sometimes attributed to Fraser–Li). Until recently it had been verified only under extra symmetry hypotheses (e.g., reflection symmetry, antipodal symmetry, or two congruent boundary components). A January 2025 preprint by L. Sun ("Free boundary minimal surfaces and the reflection principle", arXiv:2501.02700) announces a proof of the full conjecture using a reflection principle across the sphere; as of May 2026 this proof has been circulated but not yet recorded as fully peer-reviewed and accepted in the literature, so the status is best described as partially solved / claimed.

paper_title: Free Boundary Minimal Surfaces in the Unit Ball: Recent Advances and Open Questions
original_question: Let Σ be an embedded free boundary minimal hypersurface in the Euclidean unit ball B^n. Since the coordinate functions restricted to Σ are Steklov eigenfunctions with eigenvalue 1, one always has σ_1(Σ) ≤ 1. Must the first nonzero Steklov eigenvalue actually satisfy the sharp equality σ_1(Σ) = 1 for every such embedded free boundary minimal hypersurface?
self_contained_problem:
Let $B^n \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ denote the closed Euclidean unit ball with boundary $S^{n-1}$. A smooth, properly embedded hypersurface $\Sigma \subset B^n$ with boundary $\partial\Sigma \subset S^{n-1}$ is called a free boundary minimal hypersurface if $\Sigma$ has zero mean curvature in $B^n$ and meets $S^{n-1}$ orthogonally along $\partial\Sigma$. For such $\Sigma$, the Dirichlet-to-Neumann (Steklov) operator on $\partial\Sigma$ is defined by $u \mapsto \partial_\nu \hat u\big|_{\partial\Sigma}$, where $\hat u$ is the harmonic extension of $u\in C^\infty(\partial\Sigma)$ to $\Sigma$ (i.e., $\Delta_\Sigma \hat u=0$ with $\hat u|_{\partial\Sigma}=u$) and $\nu$ is the outward unit conormal of $\partial\Sigma$ in $\Sigma$. Let $\sigma_1(\Sigma)$ denote the first nonzero eigenvalue of this Steklov operator. Because the coordinate functions of $\mathbb{R}^n$ restricted to $\Sigma$ are Steklov eigenfunctions with eigenvalue $1$, one has $\sigma_1(\Sigma) \le 1$.

Prove or disprove: for every embedded free boundary minimal hypersurface $\Sigma \subset B^n$, $\sigma_1(\Sigma) = 1$.
category_tag: Steklov eigenvalues of free boundary minimal surfaces
status_search_result: This is the Fraser–Li conjecture. It remains open in general; verifications exist for various known examples (e.g., work by McGrath and others), and it has been used as a hypothesis in conditional results, but no general proof or counterexample is known.

original_question: Let Σ^k be an immersed free boundary minimal submanifold of the Euclidean unit ball B^n, and let f: B^n → B^n be a conformal diffeomorphism. Is the (k−1)-dimensional volume of the boundary maximal within its conformal orbit, in the sense that |f(∂Σ)| ≤ |∂Σ| always holds?
self_contained_problem:
Let $B^n = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : |x| \le 1\}$ denote the closed Euclidean unit ball, and let $\Sigma^k \subset B^n$ be an immersed free boundary minimal submanifold of dimension $k$; that is, $\Sigma$ is a minimal $k$-dimensional immersed submanifold whose boundary $\partial\Sigma$ lies on $\partial B^n = S^{n-1}$ and meets $S^{n-1}$ orthogonally. Let $f : B^n \to B^n$ be a conformal diffeomorphism (the group of such maps coincides with the Möbius transformations of the ball). Denote by $|\cdot|$ the $(k-1)$-dimensional Hausdorff volume.

Determine whether the inequality
$$|f(\partial \Sigma)| \le |\partial \Sigma|$$
holds for every such $\Sigma$ and every conformal diffeomorphism $f : B^n \to B^n$; equivalently, whether the boundary volume of a free boundary minimal submanifold is maximal within its conformal orbit.
status_search_result: The question is listed as an open question in the survey on free boundary minimal surfaces in the unit ball. A web search did not turn up any subsequent paper resolving the conformal monotonicity of boundary volume for general free boundary minimal submanifolds; related work addresses linear isoperimetric inequalities, monotonicity formulae, and widths, but not this specific conjecture. The status thus appears to remain open.

context_brief: Asymptotic lower bound for computing X_alpha
original_question: In the linear model where an algorithm for a transformation is a product of matrices R_t and each step R_t is block diagonal with n-2 identity blocks and one 2x2 unitary block acting on only two coordinates, let F be the normalized n x n Fourier transform, let G = [[0, F], [-F^*, 0]], and define X_alpha = (cos alpha) Id + (sin alpha) G on C^(2n). What is the true asymptotic lower bound, as alpha tends to 0, on the number of such two-coordinate unitary steps required to compute X_alpha? In particular, can one prove that computing X_alpha requires essentially Omega(n log n) steps rather than only the currently derived Omega(alpha^2 n log n) or Omega(alpha n log n) lower bounds?
self_contained_problem:
Fix an integer n ≥ 1 and let F denote the normalized n×n discrete Fourier transform matrix, i.e. the unitary matrix with entries F_{jk} = (1/√n) exp(2πi jk/n) for 0 ≤ j,k ≤ n−1. Let F* denote its conjugate transpose. Define the 2n×2n unitary block matrix

   G = [[0, F], [−F*, 0]],

and, for a real parameter α, the 2n×2n unitary matrix

   X_α = (cos α) I_{2n} + (sin α) G.

Consider the following linear computational model. An "algorithm" computing a 2n×2n unitary U is a factorization U = R_T R_{T−1} ⋯ R_1, where each R_t is a 2n×2n unitary that is, up to permutation of coordinates, block-diagonal with one nontrivial 2×2 unitary block acting on two coordinates and the identity on the remaining 2n−2 coordinates. The cost of the algorithm is T, the number of such two-coordinate steps. Let c(U) denote the minimum cost over all such factorizations of U.

It is known that c(F) = Ω(n log n), and that c(X_α) ≥ Ω(α² n log n) and c(X_α) ≥ Ω(α n log n) can be established for small α > 0.

Determine the true asymptotic behavior of c(X_α) as α → 0 (with n → ∞). In particular, prove or disprove the conjecture that

   c(X_α) = Ω( (n log n) / log(1/α) ),

and decide whether c(X_α) = Ω(n log n) holds, i.e. whether the dependence on α can be eliminated entirely from the lower bound.
status_search_result: Obtaining tight super-linear lower bounds for computing Fourier-type unitaries in the 2×2 unitary gate linear model is a longstanding open problem. Ailon's matrix-entropy method gives Ω(n log n) for F itself and Ω((n log n)/R) in R-well-conditioned models, but the conjectured Ω((n log n)/log(1/α)) bound for X_α and the question of whether α-independent Ω(n log n) holds appear not to have been resolved in the available literature.

original_question: Even when the angle is fixed at alpha = pi/4 instead of tending to 0, can one prove a nontrivial lower bound for computing X_(pi/4) in the two-coordinate unitary-step model that is better than (1/(2 sqrt(2))) n log_2 n, which the paper states is the best bound obtainable from the vanilla entropy potential Phi?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let n be a positive even integer. Consider the "two-coordinate unitary-step" computational model for n×n unitary matrices: an algorithm is a finite sequence of elementary steps U_1, U_2, …, U_T, where each U_t is an n×n unitary matrix that acts non-trivially on at most two coordinates (i.e., its restriction to some pair of coordinates {i,j} is an arbitrary 2×2 unitary, and it is the identity on the remaining n−2 coordinates). The algorithm computes the unitary U_T U_{T−1} ⋯ U_1, and its cost is the number of steps T. For an n×n unitary M, let C(M) denote the minimum cost over all algorithms computing M exactly.

For a real angle α, let R(α) = [[cos α, −sin α],[sin α, cos α]] denote the 2×2 rotation, and define the n×n unitary
   X_α = R(α) ⊕ R(α) ⊕ ⋯ ⊕ R(α)   (n/2 blocks on the diagonal).

Define the entropy potential Φ on n×n unitaries by
   Φ(U) = ∑_{i,j=1}^{n} h(|U_{ij}|^2),   where h(x) = −x log_2 x   (with h(0)=0).
A standard estimate shows that any single two-coordinate unitary step changes Φ by at most a bounded amount, and using only this potential one can derive the lower bound
   C(X_{π/4}) ≥ (1/(2√2)) · n log_2 n.

Question. Prove or disprove: there exists a constant c > 1/(2√2) such that, for all sufficiently large even n,
   C(X_{π/4}) ≥ c · n log_2 n.
Equivalently, can one establish a lower bound on the two-coordinate unitary-step complexity of X_{π/4} that strictly improves the constant 1/(2√2) obtained from the vanilla entropy potential Φ?

Web searches do not surface any subsequent work that improves the 1/(2√2) n log_2 n constant for X_{π/4}; related literature on Ω(n log n) lower bounds in this model has not been reported as having sharpened this specific constant.

context_brief: Singer transfer injectivity beyond rank four
original_question: Let Tr_d denote Singer's algebraic transfer from GL_d-coinvariants of A_2-annihilated classes in H_*(B(ℤ/2)^d) to Ext^{d,d+*}_{A_2}(F_2,F_2). Is Tr_d a monomorphism for every rank d > 4? The paper states that Singer proposed injectivity for all positive integers d, but that this prediction is still unresolved in the range d > 4.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{F}_2$ denote the field of two elements and let $A = A_2$ be the mod-2 Steenrod algebra. For a positive integer $d$, let $V_d = (\mathbb{Z}/2)^d$ and consider its classifying space $BV_d$. The mod-2 homology $H_*(BV_d;\mathbb{F}_2)$ carries a natural left action of $A$, and the general linear group $GL_d := GL_d(\mathbb{F}_2)$ acts on $H_*(BV_d;\mathbb{F}_2)$ by permuting/transforming the generators.

Let $P_A H_*(BV_d;\mathbb{F}_2)$ denote the subspace of $A$-annihilated elements (the primitives under the action of positive-degree Steenrod operations), and let
$$\bigl(\mathbb{F}_2 \otimes_{GL_d} P_A H_*(BV_d;\mathbb{F}_2)\bigr)_n$$
denote its $GL_d$-coinvariants in internal degree $n$.

Singer's algebraic transfer is a homomorphism
$$Tr_d : \bigl(\mathbb{F}_2 \otimes_{GL_d} P_A H_*(BV_d;\mathbb{F}_2)\bigr)_n \;\longrightarrow\; \mathrm{Ext}_{A}^{d,\,d+n}(\mathbb{F}_2,\mathbb{F}_2),$$
defined for every $d \geq 1$ and every $n \geq 0$.

Question: Is $Tr_d$ a monomorphism for every integer $d > 4$ and every $n \geq 0$?
status_search_result: The conjecture is trivial for d ≤ 3 and was confirmed for d = 4. For d > 4, it had remained open in general; however, recent work (2025) claims a counterexample disproving Singer's conjecture in rank 6 at bidegree (6, 6+36). Thus the original prediction of injectivity for all d > 4 is now reported to be false in general, though for d = 5 and other ranks the question remains unresolved.

context_brief: Whether the fifth Singer transfer stays an isomorphism for t at least two
original_question: For every integer t ≥ 2, is the rank-5 Singer transfer Tr_5 an isomorphism in bidegree (5, 5 + (13·2^t - 5))? Using the reductions explained in the paper, this amounts to determining the GL_5-invariants of (QP_5)_{47}, where QP_5 = P_5/A_2^+P_5 for P_5 = F_2[x_1,…,x_5], and in particular understanding whether the invariant subspace of Ker((Sqg^0_*)(5,47)) vanishes. The paper also highlights a more interesting alternative in which this kernel has nontrivial GL_5-invariants and dim((QP_5)^{GL_5}_{47}) is not equal to 1.
self_contained_problem:
Work over the field $\mathbb{F}_2$. Let $\mathcal{A}$ denote the mod-2 Steenrod algebra and let $P_h = \mathbb{F}_2[x_1,\dots,x_h]$ be the polynomial algebra on $h$ generators of degree 1, regarded as a left $\mathcal{A}$-module. Let $\mathcal{A}_2^+ \subset \mathcal{A}$ denote the augmentation ideal, and define the "hit quotient"
$$QP_h \;=\; P_h/\mathcal{A}_2^+ P_h \;=\; \mathbb{F}_2 \otimes_{\mathcal{A}} P_h.$$
The general linear group $GL_h = GL_h(\mathbb{F}_2)$ acts on $P_h$ by linear substitution and this action descends to $QP_h$; write $(QP_h)^{GL_h}_d$ for the subspace of $GL_h$-invariants in internal degree $d$. Singer's algebraic transfer is a homomorphism
$$Tr_h : (\mathbb{F}_2 \otimes_{GL_h} (QP_h)^*)_d \longrightarrow \operatorname{Tor}^{\mathcal{A}}_{h, h+d}(\mathbb{F}_2, \mathbb{F}_2),$$
defined for each rank $h \geq 1$ and each internal degree $d \geq 0$. Let $Sq^0_*$ denote the classical squaring (Kameko) operation acting on $QP_h$ in the relevant degrees, and let $\bigl(\operatorname{Ker}(Sq^0_*)\bigr)(h, d)$ be its kernel in bidegree $(h,d)$.

Question. For every integer $t \geq 2$, is the rank-5 Singer transfer
$$Tr_5 : \bigl(\mathbb{F}_2 \otimes_{GL_5} (QP_5)^*\bigr)_{13\cdot 2^t - 5} \longrightarrow \operatorname{Tor}^{\mathcal{A}}_{5,\, 5 + (13\cdot 2^t - 5)}(\mathbb{F}_2, \mathbb{F}_2)$$
an isomorphism? Equivalently, determine the $GL_5$-invariants $(QP_5)^{GL_5}_{13\cdot 2^2 - 5} = (QP_5)^{GL_5}_{47}$, and in particular decide whether
$$\bigl(\operatorname{Ker}(Sq^0_*)(5, 47)\bigr)^{GL_5} \;=\; 0,$$
in which case $Tr_5$ is an isomorphism in bidegree $(5,\, 5+(13\cdot 2^t - 5))$ for every $t \geq 2$. Alternatively, exhibit the more interesting situation in which this kernel of $GL_5$-invariants is nontrivial and $\dim (QP_5)^{GL_5}_{47} \neq 1$.
status_search_result: Web searches turned up many recent works on Singer's conjecture for the algebraic transfer (rank 4 confirmed, rank 5 known to fail in internal degree 108, rank 6 negation results), but none of the located sources explicitly settle whether $Tr_5$ is an isomorphism in bidegree $(5,\,5+(13\cdot 2^t-5))$ for all $t\geq 2$, nor whether $(\operatorname{Ker}(Sq^0_*)(5,47))^{GL_5}=0$. The status of this specific family of bidegrees could not be confirmed from the search.

paper_title: Some open problems in the context of skew PBW extensions and semi-graded rings
context_brief: Gelfand-Kirillov conjecture for skew PBW extensions
original_question: If A is a bijective skew PBW extension over an Ore domain, can one prove a Gelfand-Kirillov-type description of its total ring of fractions, and in particular does one have an isomorphism between the total ring of fractions of the center and the center of the total ring of fractions, Q(Z(A)) ≅ Z(Q(A))?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let R be an Ore domain (an associative ring with no zero divisors in which every pair of nonzero elements has a common nonzero left and right multiple). A skew PBW extension of R is a ring A containing R together with finitely many indeterminates x_1,...,x_n such that:
(i) A is a free left R-module with basis the standard monomials x_1^{α_1}···x_n^{α_n}, α_i ∈ ℕ;
(ii) for every r ∈ R\{0} and every i, there exists c_{i,r} ∈ R\{0} with x_i r − c_{i,r} x_i ∈ R;
(iii) for every 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n, there exists c_{i,j} ∈ R\{0} with x_j x_i − c_{i,j} x_i x_j ∈ R + Rx_1 + ··· + Rx_n.
The extension A is called bijective if each map r ↦ c_{i,r} is bijective and each c_{i,j} is invertible in R.

Under these hypotheses A is known to be an Ore domain, so its total (two-sided) ring of fractions Q(A) exists. Let Z(A) denote the center of A, and Q(Z(A)) its field of fractions, and Z(Q(A)) the center of Q(A).

Problem. For every bijective skew PBW extension A of an Ore domain R:
(a) Establish a Gelfand–Kirillov-type description of Q(A), i.e., realize Q(A) as a skew field of fractions of an iterated Ore extension of a purely transcendental extension of an appropriate base division ring.
(b) Prove (or disprove) that the natural embedding Q(Z(A)) ↪ Z(Q(A)) is an isomorphism, i.e.,
   Q(Z(A)) ≅ Z(Q(A)).
category_tag: Skew PBW extensions and Gelfand-Kirillov conjecture
status_search_result: Listed as an open problem in surveys on skew PBW extensions and semi-graded rings. Partial results exist: the Gelfand–Kirillov conjecture has been verified for specific subclasses such as skew quantum polynomials and certain quantum algebras, but a general proof for all bijective skew PBW extensions over Ore domains, together with the isomorphism Q(Z(A)) ≅ Z(Q(A)), has not been established.

paper_title: Some open problems in the context of skew PBW extensions and semi-graded rings
original_question: If B is a left semi-graded Artin-Schelter regular algebra (SAS) with finite Gelfand-Kirillov dimension, must B be a left noetherian domain?
self_contained_problem:
Let $B$ be an associative $\mathbb{K}$-algebra over a field $\mathbb{K}$. We say $B$ is left semi-graded if there exists an ascending filtration $\{B_n\}_{n\geq 0}$ of $\mathbb{K}$-subspaces with $B_0 = \mathbb{K}$, $B = \bigcup_{n\geq 0} B_n$, $B_m \cdot B_n \subseteq B_{m+n}$, and each $B_n$ finite-dimensional, where the associated graded structure need not be connected graded in the classical sense (so the multiplication of homogeneous components $B_n^{sg} := B_n/B_{n-1}$ may include lower-degree contributions). Define the Gelfand–Kirillov (GK) dimension of $B$ in the usual way via $\mathrm{GKdim}(B) = \limsup_{n\to\infty} \log_n \dim_{\mathbb{K}} B_n$. 

A left semi-graded algebra $B$ is called left semi-graded Artin–Schelter regular (left SAS regular) if:
(i) $B$ has finite left global dimension $d$;
(ii) $\mathrm{Ext}^i_B(\mathbb{K}, B) = 0$ for $i \neq d$ and $\mathrm{Ext}^d_B(\mathbb{K}, B) \cong \mathbb{K}$ (Gorenstein-type condition adapted to the semi-graded setting), where $\mathbb{K}$ denotes the trivial left $B$-module $B/B_{>0}$.

Question: If $B$ is a left SAS regular algebra with $\mathrm{GKdim}(B) < \infty$, must $B$ be a left noetherian domain?
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in the context of semi-graded rings and skew PBW extensions. Web searches turn up no published proof or counterexample resolving whether every left SAS regular algebra of finite GK dimension is a left noetherian domain; partial results exist for skew PBW extensions over noetherian domains, but the general semi-graded SAS case appears unresolved.

paper_title: Evolutionary Dynamics of Cancer: From Epigenetic Regulation to Cell Population Dynamics—Mathematical Model Framework, Applications, and Open Problems
context_brief: Steady states of the heterogeneous stem-cell regeneration equation
original_question: Consider a nonnegative density Q(t,x) of resting-phase stem cells indexed by a one-dimensional epigenetic state x in Ω⊂R+, with effective cytokine signal Q̂(t)=∫Ω Q(t,x)ζ(x)dx. In the delay-free version of the heterogeneous stem-cell regeneration model, ∂Q(t,x)/∂t = −Q(t,x)(β(Q̂(t),x)+κ(x)) + 2∫Ω β(Q̂(t),y)Q(t,y)e^{−μ(y)}p(x,y)dy, where β, κ, μ, ζ are nonnegative and p(x,y) is a transition probability satisfying 0≤p(x,y)≤1 and ∫Ω p(x,y)dx=1 for each mother state y. At steady state, Q(x) must solve L_{Q̂}[Q](x)=2∫Ω β(Q̂,y)e^{−μ(y)}p(x,y)Q(y)dy − (β(Q̂,x)+κ(x))Q(x)=0 together with Q̂=∫Ω Q(x)ζ(x)dx. In the general case, especially when β depends on x and p(x,y) depends on the mother state y, does there exist a positive eigenvalue Q̂ with a nonnegative eigenfunction Q(x), is the resulting steady state unique, and under what conditions is it stable?
self_contained_problem:
Let Ω ⊂ R_+ be a measurable set parametrizing a one-dimensional epigenetic state x. Consider the nonnegative density Q(t,x) of resting-phase stem cells governed by the delay-free heterogeneous stem-cell regeneration equation

  ∂Q(t,x)/∂t = −Q(t,x)(β(Q̂(t),x) + κ(x)) + 2 ∫_Ω β(Q̂(t),y) Q(t,y) e^{−μ(y)} p(x,y) dy,

where:
 • Q̂(t) = ∫_Ω Q(t,x) ζ(x) dx is the effective cytokine signal,
 • β: R_+ × Ω → R_+ is a proliferation rate (in general depending on both Q̂ and the epigenetic state x),
 • κ: Ω → R_+ is a death/clearance rate,
 • μ: Ω → R_+ is a mitotic loss rate (e^{−μ(y)} ∈ (0,1]),
 • ζ: Ω → R_+ is a nonnegative weighting function,
 • p(x,y) is a transition (inheritance) kernel with 0 ≤ p(x,y) ≤ 1 and ∫_Ω p(x,y) dx = 1 for each mother state y ∈ Ω.

A steady state is a nonnegative function Q(x) on Ω together with a scalar Q̂ ≥ 0 satisfying the coupled system

  L_{Q̂}[Q](x) := 2 ∫_Ω β(Q̂,y) e^{−μ(y)} p(x,y) Q(y) dy − (β(Q̂,x) + κ(x)) Q(x) = 0,
  Q̂ = ∫_Ω Q(x) ζ(x) dx.

Equivalently, one seeks a positive scalar Q̂ such that the linear operator L_{Q̂} has 0 as an eigenvalue with a corresponding nonnegative eigenfunction Q(x), normalized by ∫_Ω Q(x) ζ(x) dx = Q̂.

Questions, in the general setting where β genuinely depends on x and the kernel p(x,y) genuinely depends on the mother state y:

(i) Determine sufficient conditions on β, κ, μ, ζ, p ensuring the existence of a positive Q̂ admitting a nonnegative eigenfunction Q(x) of L_{Q̂}.
(ii) Determine sufficient conditions guaranteeing uniqueness of such a steady state.
(iii) Determine sufficient conditions under which a steady state is (locally or globally) asymptotically stable for the time-dependent evolution.

(The special case in which p(x,y) = p(x) is independent of the mother state y has been treated previously; the question concerns the general mother-state-dependent case.)
status_search_result: Available literature on the heterogeneous stem-cell regeneration framework treats the homogeneous G0 case and the special case p(x,y)=p(x) (mother-independent inheritance), where existence, uniqueness and stability of positive steady states have been established. For the general mother-state-dependent kernel p(x,y) with x-dependent proliferation rate β, no rigorous existence/uniqueness/stability theorem appears in the located sources; subsequent works rely on stochastic simulations rather than analytical proofs, and surveys explicitly list this as remaining open.

paper_title: Evolutionary Dynamics of Cancer: From Epigenetic Regulation to Cell Population Dynamics—Mathematical Model Framework, Applications, and Open Problems
context_brief: Inverse estimation of transition and rate functions from cancer data
original_question: In the heterogeneous cancer-development model, x denotes a cellular epigenetic state, Q(t) or tumor volume gives total population size, f(t,x) gives the fraction of cells in state x, β, κ, μ, and ζ are the proliferation, differentiation/death/senescence, apoptosis, and cytokine-secretion rate functions, and p(x,y) is the probability that a daughter cell has state x given a mother cell with state y. Because p(x,y) is usually unknown and cannot be measured directly, how can experimental data such as imaging, liquid biopsies, biomarker measurements, single-cell sequencing, tissue, blood, and molecular data be used to infer p(x,y) and the rate functions β, κ, μ, and ζ well enough to build personalized predictive models and support optimal clinical decisions for cancer development?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a heterogeneous cell population model in which each cell is characterized by an epigenetic state x belonging to a state space Ω ⊂ ℝ^d. Let Q(t) > 0 denote the total population size (e.g., tumor volume) at time t, and let f(t,x) ≥ 0 denote the fraction of cells in state x at time t, so that ∫_Ω f(t,x) dx = 1. The dynamics are governed by four nonnegative rate functions on Ω:
  • β(x): proliferation rate,
  • κ(x): differentiation/death/senescence (exit) rate,
  • μ(x): apoptosis rate,
  • ζ(x): cytokine-secretion rate,
and by a transition kernel p(x, y) ≥ 0, where p(x, y) is the conditional probability density that a daughter cell has state x given that the mother cell had state y, satisfying ∫_Ω p(x,y) dx = 1 for every y ∈ Ω.

The pair (Q(t), f(t,x)) evolves according to a structured population equation in which new cells of state x are produced at rate ∫_Ω β(y) p(x,y) f(t,y) dy · Q(t), and cells of state x are removed at rate (κ(x) + μ(x)) f(t,x) Q(t), with cytokine production proportional to ∫_Ω ζ(x) f(t,x) dx · Q(t).

Assume one is given (possibly noisy, partial, multimodal) longitudinal observations of the population: for example, total volume measurements Q(t_i), empirical state distributions sampled from f(t_i, ·) via single-cell sequencing, biomarker concentrations, imaging-derived spatial information, and liquid-biopsy data, collected at finitely many times t_1 < t_2 < ⋯ < t_N.

Problem. Develop a mathematically rigorous inverse-problem framework that, from such observational data, identifies (or estimates with quantified uncertainty) the rate functions β(x), κ(x), μ(x), ζ(x) and the transition kernel p(x, y). Specifically:
  (a) Determine conditions on the observation operators and data under which the parameters (β, κ, μ, ζ, p) are uniquely identifiable from the observed data.
  (b) Construct a stable reconstruction procedure (e.g., regularized variational, Bayesian, or learning-based) that recovers (β, κ, μ, ζ, p) and provide convergence and stability estimates as data resolution increases.
  (c) Establish error bounds on predictions of (Q(t), f(t,x)) for t beyond the observation window, sufficient to support personalized predictive modeling and optimal treatment-decision problems.
category_tag: inverse problems in cell population dynamics
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open challenge in mathematical oncology: identifying the transition kernel p(x,y) and the rate functions in heterogeneous cell-population models from multimodal clinical/experimental data. While related inverse problems for structured population equations (e.g., size-structured or age-structured models) have partial results, no general framework solving identification of p(x,y) together with all rate functions from realistic cancer data is established. The problem remains open.

paper_title: A Survey on LoRa Networking: Research Problems, Current Solutions and Open Issues
context_brief: Optimal multi-gateway placement for LoRa deployments
original_question: For LoRa networks, where battery-powered Internet-of-Things end-devices collect information and send it to gateways that relay messages to network and application servers, how can one design a generic method for choosing the number and physical placement of multiple gateways for each category of application and each set of hardware constraints, so that scalability, interference reduction, coverage, energy use, and overall network performance are improved?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a LoRa (Long Range) wireless network architecture consisting of: (i) battery-powered end-devices that periodically transmit short uplink packets, (ii) a set of gateways that receive these packets and forward them to (iii) a network server / application server backbone. Each gateway has a finite reception capacity, a propagation-dependent coverage region (parameterized by spreading factor, transmit power, bandwidth, and channel model), and known hardware constraints (e.g., number of demodulator chains, antenna gain, deployment cost). Each end-device is characterized by its location, traffic pattern (arrival rate, payload size), required quality-of-service (delivery ratio, latency, lifetime), and energy budget.

Given a deployment region with a spatial distribution of end-devices and an application category C (e.g., smart agriculture, smart city, industrial monitoring, asset tracking) specifying the QoS targets and hardware constraint set H_C, design a generic algorithmic method that, taking (C, H_C, the end-device distribution, and the propagation environment) as input, outputs:

  (a) the number N of gateways to deploy, and
  (b) the physical placement {x_1, ..., x_N} of these gateways within the region,

such that the resulting deployment simultaneously:
  1. maximizes scalability (number of supported end-devices),
  2. minimizes inter-device and inter-gateway interference / collision rate,
  3. maximizes coverage of the end-device population,
  4. minimizes end-device energy consumption (extending battery lifetime),
  5. optimizes overall network performance metrics such as packet delivery ratio and throughput.

The required method must be generic in the sense that the same procedure, instantiated with the parameters of any application category C and hardware-constraint set H_C, yields a Pareto-optimal (or provably near-optimal) (N, {x_i}) configuration. Formulate such a method and establish its optimality guarantees.
status_search_result: Multiple recent works address specific instances of LoRa multi-gateway placement using bio-inspired/evolutionary algorithms (EPSO), clustering-based models (DPLACE using Gap-statistics), ray-tracing channel models, and PDR/CAPEX-OPEX multi-objective optimization. These provide application-specific or scenario-specific solutions (e.g., smart campus in wooded areas, dynamic IoT, smart cities), but a single generic method that uniformly handles all application categories and hardware-constraint sets with provable optimality has not been established. The problem is therefore partially solved.

paper_title: A Survey on LoRa Networking: Research Problems, Current Solutions and Open Issues
context_brief: Dynamic retransmission policies for constrained LoRa hardware
original_question: How can LoRa networks set retransmission timers dynamically, across different deployment scenarios, so that end-devices do not retransmit messages that were already received correctly but whose acknowledgments were delayed or corrupted? A satisfactory policy should account for experimentally identified retransmission triggers, work on constrained LoRa hardware, and remain modular rather than depending necessarily on computationally expensive combinations of retransmission, channel coding, and compression.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a low-power wide-area network in which end-devices transmit uplink messages to a gateway over a lossy wireless channel and expect downlink acknowledgments (ACKs) within a retransmission timer T. If an ACK is not received before T expires, the device retransmits the message; this wastes energy and channel time when the original message was in fact received correctly but its ACK was delayed beyond T or corrupted in transit. Each end-device has tight constraints on memory, computation, and energy, and the channel exhibits highly variable delay distributions across different deployment scenarios (e.g., urban, rural, indoor, mobile).

Design a dynamic retransmission-timer policy T = T(state) — where 'state' may include locally observable quantities such as past ACK round-trip times, recent loss/duplicate-ACK events, spreading factor, duty-cycle constraints, and coarse load indicators — with the following requirements:

1. Trigger awareness: the policy must explicitly mitigate retransmissions whose triggering cause is a delayed or corrupted ACK rather than a lost uplink message, using empirically identifiable retransmission triggers.
2. Hardware feasibility: the policy must be implementable on resource-constrained end-device hardware (limited RAM, no floating-point unit, limited energy budget) and produce decisions in real time.
3. Modularity: the policy must function as a stand-alone retransmission mechanism, without requiring joint operation with channel coding or payload compression.
4. Cross-scenario robustness: the policy must achieve, across heterogeneous deployment scenarios, a provable or empirically demonstrated improvement over any static choice of T in terms of expected number of redundant retransmissions per successfully delivered message, while keeping the message delivery probability and end-to-end latency at least as good as a tuned static baseline.

Provide such a policy together with an analysis (or testbed-validated evaluation) establishing properties (1)–(4).
status_search_result: A targeted search did not surface a published dynamic LoRa retransmission-timer policy that simultaneously satisfies all four requirements (empirically grounded trigger awareness, constrained-hardware implementation, modularity independent of joint channel coding/compression, and cross-scenario robustness). Subsequent literature on LoRaWAN ADR and reliability typically addresses adaptive data rate, ACK-less reliability, or joint coding schemes rather than a stand-alone dynamic retransmission timer of the form requested. The problem therefore appears to remain open.

paper_title: A Survey on LoRa Networking: Research Problems, Current Solutions and Open Issues
context_brief: Scenario-specific LoRa security and key management
original_question: What security architecture, key-management mechanisms, and per-application security requirements are needed to secure LoRa networks against remaining attacks such as node impersonation, eavesdropping, black-hole attacks, wormhole attacks, jamming, replay attacks, beacon-synchronization attacks, traffic analysis, man-in-the-middle attacks, and compromised keys? In deployment scenarios where the application service provider and the network service provider are different organizations, how should the Application Session Key and Network Session Key be generated, updated, separated, and kept confidential from the inappropriate party?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a LoRaWAN-style low-power wide-area network consisting of: (i) a set of end devices D, (ii) one or more gateways, (iii) a Network Server (NS) operated by a network service provider, and (iv) an Application Server (AS) operated by an application service provider, where NS and AS may belong to distinct administrative organizations. Each end device d ∈ D shares two symmetric session keys: a Network Session Key NwkSKey_d (used for MAC-layer integrity/authentication between d and NS) and an Application Session Key AppSKey_d (used for end-to-end payload confidentiality between d and AS). In current deployments these keys are derived once (e.g., from a root key during a Join procedure) and are never refreshed, and both NS and AS are structurally able to compute, or have access to, both keys.

Design a security architecture and key-management protocol for such a network that simultaneously satisfies all of the following requirements:

1. Key separation and confidentiality across organizations: AppSKey_d must remain unknown to the NS, and NwkSKey_d must remain unknown to the AS, even though both servers participate in delivering each uplink/downlink frame.
2. Key generation and periodic key update: provide explicit mechanisms by which NwkSKey_d and AppSKey_d (and any underlying root keys) are generated at session establishment and rotated during the lifetime of a device, including rekeying triggers and synchronization between d, NS, and AS.
3. Optional trusted third-party authorization: specify how a trusted Key Management Server, distinct from NS and AS, can mediate join, key derivation, and key update so that neither NS nor AS learns the other's session key.
4. Resistance to the following attack classes, each of which must be formally characterized by an adversary model and against which the protocol must be proven (or argued) secure:
   (a) node impersonation, (b) passive eavesdropping, (c) black-hole attacks, (d) wormhole attacks, (e) jamming, (f) replay attacks, (g) beacon-synchronization attacks, (h) traffic analysis, (i) man-in-the-middle attacks, and (j) compromise of one or more session keys (forward and backward secrecy under key compromise).
5. Per-application differentiation: provide a methodology for tailoring the above mechanisms to the heterogeneous security requirements of distinct LoRa application classes (e.g., metering, healthcare, industrial control, smart agriculture), including how requirements such as confidentiality, integrity, availability, and privacy are quantified and mapped to concrete protocol parameters.

Produce such an architecture together with a security proof (or rigorous justification) of the claimed properties under standard cryptographic assumptions, and analyze its overhead in terms of the constrained energy, bandwidth, and duty-cycle budget characteristic of LoRa end devices.
status_search_result: Recent literature (2020–2025) on LoRaWAN security continues to propose partial solutions—e.g., third-party key management schemes, blockchain-based join procedures, and rekeying protocols—but no single architecture has been established that simultaneously addresses key separation between distinct network and application providers, periodic key update, and the full catalogue of attacks listed (jamming, wormhole, beacon-sync, traffic analysis, key compromise, etc.). Surveys consistently flag these as remaining open issues.

paper_title: A Survey on LoRa Networking: Research Problems, Current Solutions and Open Issues
original_question: How can interference-cancellation techniques for LoRa recover data from collided signals at the scale required by dense LoRa deployments with thousands of end-devices connected to a single gateway, when existing channel coding cannot guarantee recovery for collisions and an existing distributed-coding/backscatter approach decodes 256 concurrent transmissions, which is still below the scale needed for some deployments?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a LoRa (Long Range, Chirp Spread Spectrum based) wireless network in which a single gateway must receive uplink transmissions from a very large population of end-devices (on the order of thousands) that may transmit simultaneously on the same frequency band, producing colliding signals at the gateway. Assume the standard LoRa physical layer: each end-device modulates data using up-chirp symbols parameterized by a spreading factor SF (so each symbol carries SF bits and lasts 2^SF / BW seconds for bandwidth BW), and the gateway demodulates by dechirping followed by an FFT. Channel coding (e.g., Hamming codes used in LoRaWAN) cannot in general guarantee recovery of payload bits from collided symbols, and known distributed-coding / backscatter-style schemes based on chirp spread spectrum can demonstrably resolve at most on the order of 256 concurrent transmissions in a single FFT operation.

Design and analyze an interference-cancellation scheme for the LoRa physical layer that, given the superposition signal received at one gateway from N end-devices transmitting concurrently (with possibly different starting times, carrier frequency offsets, and received powers, and possibly with some signals below the noise floor), recovers each device's payload with high probability for N scaling to the thousands. Specifically, exhibit a decoding algorithm together with rigorous performance guarantees (in terms of bit/packet error rate as a function of N, SF, SNR distribution, and timing/frequency offset distribution) that strictly improves the achievable concurrency beyond the 256-user regime, or prove an information-theoretic upper bound showing that no such scheme can scale to thousands of concurrent LoRa transmissions on a single gateway under realistic channel conditions.
status_search_result: Subsequent work has substantially advanced LoRa concurrent decoding beyond the 256-transmission benchmark of NetScatter. Concurrent Interference Cancellation (CIC, SIGCOMM 2021) reportedly increases capacity up to 10x over standard LoRa and 4x over prior art; PCube (ACM TOSN 2022) uses multi-antenna reception diversity to scale concurrent transmissions; and more recent systems (e.g., Canas, and large-scale parallel decoding work in IEEE TMC 2024) push concurrency further by orthogonalizing many logical channels. However, no scheme has been proven to provably and reliably decode thousands of simultaneous LoRa transmissions at a single gateway under general conditions, so the underlying problem of fully scalable LoRa interference cancellation remains only partially solved.

paper_title: A Survey on LoRa Networking: Research Problems, Current Solutions and Open Issues
original_question: How should LoRa networks dynamically choose each end-device’s communication parameters, including spreading factor, transmission power, bandwidth, channel allocation, data rate, and frame repetition rate, so that scalability, packet reception, energy consumption, and reliability improve across indoor, outdoor, high-noise, temperature-varying, and other deployment environments? A complete answer should account for environmental factors that existing dynamic-parameter methods omit, such as ambient temperature reducing signal strength, and should avoid assuming that simply increasing spreading factor always improves communication performance.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a LoRa (Long Range) wireless network consisting of a set of end-devices E = {e_1, ..., e_N} communicating with one or more gateways. Each end-device e_i must, at every transmission instant t, choose a vector of communication parameters

  p_i(t) = (SF_i, TP_i, BW_i, CH_i, DR_i, FR_i),

where SF_i ∈ {7,8,9,10,11,12} is the spreading factor, TP_i ∈ [TP_min, TP_max] is the transmission power, BW_i ∈ {125, 250, 500} kHz is the bandwidth, CH_i is the channel index from a finite set of available channels, DR_i is the data rate, and FR_i ∈ ℕ is the frame repetition rate.

The deployment environment is described by an environmental state vector ε(t) which may include ambient temperature T(t), indoor/outdoor classification, ambient RF noise level, multipath/shadowing, and node mobility. The received signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio at the gateway and the corresponding packet reception probability depend on p_i(t), ε(t), and the joint choices {p_j(t)}_{j ≠ i} of other devices via standard LoRa link and capture models, with the additional realistic constraint that increasing T(t) decreases received signal strength, and that increasing SF does not monotonically improve link quality once interference and time-on-air are taken into account.

Define network-level objectives:
 (S) scalability: maximum number of end-devices supportable while keeping packet delivery ratio above a threshold;
 (P) packet reception ratio averaged over devices and time;
 (Q) average energy consumption per successfully delivered packet;
 (R) reliability, measured as the probability that each device achieves its target delivery ratio over a window.

Problem. Design a (possibly distributed) policy π: (history of local observations and feedback, ε(t)) → p_i(t), per end-device, such that for every environment trajectory ε(·) drawn from a class encompassing indoor, outdoor, high-noise, and temperature-varying conditions, the policy simultaneously improves S, P, Q, and R relative to any static or environment-agnostic parameter assignment, while

 (i) explicitly incorporating environmental covariates (in particular ambient temperature) into the parameter choice,
 (ii) not relying on the assumption that larger SF always yields better communication performance, and
 (iii) producing a personalized parameter vector p_i for each device rather than a network-wide uniform setting.

Characterize the existence, structure, and optimality guarantees of such a policy, and quantify the achievable trade-off region among (S, P, Q, R) as a function of the environmental class.
status_search_result: Recent literature (ADR variants, reinforcement-learning-based parameter assignment, and environment-aware schemes published through 2024–2025) continues to propose partial solutions for subsets of the parameters (mainly SF and TP) and partial environmental factors, but no scheme jointly optimizes SF, TP, BW, channel, data rate, and frame repetition while incorporating environmental effects such as ambient temperature and avoiding the higher-SF-is-better assumption. The general problem remains open.

paper_title: Kinetic plasma turbulence: recent insights and open questions from 3D3V simulations
original_question: How does free energy cascade through phase space in kinetic plasma turbulence when multiple collisionless processes are active at ion and electron scales? A satisfactory answer must explain how turbulent energy is transferred across both spatial and velocity-space structure in weakly collisional magnetized plasmas.
status_search_result: The phase-space free-energy cascade in kinetic plasma turbulence remains an active area of research. While significant progress has been made—including the entropy/phase-space cascade theory of Schekochihin et al., the "fluidization" mechanism by which nonlinear advection can suppress linear phase mixing (Schekochihin–Parker–Highcock 2016), and recent work on phase-space entropy cascade and irreversibility of stochastic heating (2024)—a unified quantitative theory accounting for the simultaneous competition of multiple collisionless channels at ion and electron scales has not been established. Recent literature continues to describe velocity-space cascade studies as being in their infancy and explicitly identifies this as an open problem.

paper_title: Kinetic plasma turbulence: recent insights and open questions from 3D3V simulations
original_question: Are sub-ion-scale field polarizations in kinetic plasma turbulence genuinely kinetic-Alfven-wave-like, or do the observed spectral ratios instead require a mixture of KAW-like fluctuations, other wave-like modes such as whistler, ion-cyclotron, or ion Bernstein fluctuations, and nonlinear effects that make the turbulence deviate from asymptotic linear KAW predictions? The question is specifically motivated by spectral ratios that are broadly consistent with KAW expectations but do not exactly match the linear-theory values.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a magnetized, weakly collisional plasma exhibiting a turbulent cascade that extends below the ion gyroradius and ion inertial scales (the "sub-ion" range). At these scales, linear Vlasov–Maxwell theory admits several wave branches, including:

(i) kinetic Alfvén waves (KAW), characterized by predicted ratios among electric, magnetic, density, and velocity fluctuations,
(ii) whistler waves,
(iii) ion-cyclotron waves, and
(iv) ion Bernstein waves.

For each linear branch one can compute predicted "spectral ratios" — e.g. the ratio of magnetic compressibility |δB_∥|²/|δB|², the density-magnetic ratio (n_e/n_0)²/(δB_∥/B_0)², and the Alfvén ratio |δu|²/|δB|² in appropriate units — as functions of the perpendicular wavenumber k_⊥ρ_i.

Suppose that in fully kinetic 3D-3V simulations (and in spacecraft observations) of sub-ion-range turbulence the measured spectral ratios are broadly close to the linear KAW predictions but do not match them exactly.

Question. Determine whether the sub-ion-scale electromagnetic and density polarizations of the turbulent fluctuations are genuinely dominated by KAW-like modes, or whether the observed deviations from linear KAW spectral ratios are produced by:
(a) an admixture of other linear wave branches (whistler, ion-cyclotron, and/or ion-Bernstein fluctuations) coexisting with KAWs in the cascade, and/or
(b) intrinsically nonlinear dynamics that drive the polarizations away from any asymptotic linear-mode prediction.

Quantify the relative contributions of (a) and (b) and identify a diagnostic, computable from the field correlation tensor of the turbulence, that unambiguously distinguishes a single-mode KAW cascade from a multi-mode and/or strongly nonlinear sub-ion cascade producing the same approximate spectral ratios.
status_search_result: Recent literature (2020–2024) continues to debate the nature of sub-ion-scale fluctuations. A 2020 Phys. Rev. Research paper argues for coexistence of KAW and ion Bernstein modes in solar-wind sub-ion compressive turbulence, while a 2024 Frontiers article presents simulations showing that even cascades initialized with whistlers evolve toward KAW-like polarizations, but with non-negligible non-KAW power. Spacecraft (MMS) measurements of Alfvén ratios likewise show approximate but imperfect agreement with linear KAW predictions. No consensus has been reached on disentangling the relative contributions of mode mixing versus nonlinear effects, so the question remains open.

paper_title: Kinetic plasma turbulence: recent insights and open questions from 3D3V simulations
original_question: Which dissipation mechanisms act on turbulent fluctuations under different plasma conditions in kinetic-range turbulence, and how do those mechanisms determine the resulting partition of energy among the different plasma species? A complete answer must connect the plasma conditions, the operative collisionless dissipation pathway, and the species-by-species outcome of turbulent heating.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a weakly collisional, magnetized plasma composed of multiple charged species (e.g., protons, electrons, and possibly heavier ions) immersed in a mean magnetic field, and driven into a statistically steady state of broadband electromagnetic turbulence whose cascade extends from magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) scales down through and below the ion kinetic scales (the ion Larmor radius ρ_i and the ion inertial length d_i). At kinetic scales, candidate collisionless dissipation channels for the turbulent fluctuations include: (i) ion and electron Landau damping, (ii) ion and electron transit-time (Barnes) damping, (iii) ion cyclotron damping, (iv) ion stochastic heating by low-frequency, large-amplitude perpendicular electric-field fluctuations, (v) collisionless magnetic reconnection in current sheets formed by the cascade, and (vi) kinetic "viscous" (pressure–strain) heating quantified via the scale-filtered Vlasov–Maxwell pressure–strain interaction Π_s = −(P_s · ∇) · u_s. The relevant plasma parameters include the ion plasma beta β_i = 8πn_i T_i / B^2, the electron-to-ion temperature ratio T_e/T_i, the fluctuation amplitude δB/B_0 at the ion gyroscale, and the propagation-angle/anisotropy of the cascade.

Problem. Determine, as a function of the plasma parameters (β_i, T_e/T_i, δB/B_0, anisotropy, and species composition), which of the above collisionless dissipation mechanisms dominate the removal of energy from turbulent fluctuations in the kinetic range, and derive the resulting partition of dissipated turbulent energy among the constituent plasma species (and between their parallel and perpendicular degrees of freedom). The answer must specify, for each region of parameter space, (a) the operative dissipation pathway(s), (b) the fractional heating rates Q_s / Σ_s' Q_s' for each species s, and (c) the consistency of (a)–(b) with the scale-by-scale energy balance dictated by the Vlasov–Maxwell equations.
status_search_result: The problem of identifying which collisionless dissipation mechanisms dominate in different plasma-parameter regimes and the resulting ion/electron (and parallel/perpendicular) energy partition remains an active open research question. Recent works (2024–2025), including studies on the fundamental parameters of astrophysical plasma turbulence, scale-filtered pressure–strain analyses, and kinetic-scale energy budgets at varying T_e/T_i, continue to investigate these issues without providing a complete, predictive parameter-space mapping.

paper_title: Kinetic plasma turbulence: recent insights and open questions from 3D3V simulations
original_question: What is the full three-dimensional anisotropic structure of energy transfer across scales in kinetic plasma turbulence? This asks for a direct characterization of how the cascade is organized in three dimensions relative to the magnetic field and local turbulent structure.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a magnetized collisionless plasma described by the Vlasov–Maxwell system in three spatial and three velocity dimensions, in a statistically homogeneous turbulent state with a mean magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_0$. In such a system energy injected at large (fluid) scales is transferred through a nonlinear cascade down to kinetic scales (ion and electron gyroradii and inertial lengths), where it is ultimately converted into particle heat.

Define the scale-dependent energy transfer rate using a generalized third-order (Yaglom-type / Kolmogorov-Hill) structure-function flux $\Pi(\boldsymbol{\ell})$, expressed as a function of the three-dimensional separation vector $\boldsymbol{\ell}$. Decompose $\boldsymbol{\ell}$ into:
- a component $\ell_\parallel$ parallel to the local mean magnetic field,
- a component $\ell_{\perp,1}$ perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}_0$ but aligned with the local fluctuation direction (e.g., the local perpendicular magnetic-field perturbation),
- a component $\ell_{\perp,2}$ perpendicular to both.

Problem. Determine the full three-dimensional anisotropic structure of the energy transfer rate $\Pi(\ell_\parallel,\ell_{\perp,1},\ell_{\perp,2})$ across the inertial, ion-kinetic, and sub-ion-kinetic ranges of a turbulent collisionless plasma. Specifically, characterize:
1. how the magnitude and direction of energy flux depend on the orientation of $\boldsymbol{\ell}$ with respect to both the local mean magnetic field and the local turbulent structure,
2. the scaling of $\Pi$ along each of the three axes as scales cross the ion gyroradius,
3. whether the cascade exhibits a single dominant transfer direction (e.g., predominantly perpendicular) or a non-trivial three-dimensional flux pattern, and
4. the relative role of the three symmetry axes in setting spectral slopes and dissipation channels.
status_search_result: The full three-dimensional anisotropic structure of the energy transfer in kinetic plasma turbulence remains an active research question. Recent work (e.g., a 2023 Phys. Rev. Lett. paper using MMS multipoint measurements to evaluate a 3D Yaglom flux, and 2024 A&A studies of ion-scale anisotropy) provides partial empirical characterizations but a complete theoretical/observational determination across inertial and kinetic ranges has not been achieved.

paper_title: Kinetic plasma turbulence: recent insights and open questions from 3D3V simulations
original_question: Over what range of temporal and spatial scales is Taylor's hypothesis valid for kinetic plasma turbulence? The open issue is whether the usual conversion between temporal spacecraft measurements and spatial structure remains reliable across the broad range of scales relevant to kinetic turbulence.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a magnetized, weakly collisional plasma exhibiting kinetic turbulence (e.g., a stellar/solar wind) advected past a stationary probe with bulk flow velocity $\mathbf{U}_0$. Taylor's hypothesis is the assumption that temporal fluctuations $\delta f(t)$ measured by the stationary probe at a fixed spatial point are dominated by the rigid advection of spatial structures past the probe, so that an observed angular frequency $\omega_{\rm sc}$ is related to a wavevector $\mathbf{k}$ in the plasma frame by $\omega_{\rm sc} = \mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{U}_0$, allowing the conversion of time series into spatial spectra via $k = \omega_{\rm sc}/U_0$.

Let $L$ denote the energy-containing (outer) scale of the turbulence, $\rho_i$ the ion gyroradius, $d_i = c/\omega_{pi}$ the ion inertial length, $\rho_e$ the electron gyroradius, and let $V_A$ be the Alfvén speed and $\delta V$ the rms turbulent velocity fluctuation amplitude at scale $\ell$. In the magnetohydrodynamic inertial range ($\ell \gg \rho_i$), the standard sufficient condition $\delta V \ll U_0$ (and, when relevant, $V_A \ll U_0$, i.e., super-Alfvénic flow) is known to render Taylor's hypothesis reliable. At sub-ion (kinetic) scales ($\ell \lesssim \rho_i$), however, dispersive wave modes (e.g., kinetic Alfvén waves, whistlers) can have intrinsic frequencies $\omega(\mathbf{k})$ comparable to or exceeding $\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{U}_0$, potentially violating the hypothesis.

Determine the precise range of temporal frequencies $\omega_{\rm sc}$ and spatial scales $\ell$ (spanning from $L$ down through $\rho_i$, $d_i$, and into the sub-electron scales $\ell \lesssim \rho_e$) over which Taylor's hypothesis $\omega_{\rm sc} = \mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{U}_0$ remains a quantitatively reliable conversion between single-point temporal measurements and spatial structure for fully developed three-dimensional kinetic plasma turbulence. Equivalently, characterize, in terms of the dimensionless parameters $\delta V/U_0$, $V_A/U_0$, $k\rho_i$, $k d_i$, $k\rho_e$, and the angle between $\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{U}_0$, the regime in which the hypothesis holds and the regime in which it fails.
status_search_result: Several studies have analyzed the validity of Taylor's hypothesis at kinetic scales: Howes et al. (2014, arXiv:1405.5460) showed it holds for kinetic Alfvén waves but can fail for whistler-supported dissipation ranges; subsequent works (Chhiber et al. 2019; Bourouaine & Perez 2018; Perez et al. 2021 for Parker Solar Probe; Zank et al. 2022 for the heliosheath) refined the conditions in terms of $\delta V/(V_A+U_0)$, dispersion, and obliquity. A complete, scale-resolved characterization spanning the full MHD-to-sub-electron range remains an active research problem with no single closed-form answer, so the question is best classified as partially solved.

paper_title: Using GANs for Sharing Networked Time Series Data: Challenges, Initial Promise, and Open Questions
original_question: When releasing synthetic networked time-series data generated by GANs, what privacy definition should be used for a given data-sharing use case, given that different release scenarios may require different protection goals and threat models?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the task of releasing synthetic networked time-series data, i.e., multi-dimensional time series records together with associated categorical/continuous metadata describing each entity (such as users, devices, or flows in a network), produced by a generative model (e.g., a generative adversarial network) trained on a sensitive dataset D. A "privacy definition" is a formal mathematical specification consisting of: (i) a threat model (the adversary's prior knowledge, auxiliary information, and computational power), (ii) a secret to be protected (e.g., membership of a record, the value of a specific attribute, presence of a temporal pattern, identity linkage across records), and (iii) a quantitative guarantee (e.g., an (ε, δ)-bound on a divergence between output distributions on neighboring datasets, a bound on an adversary's posterior advantage, or a bound on reconstruction error).

Formulate a principled framework that, given a data-sharing use case characterized by:
  - the structure of the data (per-entity time series plus metadata),
  - the intended downstream analytical tasks,
  - the assumed adversarial capabilities and auxiliary information, and
  - the utility requirements,
selects or constructs a privacy definition that is (a) semantically meaningful for the stated threat model, (b) composable under repeated releases, (c) achievable simultaneously with acceptable utility on the stated tasks, and (d) interpretable to data custodians.

Specifically: characterize, for the class of networked time-series release problems above, which privacy definitions (e.g., record-level differential privacy, user-/group-level differential privacy, Pufferfish privacy with appropriate secret/discriminative-pair structure, attribute privacy, membership-inference resistance, or task-specific indistinguishability notions) are appropriate for which use cases, and provide criteria under which one definition strictly dominates another for a given use case.
status_search_result: The question is explicitly framed as an open meta-question about choosing the right privacy definition per use case. The literature on differential privacy, Pufferfish privacy, and synthetic data continues to debate appropriate privacy notions for time-series and relational data, with no consensus framework. No source establishes a definitive resolution, so the problem remains open.

paper_title: Using GANs for Sharing Networked Time Series Data: Challenges, Initial Promise, and Open Questions
original_question: Do privacy-preserving GAN training methods achieve a privacy-fidelity tradeoff that is practical for networking datasets, where the synthetic output must preserve realistic temporal structure and cross-feature relationships while still offering meaningful privacy guarantees?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{D} = \{x^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ be a dataset of networked time series, where each $x^{(i)} = (m^{(i)}, s^{(i)}_1, s^{(i)}_2, \ldots, s^{(i)}_T)$ consists of a vector $m^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_m}$ of static metadata features and a sequence $s^{(i)}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_s}$, $t=1,\ldots,T$, of measurements. Such datasets typically exhibit (i) long-range temporal correlations within each series, (ii) heterogeneous and high-dimensional joint distributions over metadata, and (iii) strong cross-feature dependencies between metadata and the temporal signal.

A generative model $G_\theta$ trained on $\mathcal{D}$ produces synthetic samples $\tilde{x} \sim G_\theta$. Define:

1. A fidelity functional $F(G_\theta, \mathcal{D}) \in \mathbb{R}$ that measures how well synthetic samples reproduce marginal distributions of metadata, autocorrelation and spectral structure of the time series, and joint metadata–measurement statistics (for example, via a weighted sum of Wasserstein or Jensen–Shannon distances between empirical distributions of these quantities under $\mathcal{D}$ and under $G_\theta$).

2. A privacy guarantee parameterized, e.g., by $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy: the training procedure $\mathcal{A}: \mathcal{D} \mapsto \theta$ satisfies, for every pair of datasets $\mathcal{D}, \mathcal{D}'$ differing in one record and every measurable set $S$,
$$\Pr[\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}') \in S] + \delta.$$

The question is the following. Fix thresholds $\varepsilon^* > 0$, $\delta^* \in (0,1)$ regarded as "meaningful" privacy levels (e.g., $\varepsilon^* \le 10$, $\delta^* \le 1/N$), and a fidelity threshold $F^*$ regarded as "practical" for downstream networking tasks (such as preserving rank orderings of flow durations, packet-count autocorrelations, and conditional metadata–measurement statistics within a prescribed tolerance).

Does there exist a training algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ producing a generator $G_\theta$ for networked time-series data such that simultaneously
$$\mathcal{A} \text{ is } (\varepsilon, \delta)\text{-differentially private with } \varepsilon \le \varepsilon^*, \ \delta \le \delta^*, \quad \text{and} \quad F(G_\theta, \mathcal{D}) \le F^*?$$

Equivalently, characterize the achievable Pareto frontier of $(\varepsilon, F)$ pairs for differentially private GAN-style training on the class of networked time-series distributions described above, and determine whether this frontier admits points that are practical for typical networking datasets.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open research question concerning whether existing differentially private GAN training methods (e.g., DPGAN, PATE-GAN) can achieve a privacy-fidelity tradeoff suitable for networked time-series data. Subsequent work has explored DP synthetic time series and DP-GANs, but no general affirmative resolution has been established for networking datasets with long-range temporal and cross-feature structure; reported results show substantial fidelity degradation under meaningful DP budgets. The question remains open.

paper_title: Using GANs for Sharing Networked Time Series Data: Challenges, Initial Promise, and Open Questions
original_question: When a synthetic data generator models both per-sample attributes and associated time-series records, how can practitioners realistically tune the attribute distributions of the released synthetic dataset while still preserving the conditional behavior between those attributes and the generated records?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{D} = \{(a_i, x_i)\}_{i=1}^N$ be a dataset where each sample consists of an attribute vector $a_i \in \mathcal{A}$ (e.g., categorical or numerical metadata) and an associated time-series record $x_i \in \mathcal{X} = \mathbb{R}^{T \times d}$. Suppose a generative model has been trained to produce joint synthetic samples $(A, X)$ approximating the joint distribution $P(A, X) = P(A)\,P(X \mid A)$ of real data, where $P(A)$ is the marginal attribute distribution and $P(X \mid A)$ is the conditional distribution of time series given attributes.

A data publisher wishes to release synthetic data whose marginal attribute distribution matches a chosen target distribution $Q(A)$ (which may differ from the empirical $P(A)$, for instance to anonymize, rebalance rare categories, or correct sampling bias), while preserving the learned conditional behavior $P(X \mid A)$ between attributes and records.

Design and analyze a principled procedure that, given:
(i) a generator $G$ producing samples from $P(A, X)$,
(ii) a desired target attribute distribution $Q(A)$,

outputs a synthetic dataset $\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}$ whose attribute marginal converges (in a specified statistical sense, e.g., total variation or Wasserstein distance) to $Q(A)$ and whose conditional law $\widetilde{P}(X \mid A)$ remains close to the original $P(X \mid A)$. Specifically:

1. Formulate sufficient conditions on $G$, on $Q(A)$, and on the relationship between $Q(A)$ and the support of $P(A)$ under which such a procedure is well-defined and statistically consistent.
2. Provide quantitative bounds relating any divergence $D(Q \| P)$ on attributes to the achievable fidelity of the conditional $\widetilde{P}(X \mid A)$ versus $P(X \mid A)$.
3. Characterize fundamental obstructions (e.g., when $Q$ places mass on attribute regions poorly covered by training data) and propose diagnostics that detect when realistic tuning is infeasible.
status_search_result: The problem of realistically tuning attribute marginals in conditional generative models for networked/time-series data while preserving learned conditional structure remains an active research area. Subsequent work on DoppelGANger and conditional tabular/time-series GANs (e.g., CTGAN, follow-up DoppelGANger studies) discuss attribute conditioning and rebalancing, but a general principled methodology with consistency guarantees for arbitrary target attribute distributions has not been established, so the question is best characterized as still open.
