paper_title: Toward epidemic thresholds on temporal networks: a review and open questions
original_question: Network monitoring can mean either monitoring propagation on a fixed network or monitoring a network that itself changes over time. What are the precise connections between these network-surveillance problems, disease transmission, and epidemic thresholds in temporal networks?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a temporal network represented as a time-indexed sequence of graphs G_t = (V, E_t) for t in a discrete or continuous time domain T, where V is a fixed set of n nodes and E_t ⊆ V × V is the set of edges active at time t. On such a structure, consider a stochastic spreading process (e.g., a susceptible–infected–susceptible (SIS) or susceptible–infected–recovered (SIR) model) with per-contact infection rate β and recovery rate μ, where infections may propagate only along edges that are active at the moment of contact. The epidemic threshold is the critical value of β/μ (or analogous control parameter) above which the expected fraction of infected nodes remains bounded away from zero in the large-time and/or large-n limit.

Two distinct network-surveillance problems are defined on this setting:
(i) Surveillance of propagation on a fixed network: given a static graph G = (V, E), select a subset S ⊆ V (sensors) of bounded size that minimizes the expected detection time, or maximizes the probability of detection, of a spreading process initiated at an unknown source.
(ii) Surveillance of a changing network: given the temporal network {G_t}, select (possibly time-varying) sensors S_t ⊆ V to detect either anomalous changes in the network structure itself or propagation processes whose dynamics interact with the changing topology.

Problem. Establish precise mathematical relationships between problems (i) and (ii) and the epidemic threshold of the underlying spreading process on the temporal network. Specifically:
(a) Derive quantitative bounds linking optimal sensor placements (and their detection-time guarantees) in problems (i) and (ii) to spectral or combinatorial quantities that determine the epidemic threshold on {G_t}.
(b) Identify conditions under which solving (i) is equivalent to, reducible to, or strictly easier/harder than solving (ii), in terms of the temporal-network parameters that govern the threshold.
(c) Characterize how the epidemic threshold itself can be inferred or estimated from observations available through optimal surveillance schemes of types (i) and (ii).
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction concerning the connections between network-surveillance problems, disease transmission, and epidemic thresholds on temporal networks. No definitive resolution establishing the precise mathematical connections appears in the literature; subsequent reviews and works on temporal-network epidemics continue to treat these as ongoing research challenges.

paper_title: QCD, from its inception to its stubbornly unsolved problems
original_question: Can quantum chromodynamics derive Bloom-Gilman duality from first principles, where Bloom-Gilman duality is the observation that at low Q^2 a structure function shows prominent nucleon resonances that average to the scaling function measured at some higher Q_0^2 and then slide down its slope as Q^2 increases, rather than only explaining a QCD-improved realization of that behavior?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. In deep inelastic lepton–nucleon scattering, let $F(x,Q^2)$ denote a nucleon structure function depending on the Bjorken variable $x$ and the squared momentum transfer $Q^2$. At large $Q^2 \ge Q_0^2$, $F$ is well described by a smooth scaling curve $F_{\rm scaling}(x,Q^2)$ predicted by perturbative QCD with logarithmic ($Q^2$-dependent) evolution. At low $Q^2$, the same structure function (plotted, for example, versus the Nachtmann variable or as a function of the final hadronic mass $W$) exhibits prominent nucleon resonance peaks.

Bloom–Gilman duality is the empirical statement that:
(i) when averaged over a suitable interval in $W$ (or equivalently in $x$), the low-$Q^2$ resonance structure of $F(x,Q^2)$ reproduces the high-$Q^2$ scaling curve $F_{\rm scaling}(x,Q_0^2)$; and
(ii) as $Q^2$ increases, the locally averaged resonance curve smoothly slides down along the scaling curve, matching its slope, until the resonances dissolve into the scaling regime.

Problem. Starting from the QCD Lagrangian (quarks and gluons with the standard non-Abelian gauge interaction) alone, derive Bloom–Gilman duality from first principles. That is, prove rigorously, without postulating a hadronic spectrum or invoking phenomenological models of bound-state production, that the exact electromagnetic structure function of the nucleon defined by QCD necessarily exhibits the resonance/scaling matching and sliding behavior described in (i)–(ii).
status_search_result: A first-principles QCD derivation of Bloom–Gilman duality remains an open problem. Recent work (e.g., light-front holographic QCD analyses from 2021) frames it as the "mystery of Bloom–Gilman duality" and provides partial/model-based insights, while reviews state the origin lies in confinement physics not yet derived from QCD. Operator product expansion approaches reformulate but do not explain the phenomenon from first principles.

paper_title: QCD, from its inception to its stubbornly unsolved problems
original_question: How can the theoretical uncertainty in deep inelastic scattering be improved beyond the current practice of varying the renormalization and factorization scales within conventional brackets, given that the perturbative expression still contains higher-twist corrections and the source states that it is not clear how to do any better?
self_contained_problem:
In perturbative QCD applied to deep inelastic scattering (DIS), an observable such as a structure function is computed as a truncated expansion in the strong coupling $\alpha_s(\mu_R)$ together with parton distribution functions evolved at a factorization scale $\mu_F$, plus power-suppressed higher-twist corrections of the form $\mathcal{O}(\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}}^2/Q^2)$ that are not captured by the perturbative series. The standard prescription for assigning a "theoretical uncertainty" to a fixed-order prediction is to take the envelope of results obtained as $(\mu_R,\mu_F)$ vary over the conventional brackets
$$\mu_R/2 \le \mu_F \le 2\mu_R, \qquad \mu_F/2 \le \mu_R \le 2\mu_F,$$
about a central choice $\mu_R=\mu_F=Q$. This procedure has no rigorous statistical interpretation, ignores higher-twist contributions, and depends on an arbitrary factor of two.

Problem. Devise a principled, quantitatively reliable method for estimating the theoretical uncertainty of a perturbative DIS prediction that improves upon the standard scale-variation envelope. Specifically, formulate a scheme that
(i) provides an estimator of the uncertainty due to missing higher orders in $\alpha_s$ with a defensible probabilistic or otherwise rigorous interpretation,
(ii) accounts in a controlled way for unknown higher-twist (power-suppressed) corrections to the structure functions, and
(iii) yields uncertainty bands that, in the limit of arbitrarily many computed perturbative orders, converge to the true theoretical error.
Either construct such a method and prove it satisfies (i)–(iii), or demonstrate that no such improvement over the conventional bracket prescription is possible without additional nonperturbative input.
status_search_result: Recent work (NNPDF and collaborators, 2019–2024) has developed a "theory covariance matrix" approach using correlated renormalization/factorization scale variations to estimate missing-higher-order uncertainties (MHOUs) in PDF fits and DIS predictions, providing a more systematic Bayesian-flavored framework than naive bracket variation. However, no fully rigorous method that simultaneously handles higher-twist (power-suppressed) corrections has been established; treatment of nonperturbative power corrections remains process-dependent and incomplete. The problem is therefore partially addressed but not closed.

paper_title: QCD, from its inception to its stubbornly unsolved problems
original_question: Can lattice QCD devise a gauge-invariant way to characterize a confined constituent-quark propagator that peaks at a constituent mass roughly 300 MeV larger than a Lagrangian or chiral-model mass, and can it also determine whether one-gluon-exchange dominance explains mass differences between baryons with the same quark constituency but different spin or quark-spin alignments?
self_contained_problem:
In the framework of lattice quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the theory of an SU(3) gauge field coupled to quark fields with a Lagrangian (current) quark mass m_q, address the following two questions.

(a) Devise a gauge-invariant construction on the lattice of a propagator G(p) for a confined quark inside a hadron such that:
  (i) G(p) is invariant under local SU(3) gauge transformations of the quark and gluon fields;
  (ii) G(p) is well-defined and computable in pure lattice QCD (without recourse to model assumptions);
  (iii) the resulting spectral function or pole-like structure of G(p) exhibits a peak at an effective "constituent" mass M_c that exceeds the Lagrangian mass m_q (or the small chiral-model mass) by approximately 300 MeV for the light quarks (u, d).

(b) Using only first-principles lattice QCD computations, determine whether the mass splittings between baryons composed of the same quark flavor content but with different total spin or different internal quark-spin alignments (for example the N(939)–Δ(1232) splitting, or the Σ–Λ splitting) are dominantly accounted for by a single perturbative one-gluon-exchange interaction between constituent quarks (in the spirit of the De Rújula–Georgi–Glashow chromomagnetic hyperfine interaction proportional to (λ_i·λ_j)(σ_i·σ_j)/(m_i m_j)), as opposed to receiving comparable contributions from other non-perturbative or multi-gluon mechanisms.

Provide either an explicit construction and lattice measurement establishing both (a) and (b), or a proof that no such gauge-invariant constituent-quark propagator with the stated property exists, or that one-gluon-exchange dominance fails for these baryon mass splittings.
status_search_result: No gauge-invariant lattice construction of a constituent-quark propagator with a ~300 MeV mass shift over the Lagrangian mass is established in the literature; standard lattice studies of the quark propagator are performed in fixed gauges (Landau gauge), and the relation to a constituent mass remains model-dependent. Lattice studies of baryon spectroscopy reproduce N–Δ and other hyperfine splittings nonperturbatively, but a clean demonstration that one-gluon exchange alone dominates these splittings has not been given. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: QCD, from its inception to its stubbornly unsolved problems
original_question: Can QCD provide a quantitatively satisfactory first-principles account of hadronization and of the underlying event, rather than relying on phenomenological tuning, machine-learning-assisted tuning, string models, or cluster models, and can it justify factorization in this full realistic setting rather than treating factorization as an ansatz?
self_contained_problem:
Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) is the non-abelian gauge theory with gauge group SU(3) describing the strong interaction of quarks and gluons, with Lagrangian
  L = -(1/4) G^a_{μν} G^{a μν} + Σ_f \bar{ψ}_f (i γ^μ D_μ - m_f) ψ_f,
where D_μ = ∂_μ - i g_s t^a A^a_μ and G^a_{μν} is the non-abelian field strength. In high-energy hadronic collisions, observable cross sections receive contributions from (i) a perturbatively calculable hard partonic scattering, (ii) a perturbative parton shower describing collinear/soft radiation, (iii) hadronization, the non-perturbative transition from colored partons to color-singlet hadrons, and (iv) the underlying event, the additional soft activity associated with spectator partons of the colliding hadrons. In current practice, components (iii) and (iv) are modeled by phenomenological prescriptions such as the Lund string model or cluster hadronization model, with parameters fixed by tuning to data (possibly using machine learning), and the validity of factorization theorems—the statement that the cross section can be written as a convolution of process-independent non-perturbative functions (parton distributions, fragmentation functions) with perturbatively computable hard kernels—is in this full realistic setting effectively assumed as an ansatz beyond the regimes where it has been rigorously proved.

Problem. Provide a first-principles derivation, directly from the QCD Lagrangian above, that:
(a) gives a quantitatively predictive description of hadronization, i.e. computes from QCD alone (without recourse to tuned phenomenological string or cluster models) the probability distributions for a system of colored partons to evolve into a definite final state of hadrons, in agreement with experimental data;
(b) gives a first-principles description of the underlying event in hadron–hadron collisions; and
(c) establishes factorization of inclusive and semi-inclusive hadronic cross sections in this realistic full setting, including the contributions of (a) and (b), as a theorem derived from QCD rather than as an assumed ansatz.
status_search_result: Hadronization, the underlying event, and a fully general proof of factorization remain widely acknowledged open problems in QCD. Factorization theorems have been rigorously proved only for restricted classes of processes (e.g., inclusive DIS, Drell–Yan, certain semi-inclusive observables), while hadronization is still treated via phenomenological string/cluster models tuned to data, including ML-assisted tuning in modern Monte Carlo event generators. No first-principles QCD derivation of hadronization or the underlying event exists as of recent reviews.

original_question: Let M be the centered Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator on R^d, defined by M f(x) = sup_{r>0} (1/m(B(x,r))) ∫_{B(x,r)} |f(y)| dy, where B(x,r) is the open ball of center x and radius r, and let the uncentered maximal operator be defined analogously by taking the supremum over all open balls that contain x. Is the map f -> |∇M f| bounded from the Sobolev space W^{1,1}(R^d) to L^1(R^d)? Equivalently, for every f in W^{1,1}(R^d), is M f weakly differentiable and does there exist a universal constant C = C(d) such that ||∇M f||_{L^1(R^d)} <= C ||∇f||_{L^1(R^d)}? The same question is asked for the uncentered maximal operator.
self_contained_problem:
Let $d\ge 1$ and, for $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, define the centered Hardy–Littlewood maximal function
$$Mf(x)=\sup_{r>0}\frac{1}{m(B(x,r))}\int_{B(x,r)}|f(y)|\,dy,$$
where $B(x,r)$ is the open Euclidean ball of center $x$ and radius $r$ and $m$ denotes $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Define the uncentered Hardy–Littlewood maximal function $\widetilde{M}f(x)$ analogously, taking the supremum of averages $\frac{1}{m(B)}\int_B|f(y)|\,dy$ over all open balls $B\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ that contain $x$. Let $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ denote the Sobolev space of integrable functions whose distributional gradient lies in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^d;\mathbb{R}^d)$.

Prove or disprove: for every $f\in W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, the function $Mf$ is weakly differentiable, and there exists a constant $C=C(d)$, independent of $f$, such that
$$\|\nabla Mf\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)}\le C\,\|\nabla f\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)}.$$
Equivalently, decide whether the sublinear map $f\mapsto |\nabla Mf|$ is bounded from $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ to $L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)$. The same question is posed with $M$ replaced by the uncentered maximal operator $\widetilde{M}$.
category_tag: Endpoint Sobolev regularity of maximal operators
status_search_result: The problem is known in dimension one: Tanaka (and Aldaz–Pérez Lázaro with sharp constant 1) settled the uncentered case, and Kurka established the centered case in $d=1$. Partial results are known in higher dimensions for special classes (e.g., radial functions, block-decreasing functions, Hardy–Sobolev variants), but the full endpoint $W^{1,1}\to L^1$ gradient bound for both the centered and uncentered Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator in $\mathbb{R}^d$, $d\ge 2$, remains open.

original_question: For alpha >= 0, define the one-dimensional non-tangential maximal operator by M^alpha f(x) = sup_{(y,t): |x-y| <= alpha t} (1/(2t)) ∫_{y-t}^{y+t} |f(s)| ds, so that alpha = 0 gives the centered maximal operator and alpha = 1 gives the uncentered maximal operator. For functions f : R -> R of bounded variation, does the sharp inequality Var(M^alpha f) <= Var(f) hold for every 0 <= alpha < 1/3? If not, what is the smallest alpha for which that inequality is valid?
self_contained_problem:
For $\alpha \geq 0$, define the one-dimensional non-tangential Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator acting on locally integrable functions $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ by
$$M^{\alpha} f(x) \;=\; \sup_{(y,t)\in\mathbb{R}\times(0,\infty),\ |x-y|\leq \alpha t}\; \frac{1}{2t}\int_{y-t}^{y+t} |f(s)|\,ds.$$
Note that $M^{0}$ is the centered Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator and $M^{1}$ is the uncentered one. For a function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, let
$$\operatorname{Var}(f) \;=\; \sup\sum_{i=1}^{n} |f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1})|,$$
where the supremum is taken over all finite increasing sequences $x_0<x_1<\dots<x_n$ in $\mathbb{R}$, and call $f$ a function of bounded variation if $\operatorname{Var}(f)<\infty$.

Question: For every function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ of bounded variation, does the inequality
$$\operatorname{Var}(M^{\alpha} f) \;\leq\; \operatorname{Var}(f)$$
hold for all $\alpha$ with $0\leq \alpha < 1/3$? If not, determine the smallest value of $\alpha\geq 0$ for which the inequality holds for every $f$ of bounded variation.
status_search_result: Recent work (e.g., Ramos and follow-ups, including a 2025 preprint on the discrete H–L nontangential operator) establishes the sharp variation bound Var(M^α f) ≤ Var(f) for α ∈ [1/3, ∞), but the regime 0 ≤ α < 1/3 (in particular the centered case α=0) remains unresolved. No source found resolves the question for α < 1/3.

original_question: Let M_S be the spherical maximal operator on R^d, defined by taking at each x the supremum over r > 0 of the average of |f| on the sphere S^{d-1}(x,r). For dimensions d >= 2, is M_S bounded as an operator from W^{1,p}(R^d) to W^{1,p}(R^d) throughout the full endpoint range 1 < p <= d/(d-1)?
self_contained_problem:
For an integer $d\ge 2$, let $S^{d-1}(x,r)=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^d:|z-x|=r\}$ denote the $(d-1)$-dimensional sphere of center $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and radius $r>0$, equipped with its surface measure $\sigma$, and let $\omega_{d-1}$ denote the surface area of the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^d$. The spherical maximal operator $M_S$ is defined for locally integrable $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ by
$$M_S f(x)=\sup_{r>0}\frac{1}{\omega_{d-1} r^{d-1}}\int_{S^{d-1}(x,r)}|f(z)|\,d\sigma(z).$$
For $1<p<\infty$, the Sobolev space $W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ consists of those $f\in L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)$ whose distributional gradient $\nabla f$ also lies in $L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)$, with norm $\|f\|_{W^{1,p}}=\|f\|_{L^p}+\|\nabla f\|_{L^p}$.

Question: For every $d\ge 2$ and every $p$ with $1<p\le d/(d-1)$, is $M_S$ a bounded operator from $W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ to $W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^d)$?
category_tag: Spherical maximal operators on Sobolev spaces
status_search_result: Available sources indicate that boundedness of the spherical maximal operator on $\dot W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ has been established for $d/(d-1)<p<\infty$ (with appropriate dimensional restrictions), and the endpoint $p=d/(d-1)$ together with the range $1<p<d/(d-1)$ is reported as an open problem. Recent work on related (e.g., strong) spherical maximal operators continues but does not appear to resolve this endpoint Sobolev question.

original_question: For 0 <= beta < d, define the centered Hardy-Littlewood fractional maximal operator by M_beta f(x) = sup_{r>0} m(B(x,r))^{beta/d - 1} ∫_{B(x,r)} |f(y)| dy, and define the uncentered fractional maximal operator analogously by taking the supremum over balls that contain x. When 0 <= beta < 1 and q = d/(d-beta), is the map f -> |∇M_beta f| bounded from W^{1,1}(R^d) to L^q(R^d)? The same question is asked for the uncentered fractional maximal operator.
self_contained_problem:
Let $d\ge 1$ be an integer. For a locally integrable function $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ and $0\le\beta<d$, define the centered Hardy–Littlewood fractional maximal function by
$$M_\beta f(x)=\sup_{r>0}\frac{1}{m(B(x,r))^{1-\beta/d}}\int_{B(x,r)}|f(y)|\,dy,$$
where $m$ denotes Lebesgue measure and $B(x,r)$ is the open Euclidean ball of radius $r$ centered at $x$. Define the uncentered fractional maximal function $\widetilde{M}_\beta f(x)$ analogously, with the supremum taken over all open balls $B$ that contain $x$ (not necessarily centered at $x$):
$$\widetilde{M}_\beta f(x)=\sup_{B\ni x}\frac{1}{m(B)^{1-\beta/d}}\int_{B}|f(y)|\,dy.$$
Let $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ denote the Sobolev space of integrable functions whose distributional gradient is also integrable, with norm $\|f\|_{W^{1,1}}=\|f\|_{L^1}+\|\nabla f\|_{L^1}$.

Fix $0\le\beta<1$ and set $q=d/(d-\beta)$. Determine whether the map
$$f\;\longmapsto\;|\nabla M_\beta f|$$
is bounded from $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ to $L^q(\mathbb{R}^d)$, i.e. whether there exists a constant $C=C(d,\beta)$ such that
$$\bigl\||\nabla M_\beta f|\bigr\|_{L^q(\mathbb{R}^d)}\le C\,\|f\|_{W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)}\qquad\text{for all }f\in W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d),$$
and answer the analogous question with $M_\beta$ replaced by the uncentered fractional maximal operator $\widetilde{M}_\beta$.
status_search_result: Beltran, Madrid, and others (Math. Z., 2022; arXiv:2010.05561) establish that for all $0<\alpha<d$ and $1\le p<d/\alpha$, both the centered and uncentered Hardy–Littlewood fractional maximal operators $\mathcal{M}_\alpha f$ are weakly differentiable on $W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ with $\|\nabla\mathcal{M}_\alpha f\|_{p^*}\le C_{d,\alpha,p}\|\nabla f\|_p$, where $p^*=(p^{-1}-\alpha/d)^{-1}$, explicitly covering the previously unknown endpoint $p=1$ for $0<\alpha<1$ (with $W^{1,1}$ replaceable by BV). This affirmatively answers both the centered and uncentered versions of the question.

original_question: For a sequence f : Z -> R, define the one-dimensional discrete centered Hardy-Littlewood maximal function by M f(n) = sup_{r>=0} (1/(2r+1)) sum_{k=-r}^r |f(n+k)|, where the supremum is over nonnegative integers r. If f has bounded variation on Z, must the sharp inequality Var(M f) <= Var(f) hold? If not, can Temur's bound with constant 294912004 be substantially improved?
self_contained_problem:
For a function $f:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{R}$, define the one-dimensional discrete centered Hardy–Littlewood maximal function $Mf:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{R}$ by
$$Mf(n) \;=\; \sup_{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}} \frac{1}{2r+1}\sum_{k=-r}^{r} |f(n+k)|,$$
where the supremum is taken over nonnegative integers $r$. The total variation of a function $g:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{R}$ is
$$\mathrm{Var}(g) \;=\; \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} |g(n+1)-g(n)|.$$
It is known that there exists a finite constant $C$ (in particular, one may take $C = 294{,}912{,}004$) such that for every $f:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{R}$ of bounded variation,
$$\mathrm{Var}(Mf) \;\leq\; C\,\mathrm{Var}(f).$$

Question: Does the sharp inequality
$$\mathrm{Var}(Mf) \;\leq\; \mathrm{Var}(f)$$
hold for every $f:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{R}$ of bounded variation? If not, can the constant $C$ be substantially improved beyond $294{,}912{,}004$?
category_tag: discrete maximal operators and bounded variation
status_search_result: The question appears to remain open in full generality. Recent works (e.g., Bilz–Weigt and follow-ups, 2021–2025) establish the sharp inequality Var(Mf) ≤ Var(f) for indicator functions and certain piecewise constant functions in both continuous and discrete one-dimensional settings, and surveys describe the centered case as the remaining open endpoint regularity problem. No general proof or substantial improvement of Temur's constant for arbitrary BV functions on ℤ has been reported.

original_question: Let Omega be a bounded open convex subset of R^d with Lipschitz boundary and 0 in its interior. For 0 <= beta < d and f : Z^d -> R, define the discrete centered fractional maximal operator associated to Omega by M_{Omega,beta} f(n) = sup_{r>=0} N(0,r)^{beta/d - 1} sum_{m in Omega(0,r)} |f(n+m)|, where N(x,r) counts lattice points in the Omega-ball Omega(x,r). When 0 <= beta < 1 and q = d/(d-beta), does every discrete function f satisfy ||∇M_{Omega,beta} f||_{ell^q(Z^d)} <= C(d,Omega,beta) ||∇f||_{ell^1(Z^d)}? More generally, does inequality (6.4) hold for all alpha <= beta and q = d/(d-beta+alpha)? The paper asks the analogous questions for the uncentered operator as well.
self_contained_problem:
Let $d\ge 1$ and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ be a bounded open convex set with Lipschitz boundary that contains the origin in its interior. For $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $r\ge 0$ set $\Omega(x,r)=x+r\,\Omega$, and let $N(x,r)=\#(\Omega(x,r)\cap\mathbb{Z}^d)$ denote the number of lattice points in $\Omega(x,r)$.

For $0\le \beta<d$ and $f:\mathbb{Z}^d\to\mathbb{R}$, define the discrete centered fractional maximal operator associated to $\Omega$ by
$$M_{\Omega,\beta} f(n)=\sup_{r\ge 0}\frac{1}{N(0,r)^{1-\beta/d}}\sum_{m\in\Omega(0,r)\cap\mathbb{Z}^d}|f(n+m)|, \qquad n\in\mathbb{Z}^d.$$
Define the uncentered version $\widetilde{M}_{\Omega,\beta}f(n)$ analogously, taking the supremum over all $\Omega$-balls $\Omega(x,r)$ containing $n$.

For $g:\mathbb{Z}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ let $\nabla g$ denote the discrete gradient $(\nabla g)(n)=\bigl(g(n+e_i)-g(n)\bigr)_{i=1}^d$, and for $1\le q<\infty$ write $\|\nabla g\|_{\ell^q(\mathbb{Z}^d)}=\bigl(\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^d}|\nabla g(n)|^q\bigr)^{1/q}$.

(a) Let $0\le\beta<1$ and $q=d/(d-\beta)$. Does there exist a constant $C=C(d,\Omega,\beta)$ such that for every $f:\mathbb{Z}^d\to\mathbb{R}$,
$$\|\nabla M_{\Omega,\beta}f\|_{\ell^q(\mathbb{Z}^d)}\le C\,\|\nabla f\|_{\ell^1(\mathbb{Z}^d)}\,?$$

(b) More generally, given $0\le\alpha\le\beta<1$ and $q=d/(d-\beta+\alpha)$, does the inequality
$$\|\nabla M_{\Omega,\beta}f\|_{\ell^q(\mathbb{Z}^d)}\le C(d,\Omega,\beta,\alpha)\,\|\nabla f\|_{\ell^{d/(d-\alpha)}(\mathbb{Z}^d)}$$
hold for all $f:\mathbb{Z}^d\to\mathbb{R}$?

(c) Do the analogous inequalities hold with $M_{\Omega,\beta}$ replaced by the uncentered operator $\widetilde{M}_{\Omega,\beta}$?
status_search_result: Endpoint Sobolev bounds for fractional maximal operators in the continuous setting were established by Beltran–Madrid (arXiv:2010.05561, Math. Z. 2022). For the discrete setting on general convex Ω-balls in Z^d as posed here, no resolution appears in the literature; partial results exist only for specific cases (e.g., ℓ¹-balls and multisublinear variants). The problem as stated for general convex Ω with Lipschitz boundary appears to remain open.

original_question: Let M̃ be the one-dimensional uncentered Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator, and let BV(R) denote the Banach space of functions f : R -> R of bounded total variation with norm ||f||_{BV(R)} = |f(-infinity)| + Var(f). Is the map M̃ : BV(R) -> BV(R) continuous?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathrm{BV}(\mathbb{R})$ denote the Banach space of functions $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ of bounded total variation, equipped with the norm
$$\|f\|_{\mathrm{BV}(\mathbb{R})} = |f(-\infty)| + \mathrm{Var}(f),$$
where $f(-\infty) = \lim_{x\to-\infty} f(x)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(f)$ is the total variation of $f$ on $\mathbb{R}$.

Let $\widetilde{M}$ denote the one-dimensional uncentered Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator, defined for a locally integrable function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ by
$$\widetilde{M}f(x) = \sup_{I\ni x} \frac{1}{|I|}\int_I |f(y)|\,dy,$$
where the supremum is taken over all bounded open intervals $I\subset\mathbb{R}$ containing $x$.

It is known that $\widetilde{M}$ maps $\mathrm{BV}(\mathbb{R})$ into itself boundedly. Determine whether the map
$$\widetilde{M} : \mathrm{BV}(\mathbb{R}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{BV}(\mathbb{R})$$
is continuous.
status_search_result: The problem was solved affirmatively by C. González-Riquelme and D. Kosz in "BV continuity for the uncentered Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator," Journal of Functional Analysis 281 (2021), Article 109037, who proved that the map $\widetilde{M}:\mathrm{BV}(\mathbb{R})\to\mathrm{BV}(\mathbb{R})$ is continuous.

original_question: For 0 < beta < 1, let M_beta be the one-dimensional centered fractional maximal operator and let q = 1/(1-beta). Is the derivative map f -> (M_beta f)' both bounded and continuous from W^{1,1}(R) to L^q(R)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $0<\beta<1$ and set $q=1/(1-\beta)$. For $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R})$, define the one-dimensional centered Hardy–Littlewood fractional maximal function by
$$M_\beta f(x)=\sup_{r>0}\frac{1}{(2r)^{1-\beta}}\int_{x-r}^{x+r}|f(y)|\,dy,\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}.$$
Let $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R})$ denote the Sobolev space of integrable functions whose distributional derivative belongs to $L^1(\mathbb{R})$, equipped with the norm $\|f\|_{W^{1,1}}=\|f\|_{L^1}+\|f'\|_{L^1}$.

Determine whether the map
$$f\longmapsto (M_\beta f)'$$
is both bounded and continuous as a map from $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R})$ into $L^q(\mathbb{R})$.
status_search_result: Recent work has resolved analogous questions for the (non-fractional) one-dimensional centered Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator, proving continuity of f↦(Mf)' from W^{1,1}(R) to L^1(R), and for the uncentered fractional case in higher dimensions. For the centered fractional case in one dimension with 0<β<1 and q=1/(1−β), boundedness of the derivative map is conjectural; partial results show that boundedness would imply continuity, but the full boundedness/continuity statement does not appear to have been established in the literature.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: In fully decentralized federated learning without a central coordinator, how can stochastic-gradient-based training for deep models be made robust to temporary client unavailability, client dropout and joining, message loss, non-IID client data, heterogeneous update frequencies, and communication-topology choices, while still achieving good practical convergence time?
status_search_result: Recent works (e.g., DeceFL 2023, asynchronous decentralized FL with persistent dropout 2025) provide partial progress: convergence guarantees for convex/strongly-convex objectives or empirical mitigation strategies for specific subsets of the listed challenges. However, no algorithm is known that simultaneously handles all of (temporary unavailability, dropout/joining, message loss, non-IID data, heterogeneous update frequencies, topology effects) for deep non-convex SGD with provable robustness and good practical convergence time. The problem is broadly regarded as still open.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: Can split learning be parallelized effectively on resource-constrained edge devices so that different parts of the split computation can run with lower centralized training time while remaining practical in federated deployments?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning setting in which a neural network model M with L layers is trained collaboratively by a central server S and a collection of N resource-constrained edge devices D_1,...,D_N (each device having limited compute, memory, and bandwidth, and holding a private local dataset). In split learning, the model M is partitioned at a designated cut layer ℓ into a client-side sub-model M_c (layers 1,...,ℓ) executed on each edge device and a server-side sub-model M_s (layers ℓ+1,...,L) executed on S, with forward activations at layer ℓ and backward gradients exchanged between device and server. In its standard formulation, devices interact with the server sequentially, so that the centralized training time scales roughly linearly with N.

Design a parallelized variant of split learning satisfying all of the following requirements, or prove that no such variant exists:

(a) Multiple devices D_i may execute their forward and backward passes on M_c concurrently and the server may process the corresponding server-side computations on M_s in parallel, so that the total wall-clock training time per global epoch is sublinear in N (ideally O(1) up to communication and aggregation costs).

(b) The per-device computation, memory footprint, and communication volume per round remain within the budget of resource-constrained edge devices, independent of N.

(c) The trained global model achieves accuracy comparable (within a specified tolerance ε > 0) to that obtained by sequential split learning on the same data and architecture.

(d) The privacy properties of split learning (i.e., raw data never leaves any device D_i) are preserved.

Specify the protocol explicitly, including how client-side sub-model weights are synchronized across devices, how the server schedules and aggregates parallel activations and gradients, and provide a convergence analysis together with bounds on the centralized training time, communication cost, and accuracy gap relative to the sequential baseline.
status_search_result: Multiple subsequent works have proposed parallelized split-learning frameworks for resource-constrained edge devices, including SplitFed/SFL, CPSL (cluster-based parallel SL), EdgeSplit, HSFL, and ParallelSFL. These frameworks demonstrate empirically that parallelization is feasible and reduces wall-clock training time while preserving privacy and approximate accuracy. However, fully general theoretical guarantees on convergence, optimal cut-layer selection, and tight communication/computation/accuracy trade-offs under arbitrary device heterogeneity remain active research directions, so the broad open question is best characterized as partially solved.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: How can researchers characterize the real cross-client distribution shifts that appear in real-world federated datasets, and use that understanding to build controlled but realistic non-IID benchmarks that stress-test algorithms under the kinds of heterogeneity seen in deployment?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the federated learning setting in which a population of clients $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ each hold a local data distribution $P_i$ over an input-output space $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$, and the global learning task concerns the mixture $P = \sum_{i=1}^N w_i P_i$ for client weights $w_i \ge 0$ with $\sum_i w_i = 1$. Cross-client heterogeneity (non-IID-ness) can arise from several distinct mechanisms, including: (i) feature distribution skew, where the marginals $P_i(x)$ differ but $P_i(y \mid x)$ is shared; (ii) label distribution skew, where $P_i(y)$ differs but $P_i(x \mid y)$ is shared; (iii) concept drift, where $P_i(y \mid x)$ differs across clients while $P_i(x)$ is shared; (iv) concept shift, where $P_i(x \mid y)$ differs while $P_i(y)$ is shared; and (v) quantity skew, where the local sample sizes $n_i$ differ substantially.

Develop a quantitative framework that:

1. Defines measurable statistics $\{T_k(P_1, \dots, P_N)\}$ that decompose the heterogeneity present in a real-world federated dataset into contributions from the mechanisms (i)–(v) above (and possibly others, such as temporal drift within a client).

2. Estimates these statistics from samples and applies the framework to representative real-world partitioned datasets (e.g., user-keyed text, image, or sensor data) to characterize the actual mixture of effects observed in deployment.

3. Specifies a generative procedure $\mathcal{G}(\theta)$ — parameterized by a vector $\theta$ controlling the magnitudes of mechanisms (i)–(v) — that produces synthetic federated benchmarks whose statistics $\{T_k\}$ provably match (in expectation, up to a prescribed tolerance) those measured on real datasets, while also allowing controlled interpolation between IID and extreme heterogeneity regimes.

4. Demonstrates that the resulting controlled benchmarks are predictive: i.e., the relative performance of federated optimization algorithms on $\mathcal{G}(\theta_{\text{real}})$ correlates (in a precise, reported sense) with their performance on the corresponding real-world federated datasets, for a representative class of algorithms such as FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD, and personalized variants.

The problem is to provide such a characterization and benchmark-construction methodology, together with the analyses establishing properties (1)–(4).
status_search_result: The problem of fully characterizing real-world cross-client distribution shifts and building controlled, realistic non-IID federated benchmarks remains an active and open research direction. Subsequent works (e.g., LEAF, FedScale, NIID-Bench, Flamby) have proposed partial taxonomies and benchmarks based on Dirichlet label-skew sampling or specific real datasets, but no widely accepted framework matches the empirical mixture of feature/label/concept shifts seen in deployment, and recent surveys continue to list realistic non-IID benchmarking as an unresolved challenge.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: Can the multi-task or lifelong-learning perspective used for personalization and privacy in federated learning be extended to other phenomena such as concept drift, and can non-parameter-transfer lifelong-learning methods such as ProtoNets be made useful in federated learning?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the federated learning setting in which a central coordinator collaborates with a population of clients i = 1, ..., N, each holding a local data distribution D_i, to learn personalized predictive models f_i without centralizing raw data. A multi-task / learning-to-learn (LTL) viewpoint regards each client's task as drawn from a meta-distribution over tasks, and seeks shared representations or meta-parameters that transfer across clients. Concept drift refers to the phenomenon in which a client's data distribution D_i(t) changes over time t, so that the optimal predictor f_i(t) is non-stationary. Lifelong learning algorithms aim to continually learn a sequence of tasks while retaining performance on earlier ones; among them, parameter-transfer methods (e.g., MAML-style approaches) share weights across tasks, while non-parameter-transfer methods such as Prototypical Networks (ProtoNets) operate by computing class prototypes in an embedding space and classifying new points by nearest-prototype rules, without transferring task-specific parameters.

Address the following two questions:

(a) Formulate concept drift in federated learning as a lifelong-learning problem within the multi-task / LTL framework. Specifically, design an algorithmic framework and provide a theoretical analysis (e.g., generalization or regret bounds) for federated learning under client-side concept drift, treating the temporal sequence of distributions {D_i(t)} on each client as a stream of related tasks to be learned in a lifelong-learning sense.

(b) Design and analyze a federated learning algorithm based on a non-parameter-transfer lifelong-learning method such as Prototypical Networks. Determine whether such non-parameter-transfer schemes can be made useful in federated learning, and characterize conditions under which they yield provable benefits (in accuracy, communication cost, privacy, or robustness to heterogeneity) over parameter-transfer-based federated meta-learning approaches.
status_search_result: The question is posed as a forward-looking research direction in the federated learning literature. Subsequent work has explored federated continual/lifelong learning and federated prototype-based methods (e.g., FedProto and federated continual learning frameworks), but no definitive resolution of the broad questions—unifying concept drift with the multi-task/LTL framework and establishing the general usefulness of non-parameter-transfer LTL algorithms like ProtoNets in FL—has been established. The questions remain open as broad research programs.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: What privacy-preserving debugging and interpretability methods can answer practical machine-learning workflow questions on decentralized user data, such as inspecting failure cases, outliers, or bias, and how can differentially private federated generative models be improved enough to support those uses faithfully?
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Let a population of $N$ clients each hold a private local dataset $D_i$ drawn from an unknown distribution $\mathcal{P}_i$ over a common data domain $\mathcal{X}$. A central server may interact with the clients only through a federated protocol: in each round it broadcasts a message, each participating client computes a local update from its own data, and the aggregated client messages are released to the server through a mechanism $\mathcal{M}$ that is $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private at the user (client) level, i.e. for every pair of neighboring client populations differing in the data of a single user and every measurable event $S$,
$$\Pr[\mathcal{M}(\text{population}) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon}\,\Pr[\mathcal{M}(\text{neighbor}) \in S] + \delta.$$
Raw examples in any $D_i$ may never be transmitted to the server or to a human analyst.

Practical workflow questions. A machine-learning practitioner training a model $f_\theta:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ on the federation needs to perform standard debugging and interpretability tasks on the union $\bigcup_i D_i$, including:
(a) inspecting representative failure cases on which $f_\theta$ errs;
(b) detecting and characterizing outliers or distribution shift between subpopulations of clients;
(c) auditing the model and the data for bias with respect to a sensitive attribute $A$;
(d) producing human-interpretable summaries or example-level explanations of model behavior.

Problem. 
1. Design a family of $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-user-level differentially private federated procedures $\{\mathcal{A}_q\}$, one for each workflow question $q$ in (a)–(d), that produce releases $\mathcal{A}_q(D_1,\dots,D_N)$ enabling the practitioner to faithfully answer $q$, and prove formal utility guarantees relating the answers obtained from $\mathcal{A}_q$ to the answers that would be obtained from direct inspection of $\bigcup_i D_i$.

2. Consider the special case where $\mathcal{A}_q$ is implemented by training a generative model $G_\phi$ over $\mathcal{X}$ via a federated, user-level $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP optimization procedure, and then answering workflow questions by drawing synthetic samples from $G_\phi$. Define a fidelity measure $\mathrm{Fid}(G_\phi,\mathcal{P})$ (for example, the total variation or Wasserstein distance to the underlying mixture $\mathcal{P} = \tfrac{1}{N}\sum_i \mathcal{P}_i$, or the gap between expectations of a chosen test class of statistics under $G_\phi$ and under $\mathcal{P}$). Develop training algorithms and theoretical analyses showing how $\mathrm{Fid}(G_\phi,\mathcal{P})$ can be made small enough — as a function of $\varepsilon$, $\delta$, $N$, the per-client sample size, the model class, and the data dimension — that synthetic samples from $G_\phi$ faithfully support the debugging and interpretability tasks (a)–(d), in the sense that decisions made by the practitioner from $G_\phi$-samples agree with decisions that would be made from the true data with high probability.

The goal is both to identify which workflow questions admit such privacy-preserving answers and to quantitatively improve the achievable fidelity of differentially private federated generative models to the level required by these uses.

However, the literature explicitly frames raising the fidelity of DP federated generative models to the level required for faithful debugging, outlier and bias inspection on decentralized user data as an active and unresolved research direction. No general solution with formal utility guarantees covering the full range of debugging and interpretability workflows is established.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: Can interactive zero-knowledge proofs or non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs be made efficient enough for federated learning, both for proving properties of client inputs to the server and for client-side verification tasks that depend on information from multiple participants?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the federated learning setting in which a central server coordinates the training of a shared model with many clients. Each client holds private local data and computes a local update (e.g., a gradient or model delta), which is sent to the server, which aggregates the updates to produce the next global model.

Recall that an interactive zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) system allows a prover holding a secret witness w for a statement x in a language L to convince a verifier that x ∈ L through a multi-round interactive protocol, while leaking no information about w beyond this fact. A non-interactive zero-knowledge proof (NIZK) achieves the same guarantee with a single message from prover to verifier (typically in a common reference string or random oracle model). Standard requirements are completeness, computational (or statistical) soundness, and the zero-knowledge property; efficiency is measured by prover time, verifier time, proof size, and any setup/CRS cost.

Design ZKP or NIZK protocols that are simultaneously practical for the following two federated-learning tasks, and prove the corresponding completeness, soundness, and zero-knowledge properties together with concrete asymptotic and concrete efficiency bounds:

1. Server-directed proofs of input properties. For a fixed predicate P on client local inputs/updates (for example: norm bounds on a gradient, correctness of the local training procedure with respect to a published model and a committed dataset, validity of dataset format, or honest sampling from a committed local distribution), construct a NIZK such that each client can prove to the server that its submitted update u satisfies P(u) = 1 with respect to a public commitment to the client's data, while revealing nothing about the client's data or update beyond P(u) = 1. The protocol must scale to model sizes and client populations typical of federated learning, with prover cost achievable on resource-constrained client devices and aggregate verifier cost on the server sublinear or efficient in the number of clients.

2. Client-directed verification of multi-party-dependent statements. Construct a (possibly interactive) ZKP or NIZK that allows the server (or another designated prover) to convince an individual client that a statement S depending on the joint inputs of many clients holds — for instance, that the published global model was correctly aggregated from valid client updates, that a claimed differential-privacy noise was added correctly, or that a particular client's contribution was included — without revealing the other clients' inputs and while producing a statement that the verifying client can meaningfully trust given that it has no direct access to the other clients' data.

The problem is to determine whether such protocols can be instantiated with end-to-end efficiency (prover time, verifier time, proof size, setup) suitable for deployment in federated learning at realistic scales, and to provide concrete constructions together with security proofs, or alternatively to establish lower bounds ruling out such efficient constructions.
status_search_result: Recent works (2023–2025), including zkFL, ProxyZKP, VPFL, and various verifiable-FL surveys, give NIZK/zk-SNARK constructions for proving properties of client updates and for verifying aggregation, with reported speedups over generic zk-SNARKs and Bulletproofs. However, no construction is known that simultaneously delivers practical prover cost on resource-constrained clients, sublinear server verification at federated scale, and full coverage of multi-party-dependent client-side verification statements; the general question of efficient ZKP/NIZK for federated learning remains an active open research direction.

original_question: Do privacy-amplification-by-iteration results known for convex optimization extend to the non-convex federated-learning setting, and can practical protocols provide formal privacy guarantees despite dynamic user eligibility, local participation decisions, and mid-protocol dropout?

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: Is it possible to perform communication-efficient federated training of sub-models while preserving the privacy of which sub-model each client is updating, and what sparsity regimes, private retrieval mechanisms, and secure aggregation variants would make that practical?
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Consider a federated learning system with a central server and a set of clients $\{1,2,\dots,N\}$. The global model is partitioned into $M$ disjoint sub-models $\theta = (\theta_1,\dots,\theta_M)$, where $\theta_m \in \mathbb{R}^{d_m}$. Each client $i$ holds local data $\mathcal{D}_i$ that is relevant to exactly one sub-model index $s(i) \in \{1,\dots,M\}$, known only to that client. In each round, client $i$ wishes to (a) download the current value of $\theta_{s(i)}$ from the server, (b) compute a local update $\Delta_{s(i)}^{(i)}$ from $\mathcal{D}_i$, and (c) contribute this update so that the server can form an aggregated update to $\theta_{s(i)}$, without ever revealing $s(i)$ or $\Delta_{s(i)}^{(i)}$ in the clear.

Define a federated sub-model training protocol $\Pi$ to be a multi-round interactive protocol between the server and clients that, at the end of training, produces an updated global model $\hat\theta$. Let $\mathrm{Acc}(\Pi)$ denote the expected utility (e.g., test accuracy) of $\hat\theta$ on the underlying task, and let $\mathrm{Comm}(\Pi)$ denote the total expected per-client communication (uplink plus downlink) per round, measured in bits. Say that $\Pi$ is:
- communication-efficient if $\mathrm{Comm}(\Pi) = o\!\left(\sum_{m=1}^M d_m\right)$ in the relevant asymptotic regime, ideally scaling polynomially in $\max_m d_m$ rather than in the full model dimension;
- index-private if for every pair of clients $i,j$ and every adversary modeled as the server colluding with any subset $T \subset \{1,\dots,N\}\setminus\{i,j\}$ of size at most $t$, the protocol transcript reveals (in either an information-theoretic or a cryptographic sense) no more about $s(i)$ than is implied by aggregate statistics released by the protocol;
- update-private if, in addition, the individual update vector $\Delta_{s(i)}^{(i)}$ is hidden from the same adversary, except through its contribution to the aggregated sums on each sub-model.

Problem. Determine whether there exists a federated sub-model training protocol $\Pi$ that is simultaneously communication-efficient, index-private, and update-private, and that achieves utility $\mathrm{Acc}(\Pi)$ matching (up to a vanishing additive error) the utility of the non-private baseline in which each client sends $\Delta_{s(i)}^{(i)}$ in the clear together with its index $s(i)$. Specifically:

(i) Identify sparsity regimes on $(N, M, d_1,\dots,d_M)$ and on the distribution of indices $\{s(i)\}_{i=1}^N$ (e.g., heavy-tailed versus near-uniform popularity of sub-models) under which such a protocol exists.

(ii) Construct, or prove the impossibility of, a protocol combining a private information retrieval (PIR) or oblivious-RAM-style download mechanism for $\theta_{s(i)}$ with a secure aggregation scheme tolerating up to $t$ colluding parties for the upload of $\Delta_{s(i)}^{(i)}$, whose total communication is sublinear in $\sum_m d_m$.

(iii) Quantify the optimal trade-off, as a function of the sparsity parameters, the collusion threshold $t$, and the desired privacy level, between $\mathrm{Comm}(\Pi)$ and the achievable utility $\mathrm{Acc}(\Pi)$.
status_search_result: The question has stimulated an active research line. Several works (e.g., information-theoretically private federated submodel learning with multiple non-colluding databases, secure-aggregation-based private submodel updates, and hierarchical submodel training) propose protocols that target communication efficiency together with privacy of the submodel index and updates. However, no single protocol is known to simultaneously achieve sublinear communication, full index- and update-privacy under realistic single-server collusion models, and baseline utility across general sparsity regimes; trade-offs are still being mapped, so the broad question remains only partially resolved.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: Can defenses such as data sanitization and network pruning be adapted to federated learning in a way that does not require direct access to private client data, and how should the gap between data poisoning and model-update poisoning attacks be quantified under realistic federated adversary capabilities?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning setting in which a central server coordinates the training of a global model with parameters $	heta \in \mathbb{R}^d$ across $N$ clients. In each round $t$, the server broadcasts the current model $	heta_t$, a subset $S_t \subseteq \{1,\dots,N\}$ of clients each compute an update $\Delta_i^{(t)}$ from their private local dataset $D_i$, and the server aggregates these updates to obtain $	heta_{t+1} = 	heta_t + \mathrm{Agg} igl(\{\Delta_i^{(t)}\}_{i \in S_t} igr)$. The server cannot observe the client data $D_i$ nor any data drawn from the same distribution.

Two classes of adversarial behavior are considered for a fraction $ho$ of compromised clients:
(i) Data poisoning: the adversary alters the local dataset $D_i$ but the client otherwise follows the prescribed local training protocol, producing $\Delta_i^{(t)}$ honestly from the corrupted data.
(ii) Model-update poisoning: the adversary may submit any vector $\Delta_i^{(t)} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ subject to specified constraints (e.g., norm bounds or stealth constraints), without regard to any underlying dataset.

Two standard centralized defenses are:
- Data sanitization: filter or relabel training points by detecting outliers in the training data using a reference (clean) dataset.
- Network pruning: identify and remove neurons or weights that activate primarily on backdoored or anomalous inputs, using clean validation data to detect such neurons.

Both defenses, in their classical forms, require direct access to (a sample of) clean training data resembling the clients' data.

Resolve the following:

(A) Design and analyze data-sanitization-style and network-pruning-style defenses that operate in the federated setting under the constraint that the server has no access to clients' private data and no auxiliary dataset drawn from their distribution, while preserving formally stated privacy guarantees (e.g., $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy with respect to each $D_i$). Provide either (a) provable robustness guarantees—bounds on the deviation $\|	heta_T - 	heta_T^{\mathrm{clean}}\|$ or on the test risk under a specified poisoning model—matching those of the centralized analogues, or (b) impossibility results showing that the centralized guarantees cannot be achieved by any defense satisfying the stated privacy constraint, thereby establishing whether genuinely new federated-specific defenses against data poisoning are required.

(B) Formulate a quantitative measure $G(\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{data}}, \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{model}})$ of the gap between the worst-case attack success achievable by a data-poisoning adversary $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{data}}$ and a model-update-poisoning adversary $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{model}}$ operating under matched, realistic capability budgets (fraction $ho$ of corrupted clients, bounds on per-client update norm, knowledge of other clients' data and of the aggregation rule, computational budget). Prove upper and lower bounds on $G$ as a function of these capability parameters and the aggregation rule $\mathrm{Agg}$, and relate $G$ to a precise notion of relative adversarial strength between the two threat models.
status_search_result: The problem remains broadly open. Although since 2020 numerous federated defenses have appeared (FoolsGold, robust aggregation rules, anomaly-detection-based filtering, federated data sanitization variants such as FDSD, pruning-style backdoor mitigation), there is no defense that simultaneously matches centralized data-sanitization/network-pruning guarantees while provably respecting client privacy, and recent work continues to break state-of-the-art defenses with optimization-based attacks. No widely accepted quantitative theory of the data-poisoning vs. model-update-poisoning gap under matched federated capabilities has been established.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: To what extent can bias that originates in the data-generating process be detected or mitigated in federated learning, and what methods can apply post-hoc fairness corrections to models learned from potentially biased decentralized interaction data?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning setting in which a set of clients $\{C_1, \ldots, C_K\}$ each holds a local dataset $D_k = \{(x_{k,i}, y_{k,i})\}_{i=1}^{n_k}$ drawn from a (possibly client-specific) distribution $\mathcal{P}_k$ over an input space $\mathcal{X}$ and label space $\mathcal{Y}$, together with a sensitive attribute $a_{k,i} \in \mathcal{A}$. A global model $f_\theta : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}$ is trained collaboratively (without centralizing the raw data) by minimizing some federated objective such as $\sum_k \tfrac{n_k}{N} \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim \mathcal{P}_k}[\ell(f_\theta(x), y)]$. Assume that the data-generating processes $\mathcal{P}_k$ may themselves be biased, in the sense that there exist measurable disparities in conditional distributions across values of the sensitive attribute (e.g., $\mathcal{P}_k(y \mid a = a_0) \neq \mathcal{P}_k(y \mid a = a_1)$) arising from the collection or interaction mechanism rather than from sampling noise.

(a) Develop a rigorous framework, compatible with the federated constraints (clients do not share raw data, communication is limited, and individual data may be subject to privacy mechanisms such as differential privacy), under which one can detect biases that originate in the data-generating processes $\{\mathcal{P}_k\}$. Specifically, give procedures and provable guarantees for identifying when observed disparities in the trained model $f_\theta$ are attributable to bias in $\{\mathcal{P}_k\}$ rather than to optimization, heterogeneity, or finite-sample effects.

(b) Develop federated training algorithms that provably mitigate such data-generation bias under standard fairness criteria (e.g., demographic parity, equalized odds, calibration), with quantitative trade-offs between fairness, accuracy, communication, and privacy.

(c) Develop post-hoc correction methods that, given an already-trained federated model $f_\theta$ and limited (possibly decentralized and privacy-protected) access to client data or summary statistics, produce a corrected predictor $\tilde f$ satisfying a prescribed fairness criterion, with guarantees on the deviation from $f_\theta$ in predictive performance.

Provide methods for (a), (b), and (c), or establish impossibility results delineating the limits of bias detection and mitigation under federated, decentralized interaction-data settings.
status_search_result: This is a broad open research direction concerning fairness and bias in federated learning. While numerous partial results have appeared (e.g., fair federated averaging variants, client-fairness reweighting schemes, and post-hoc fairness calibration in centralized settings), no comprehensive solution providing detection, mitigation, and post-hoc correction guarantees specifically for biases originating in decentralized data-generating processes has been established. The problem remains open as a research program.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: How do client-sampling constraints and decentralized data collection affect fairness in federated learning, and under what assumptions can fairness-improving methods from centralized learning be adapted to the federated setting?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning system consisting of a central server and a population of clients $\mathcal{C} = \{1,2,\dots,N\}$. Each client $i \in \mathcal{C}$ holds a local data distribution $\mathcal{D}_i$ over an input-label-attribute space $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{A}$, where $\mathcal{A}$ encodes a protected attribute (e.g. demographic group). At each round $t$, a (possibly biased) sampling mechanism selects a subset $S_t \subseteq \mathcal{C}$ of clients according to a distribution $q_t$ that may depend on availability constraints, device characteristics, network connectivity, time zone, or other systematic factors that cause $q_t$ to deviate from the uniform distribution. The server then aggregates locally trained updates from clients in $S_t$ to produce a global model $h:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$.

Fix a fairness criterion $\mathcal{F}(h)$ for centralized learning (e.g. demographic parity, equalized odds, calibration, or individual fairness with respect to a metric on $\mathcal{X}$), defined as a functional of $h$ and a global data distribution $\mathcal{D}^* = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{D}_i$. Suppose that in the centralized setting (where a learner has direct sample access to $\mathcal{D}^*$) there exists a known algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\text{cen}}$ that produces a model $h$ achieving $\mathcal{F}(h) \le \varepsilon$ while attaining utility within $\delta$ of the unconstrained optimum.

Address the following:

1. Quantify, as a function of the divergence between $q_t$ and the uniform distribution and of the heterogeneity among the $\mathcal{D}_i$, how client-sampling bias and decentralized data collection degrade $\mathcal{F}(h)$ for the model produced by standard federated aggregation (e.g. FedAvg).

2. Identify minimal assumptions on (a) the sampling distributions $\{q_t\}$, (b) the inter-client heterogeneity (e.g. bounded $\chi^2$ or KL divergence between $\mathcal{D}_i$ and $\mathcal{D}^*$), (c) the availability of protected-attribute information at clients or server, and (d) the communication and privacy constraints (such as differential privacy or secure aggregation), under which $\mathcal{A}_{\text{cen}}$ can be adapted into a federated algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\text{fed}}$ that, with high probability, returns a global model $h$ satisfying $\mathcal{F}(h) \le \varepsilon + o(1)$ while preserving utility within $\delta + o(1)$ of the federated optimum.

3. Either construct such an adaptation $\mathcal{A}_{\text{fed}}$ for a representative class of fairness criteria, or prove an impossibility result showing that under the stated constraints no federated algorithm can simultaneously achieve approximate fairness, approximate utility, and the required privacy/communication guarantees.
status_search_result: Fairness under client-sampling bias in federated learning remains an active research area. Subsequent works (e.g., q-FFL, AFL, FairFed, and various papers on fairness-aware federated optimization through 2023–2025) have proposed partial solutions for specific fairness notions and sampling models, but a general theory characterizing when centralized fairness algorithms can be lifted to the federated setting under heterogeneity, biased participation, and privacy/communication constraints is not yet established. The problem is therefore considered open in its general form.

paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
original_question: What composite objective functions should be optimized when tuning federated learning systems that must trade off model quality, throughput, convergence speed, fairness, privacy, robustness, and resource use, and how can those settings be tuned automatically rather than manually?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning system in which a central coordinator orchestrates training of a shared model across a large population of distributed clients. The performance of such a system can be characterized by multiple, often competing, criteria, including: (i) model quality Q (e.g., validation accuracy or loss), (ii) throughput T (e.g., updates processed per unit time), (iii) convergence speed C (e.g., wall-clock time or rounds to reach a target quality), (iv) fairness F across clients (e.g., variance of per-client performance, or worst-client utility), (v) a privacy guarantee P (e.g., the (ε, δ) parameters of a differential-privacy mechanism, or a bound on information leakage), (vi) robustness R against adversarial or Byzantine clients and against client drift, and (vii) resource use U (communication bandwidth, on-device compute, energy). Each of these is itself a function of a vector θ of tunable system parameters (number of clients sampled per round, local epochs, learning rates, batch sizes, compression and quantization levels, noise multipliers, aggregation rules, secure-aggregation thresholds, dropout-tolerance settings, etc.).

Formalize and solve the following:

1. Design a family of composite objective functions Φ(θ) = Φ(Q(θ), T(θ), C(θ), F(θ), P(θ), R(θ), U(θ)) suitable for use as optimization targets when tuning a federated learning system, such that Φ encodes principled trade-offs among the seven criteria above and admits meaningful Pareto analysis.

2. Provide algorithms that, given only black-box (and noisy) access to the criteria via system runs or simulations, automatically select θ to optimize Φ — replacing manual tuning — and prove guarantees on their sample complexity, regret, or convergence to (approximate) Pareto-optimal configurations under appropriate assumptions on the criteria as functions of θ.

The task is to produce both the principled construction of Φ and the accompanying automatic-tuning algorithms with formal guarantees.
status_search_result: The question is an open-ended research direction in federated learning systems. Surveys and follow-up works through 2024–2025 still describe automated multi-objective tuning of FL systems (balancing accuracy, communication, privacy, fairness, robustness) as an active and unresolved area, with various partial heuristics (Bayesian optimization, multi-objective NAS, AutoFL) but no general principled composite objective or tuning algorithm with guarantees.

paper_title: A Collection of Open Problems
context_brief: How many triangles must concentrate on one edge in a dense graph?
original_question: Fix a constant c > 0. For a graph on n vertices with cn^2 edges, assume every edge belongs to at least one triangle. Let f(n; c) be the largest integer such that some edge of the graph is contained in at least f(n; c) triangles. Determine f(n; c) as sharply as possible, from above and below, as a function of n and c.
self_contained_problem:
Fix a constant $c>0$. For each integer $n\ge 1$, consider all simple graphs $G$ on $n$ vertices with at least $cn^2$ edges such that every edge of $G$ belongs to at least one triangle (a triangle being a set of three pairwise adjacent vertices). Define
\[
 f(n;c) \;=\; \min_{G}\;\max_{e\in E(G)} \, t_G(e),
\]
where $t_G(e)$ denotes the number of triangles in $G$ containing the edge $e$, the minimum is taken over all such graphs $G$ on $n$ vertices, and the maximum is taken over all edges $e$ of $G$. Determine the asymptotic behavior of $f(n;c)$ as $n\to\infty$ as sharply as possible, providing matching upper and lower bounds as functions of $n$ and $c$.
category_tag: extremal graph theory: triangles per edge
status_search_result: For c < 1/4, Fox and Loh (2012) showed that f(n;c) = n^{O(1/log log n)}, refuting the conjecture that f(n;c) > n^ε for some ε>0. For c > 1/4, a classical result guarantees an edge in at least n/6 triangles. So qualitatively the question is largely resolved (the polynomial growth conjecture is disproved and matching super-polylogarithmic lower bounds are known), but the precise asymptotic behavior of f(n;c) is not fully pinned down, so the sharp form remains open.

paper_title: A Collection of Open Problems
context_brief: Sparse-incidence clique coverings of almost all graphs.
original_question: For almost every graph on n vertices, does there exist a collection of cliques such that each vertex belongs to only o(n) of the chosen cliques while all but o(n^2) edges are covered by those cliques? More sharply, can one achieve a per-vertex bound of order O(n / log n)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G(n,1/2)$ denote the random graph on the vertex set $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ in which each pair of distinct vertices is joined by an edge independently with probability $1/2$. A clique of $G$ is a subset of vertices that is pairwise adjacent. A clique covering of $G$ is a collection $\mathcal{C}$ of cliques of $G$ whose union of edge sets covers some subset of the edges of $G$; an edge of $G$ is said to be covered by $\mathcal{C}$ if it is contained in at least one clique of $\mathcal{C}$. For a vertex $v$, let $d_{\mathcal{C}}(v)$ denote the number of cliques in $\mathcal{C}$ that contain $v$.

Prove or disprove: with probability tending to $1$ as $n 	o \infty$, the random graph $G(n,1/2)$ admits a collection of cliques $\mathcal{C}$ such that

(i) $\max_{v} d_{\mathcal{C}}(v) = o(n)$, and

(ii) all but $o(n^2)$ edges of $G$ are covered by $\mathcal{C}$.

Moreover, determine whether one can sharpen (i) to $\max_{v} d_{\mathcal{C}}(v) = O(n/\log n)$, while still satisfying (ii).
status_search_result: Related results are known: Bollobás–Erdős–Spencer–West (1993) bounded the total number of cliques needed to cover almost all edges of $G(n,1/2)$, and Frieze–Reed (1995) determined that the clique cover number of $G(n,1/2)$ is $\Theta(n^2/\log^2 n)$. However, no source explicitly confirms a per-vertex incidence bound of the form $O(n/\log n)$ while leaving only $o(n^2)$ edges uncovered. The sharp form of the question therefore appears not to be definitively settled in accessible literature.

paper_title: A Collection of Open Problems
context_brief: Threshold-graph covering and density extremal questions.
original_question: Using threshold graphs instead of cliques, determine the correct extremal behavior of threshold-graph coverings and large threshold subgraphs. In particular: (i) if a graph family has nth member edge-coverable by 2n threshold graphs but requiring 3n threshold graphs for an edge-partition, is that 3n requirement best possible? and (ii) if a graph with 2n vertices and n^2 + 1 edges must contain a threshold subgraph with n(1 + 1/2) edges, what is the correct constant c for which one can force a threshold subgraph with cn edges?
self_contained_problem:
A threshold graph is a graph that can be constructed from a single vertex by repeatedly adding either an isolated vertex or a dominating vertex (one adjacent to all existing vertices). Equivalently, threshold graphs are exactly the graphs containing no induced subgraph isomorphic to 2K_2, P_4, or C_4.

Consider the following two extremal questions about threshold graphs.

(i) Cover vs. partition. Suppose there exists a family of graphs {G_n} such that, for every n, the edge set E(G_n) can be covered by the edge sets of 2n threshold subgraphs of G_n (these threshold subgraphs may overlap), but any partition of E(G_n) into edge-disjoint threshold subgraphs requires at least 3n parts. Determine whether the ratio 3n/2n = 3/2 is the largest possible separation. More precisely, find the supremum of constants c such that there exists a graph family in which the minimum size of a threshold edge-cover is m_n while the minimum size of a threshold edge-partition is at least c·m_n + o(m_n).

(ii) Large threshold subgraphs in dense graphs. Determine the largest constant c with the following property: every graph on 2n vertices with at least n^2 + 1 edges contains a threshold subgraph with at least cn edges. Equivalently, find
   c* = lim inf_{n→∞} (1/n) · min { t(G) : |V(G)| = 2n, |E(G)| ≥ n^2 + 1 },
where t(G) denotes the maximum number of edges in a threshold subgraph of G.
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not surface a definitive resolution of either the cover-versus-partition ratio question or the precise extremal constant for forcing a large threshold subgraph in graphs on 2n vertices with more than n^2 edges. General references on extremal graph theory and edge partitions appear, but none specifically settle these threshold-graph problems, so the current status is inconclusive.

paper_title: A Collection of Open Problems
original_question: Color the unit interval by k measurable color classes. An m-partition is a partition of the interval into m disjoint subsets, each a finite union of intervals, such that every part captures exactly 1/m of the measure of each color. Let c(m, k) be the smallest number of cuts needed, in the worst case, to produce such an m-partition. Is c(m, k) = (m - 1)k for all m and k?
self_contained_problem:
Let $k, m \ge 1$ be integers. Suppose the unit interval $[0,1]$ is partitioned into $k$ measurable subsets $C_1, \dots, C_k$ (the "color classes"), each of positive Lebesgue measure $|C_i|$. An $m$-partition of $[0,1]$ consists of $m$ pairwise disjoint subsets $A_1, \dots, A_m$ whose union is $[0,1]$, where each $A_j$ is a finite union of subintervals of $[0,1]$, and such that for every color $i \in \{1,\dots,k\}$ and every part $j \in \{1,\dots,m\}$,
$$|A_j \cap C_i| = \frac{1}{m} |C_i|.$$
The number of cuts of such an $m$-partition is the number of interior endpoints of the constituent subintervals (equivalently, the minimum number of points in $(0,1)$ at which $[0,1]$ must be cut so that the resulting open intervals can be reassembled into the parts $A_1,\dots,A_m$).

Define $c(m,k)$ to be the smallest integer $N$ such that, for every choice of $k$ measurable color classes $C_1,\dots,C_k$ partitioning $[0,1]$, there exists an $m$-partition using at most $N$ cuts.

Prove or disprove: $c(m,k) = (m-1)k$ for all positive integers $m$ and $k$.
status_search_result: This is the continuous necklace-splitting problem. The upper bound $c(m,k)\le (m-1)k$ was established by Noga Alon (1987) using a Borsuk–Ulam type argument, matching the easy lower bound. The conjecture is therefore considered solved.

paper_title: A Collection of Open Problems
context_brief: Increasing-label paths in edge-labeled complete graphs.
original_question: Label the edges of the complete graph K_n bijectively by 1, 2, ..., binom(n, 2). For a labeling lambda, let l(lambda) be the length of the longest simple path whose edge labels strictly increase along the path, and let f(n) be the minimum of l(lambda) over all such labelings. Determine the growth of f(n), in particular whether f(n) = o(n) and whether f(n) > n^(1/2 + epsilon) for some epsilon > 0.
self_contained_problem:
For an integer n ≥ 2, consider all bijective labelings λ : E(K_n) → {1, 2, …, C(n,2)} of the edges of the complete graph on n vertices. For such a labeling λ, let ℓ(λ) be the length (number of edges) of the longest simple path v_0 v_1 … v_k in K_n whose edge labels are strictly increasing, i.e. λ(v_0 v_1) < λ(v_1 v_2) < … < λ(v_{k-1} v_k). Define
   f(n) = min_λ ℓ(λ),
the minimum being taken over all bijective edge-labelings of K_n.

Determine the asymptotic growth rate of f(n). In particular:
(a) Is f(n) = o(n)?
(b) Does there exist ε > 0 such that f(n) > n^{1/2 + ε} for all sufficiently large n?

Bucić, Kwan, Pokrovskiy, Sudakov, Tran, and Wagner (2018/2020, "Nearly-linear monotone paths in edge-ordered graphs", Israel J. Math.) proved f(n) ≥ n^{1-o(1)}, which in particular answers (b) affirmatively for every ε < 1/2. The original conjecture that f(n) is linear in n, and the question whether f(n) = o(n), remain open.

paper_title: A Collection of Open Problems
context_brief: Highly connected graphs with highly connected spanning bipartite subgraphs.
original_question: For each integer k >= 1, is it true that every (2k - 1)-connected graph contains a spanning bipartite subgraph that is k-connected?
self_contained_problem:
A graph $G$ is said to be $m$-connected if it has more than $m$ vertices and remains connected after the removal of any set of fewer than $m$ vertices. A spanning subgraph of $G$ is a subgraph containing every vertex of $G$. A graph is bipartite if its vertex set can be partitioned into two parts so that every edge has one endpoint in each part.

Question: For every integer $k \geq 1$, is it true that every $(2k-1)$-connected graph $G$ contains a spanning bipartite subgraph that is $k$-connected?
status_search_result: This is a conjecture commonly attributed to Thomassen. It remains open in general. Recent work (e.g., a 2024 Electronic Journal of Combinatorics paper, "Highly Connected Graphs Have Highly Connected Spanning Bipartite Subgraphs") establishes that every t-connected graph has a k-connected spanning bipartite subgraph for some t = t(k,n) bounded above by a function such as O(k^2 log n), but the linear bound 2k-1 (independent of n) is not known. Thus the original question is unresolved.
