paper_title: ALGORITHMIC INFORMATION THEORY: OPEN PROBLEMS
original_question: Define and study symmetry for random strings and random sequences. Is lack of symmetry a sign of non-randomness?
self_contained_problem:
Work in the setting of algorithmic information theory. For a finite binary string $x \in \{0,1\}^*$, let $K(x)$ denote its prefix-free Kolmogorov complexity. Call a string $x$ of length $n$ (Kolmogorov-)random if $K(x) \ge n - O(1)$, and call an infinite binary sequence $X \in \{0,1\}^\omega$ (Martin-Löf) random if there is a constant $c$ such that $K(X\!\upharpoonright\!n) \ge n - c$ for all $n$.

Introduce a general notion of "symmetry" for finite strings and infinite sequences. By a symmetry of a string $x$ of length $n$ one may understand, for instance, a nontrivial permutation $\sigma \in S_n$ such that $x_{\sigma(i)} = x_i$ for all $i$, or more generally invariance of $x$ under some structured family of transformations (reflections, rotations, block permutations, affine maps on indices, etc.); analogous definitions can be formulated for infinite sequences via shift-, reflection-, or block-invariances on initial segments.

The problem is twofold:

(a) Propose a mathematically robust definition of symmetry (and of a quantitative measure of symmetry, e.g.\ the size or descriptive complexity of the group of symmetries of $x$) for random finite strings and for random infinite sequences.

(b) Under such a definition, determine whether the absence of symmetry is a necessary feature of randomness. Specifically: is it true that every Kolmogorov-random string, respectively every Martin-Löf random infinite sequence, has only trivial symmetries (in the proposed sense), and conversely does the presence of nontrivial symmetry imply a quantifiable defect in randomness (e.g.\ a bound $K(x) \le n - f(x)$ where $f(x)$ grows with the amount of symmetry)?
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open question in algorithmic information theory attributed to C. Calude. No published resolution defining symmetry for random strings/sequences and establishing the symmetry/non-randomness equivalence appears in standard sources; the problem remains open.

paper_title: ALGORITHMIC INFORMATION THEORY: OPEN PROBLEMS
original_question: Let M be an arbitrary finite set of strings. Extend the notion of the degree of randomness of a string x, which compares the complexity of x with the complexities of all strings of the same length, so that randomness can be defined with respect to M. The desired extension should preserve the intuition that if M has m elements, m is very large, and M can be described by a program whose length is negligible compared with log m, then almost all elements of M should have maximal complexity close to log m and therefore count as random with respect to M.
self_contained_problem:
Background. For a binary string x, let C(x) denote its (plain or prefix-free) Kolmogorov complexity, i.e. the length of the shortest program (in a fixed universal Turing machine) that outputs x. For strings of length n, one classical measure of the "degree of randomness" of x compares C(x) with n = log|{0,1}^n|: x is considered (highly) random when C(x) is close to n. More generally, for a finite set M of strings, one can compare C(x) (or the conditional complexity C(x | M), given a description of M) with log|M|.

Problem. Define a notion of "degree of randomness of a string x with respect to an arbitrary finite set M of strings" that extends the usual notion (recovered when M = {0,1}^n) and that satisfies the following requirement: whenever M is a finite set of strings with |M| = m, m is very large, and M admits a program description whose length is negligible compared with log m, then almost every element x ∈ M should be assigned the maximal degree of randomness with respect to M, i.e. its complexity should be close to log m, so that almost all elements of M are "random with respect to M".

Provide such a definition and prove that it has the stated property.
status_search_result: A targeted search did not surface a definitive resolution of this specific formulation (attributed to C. Calude) asking for a satisfactory notion of randomness of a string with respect to an arbitrary finite set. Related work exists on conditional Kolmogorov complexity, randomness deficiency relative to computable measures, and Kolmogorov's structure function, but no clearly identified solution to this exact problem was located. Status is therefore reported as unknown.

paper_title: Observational Cosmology: caveats and open questions in the standard model
original_question: Can the Tolman surface-brightness test provide a decisive observational distinction between an expanding universe and a non-expanding universe when the observed surface-brightness dependence on redshift must be disentangled from galaxy luminosity evolution, intergalactic absorption by metals or dust, and possible methodological errors?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider two competing cosmological hypotheses for a population of galaxies observed at varying redshifts z:

(A) An expanding-universe hypothesis, in which the bolometric surface brightness (flux per unit solid angle) of a galaxy of intrinsic luminosity and physical size satisfies the relation SB(z) ∝ (1+z)^(−4) at fixed rest-frame band, in addition to any intrinsic evolution of the source.

(B) A non-expanding (static) universe hypothesis, in which cosmological redshift arises from some non-expansion mechanism and the surface brightness has at most a mild redshift dependence (e.g. SB(z) ∝ (1+z)^0 or (1+z)^(−1) depending on the assumed photon mechanism), modulo intrinsic evolution and absorption.

Let m(z) denote the observed mean surface brightness of a chosen class of galaxies (e.g. early-type galaxies or another standard set) as a function of redshift. Suppose the observed signal decomposes as
   m(z) = T(z) + E(z) + A(z) + η(z),
where T(z) is the cosmological Tolman term (which differs between hypotheses (A) and (B)), E(z) is the contribution from intrinsic luminosity and size evolution of the galaxy population, A(z) is dimming due to intergalactic absorption by dust and metals, and η(z) represents systematic and methodological errors (e.g. point-spread function effects, ellipticity, selection, K-corrections).

Problem. Determine whether, on the basis of currently available or foreseeable photometric data over a wide range of redshifts, the Tolman surface-brightness test can in principle yield a statistically decisive observational discrimination between hypotheses (A) and (B). Specifically:

1. Identify whether E(z), A(z), and η(z) can be independently constrained to a precision sufficient that the residual m(z) − E(z) − A(z) − η(z) distinguishes the predicted (1+z)^(−4) law from the static-universe prediction at high confidence.

2. If not, exhibit a model-independent argument or example showing that any expansion signature can be mimicked by an admissible choice of luminosity evolution E(z) (together with absorption A(z)), so that the test cannot separate cosmological expansion from galaxy evolution.

State precisely the conditions on E(z), A(z), and the observational sample under which the Tolman test is or is not a decisive cosmological discriminator.
status_search_result: The question remains actively debated. Recent analyses (including JWST-era studies in 2024–2026 using thousands of spectroscopically confirmed galaxies) report that observed surface-brightness trends with redshift depart from the (1+z)^(−4) prediction of the expanding-universe model, but the interpretation is still confounded by uncertain galaxy luminosity/size evolution and intergalactic absorption. No consensus has emerged that the Tolman test decisively distinguishes expanding from non-expanding cosmologies; the degeneracy with evolution remains the central obstacle.

paper_title: Observational Cosmology: caveats and open questions in the standard model
original_question: Do absorption-line measurements in high-redshift clouds demonstrate that the cosmic microwave background radiation temperature increases with redshift as T proportional to 1 + z, or are those inferred temperatures too dependent on collisional excitation, ultraviolet pumping, infrared dust emission, and other local excitation mechanisms to serve as a definitive test?
self_contained_problem:
In the standard hot Big Bang cosmology, the cosmic microwave background (CMB) is predicted to be a blackbody whose temperature scales with redshift as
$$T_{\rm CMB}(z) = T_0\,(1+z),\qquad T_0 = 2.725\,\text{K}.$$
One observational test of this prediction uses quasar absorption-line systems at high redshift: the relative populations of fine-structure or rotational levels of species such as C I, C II, CN, CO, or H2O in intervening or associated clouds are measured, and an excitation temperature is inferred. If the CMB is the dominant excitation source, this excitation temperature equals $T_{\rm CMB}(z)$; otherwise additional local mechanisms (collisional excitation by particles in the cloud, ultraviolet pumping by ambient radiation, infrared pumping by dust emission, and other excitation channels) contribute and must be modeled and subtracted.

Question: Do the available absorption-line excitation-temperature measurements in high-redshift clouds constitute a definitive demonstration that $T_{\rm CMB}(z) = T_0(1+z)$, or are the inferred temperatures sufficiently dependent on the modeling of collisional excitation, UV pumping, IR dust emission, and other local excitation mechanisms that they cannot yet conclusively confirm or rule out this scaling law? More precisely, determine whether observations exist (or design observations) that establish the $(1+z)$ scaling of $T_{\rm CMB}$ from absorption-line data in a manner independent of, or robust to, uncertainties in such local excitation contributions.
status_search_result: Since 2003, absorption-line measurements have substantially improved. CO rotational excitation in quasar absorption systems up to z~3 (Noterdaeme et al. 2011) yields T_CMB(z) = 2.725(1+z)^{1-β} with β = -0.007 ± 0.027, consistent with the standard (1+z) scaling. A precise determination at z=0.89 (Muller et al. 2013) and an H2O absorption measurement at z=6.34 (Riechers et al. 2022) further support the linear scaling within errors. Local-excitation modeling (collisions, UV/IR pumping) remains a systematic that authors explicitly account for, but current constraints meaningfully confirm the (1+z) law in the redshift ranges probed; deviations are not detected and the original concern is partially resolved.

paper_title: Observational Cosmology: caveats and open questions in the standard model
original_question: Does the temperature of the intergalactic medium, as inferred from the small-scale falloff of the Lyman-alpha forest power spectrum, evolve with redshift as expected from adiabatic cooling in an expanding universe, or is the reported absence of redshift evolution evidence that requires another explanation?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the diffuse intergalactic medium (IGM), the low-density baryonic gas pervading the universe between galaxies, whose thermal state can be probed observationally through the Lyman-alpha forest: the dense series of absorption lines blueward of the Lyman-alpha emission of distant quasars produced by neutral hydrogen along the line of sight. On small spatial scales, the one-dimensional flux power spectrum of the Lyman-alpha forest exhibits a high-wavenumber cutoff arising from thermal Doppler broadening and pressure (Jeans) smoothing, from which one can infer a characteristic IGM temperature T_0 at the cosmic mean density as a function of redshift z.

In a homogeneous, isotropically expanding universe with scale factor a(t), a non-relativistic ideal gas that is thermally decoupled and undergoes no additional heating or cooling cools adiabatically as T ∝ a^{-2} ∝ (1+z)^2, so T_0(z) should decrease monotonically toward lower redshift in the absence of compensating heat sources.

Question: Does the IGM temperature T_0(z), as inferred from the small-scale cutoff of the Lyman-alpha forest flux power spectrum across the observable redshift range (roughly 2 ≲ z ≲ 5), evolve with redshift in a manner consistent with adiabatic cooling in an expanding Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker universe (possibly modified by photoionization heating during and after hydrogen and helium reionization, Compton cooling off the cosmic microwave background, and structure-formation shock heating)? Equivalently, can the observed redshift dependence of T_0 inferred from the Lyman-alpha forest be reproduced by a standard thermal-history model in an expanding universe, or does it require some non-standard explanation?
status_search_result: Recent measurements of the Lyman-alpha forest 1D flux power spectrum (e.g., Walther et al. 2019 and subsequent work) have constrained IGM thermal evolution from z ≈ 5.4 down to z ≈ 1.8 and find a redshift evolution of T_0 broadly consistent with standard thermal-history models that include hydrogen and helium reionization heating followed by cooling. Tensions remain at the highest redshifts (z ≳ 5) where inferred temperatures are lower than expected. The early claim of "no redshift evolution" has not been supported by later, more precise measurements; the question is largely resolved in favor of standard expanding-universe thermal histories, though detailed thermal modeling is ongoing.

paper_title: Observational Cosmology: caveats and open questions in the standard model
original_question: Are high-redshift quasars, or quasi-stellar objects, physically associated with and possibly ejected from nearby low-redshift active galaxies, with intrinsic or quantized redshift components, rather than lying at the large cosmological distances implied by their observed redshifts?
self_contained_problem:
Quasi-stellar objects (QSOs), commonly called quasars, are compact extragalactic sources whose optical spectra exhibit large redshifts z. Under the standard cosmological interpretation, these redshifts arise from the expansion of the Universe (Hubble flow), placing the QSOs at large cosmological distances. An alternative, non-standard hypothesis asserts that a significant population of high-redshift QSOs is physically associated with, and possibly has been ejected from, nearby low-redshift active galaxies, so that the QSOs lie at essentially the same distance as those host galaxies. Under this hypothesis a substantial part of an observed QSO redshift would be non-cosmological in origin, having an intrinsic component (for example, a discrete or "quantized" contribution depending only on the source), rather than being due to recessional motion.

Determine whether such physical QSO–galaxy associations exist as a generic phenomenon: that is, decide whether high-redshift QSOs found in apparent proximity (including cases showing morphological bridges or filamentary connections) to low-redshift active galaxies are genuinely physically associated with those galaxies and carry intrinsic/non-cosmological redshift components, or whether all such configurations are chance projections of background QSOs whose redshifts are purely cosmological.

paper_title: Observational Cosmology: caveats and open questions in the standard model
original_question: What physically coherent model of quasars at cosmological distances can jointly explain their required luminosities in compact variable regions, apparently superluminal radio motions, lack of expected time dilation, Faraday-rotation behavior with redshift, high metallicity and dust content at high redshift, and the failure or uniformity problems of damped Lyman-alpha absorber detections?
self_contained_problem:
Assume that quasi-stellar objects (QSOs) lie at the cosmological distances inferred from interpreting their observed spectral redshifts $z$ as due to the expansion of a Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker universe. Under this assumption, construct a single, physically self-consistent model of QSOs that simultaneously accounts for all of the following observational features:

1. The very high bolometric luminosities required of the compact, rapidly variable central emitting regions, given the short variability timescales (which constrain the emitting region's size via light-travel arguments).
2. The apparently superluminal transverse motions observed between radio-emitting components, i.e. angular separation rates $\omega$ that, when multiplied by the cosmological distance $D$, yield apparent transverse speeds $v_{\rm app}=D\omega>c$.
3. The apparent absence or strong attenuation of the expected cosmological time dilation by a factor $(1+z)$ in the temporal statistics of QSO light curves.
4. The observed dependence (or lack thereof) of Faraday rotation measures of QSO radio emission on redshift.
5. The presence of high metallicity and substantial dust content inferred for QSO environments at high redshift, despite the limited cosmic time available since the Big Bang for stellar nucleosynthesis and dust production.
6. The difficulties in directly imaging the galaxies hosting damped Lyman-$\alpha$ absorption systems seen in QSO spectra, together with the surprising uniformity of relative elemental abundances in these absorbers and the apparent constancy of their inferred temperatures with redshift.

Specify the model's geometric, dynamical, radiative, and statistical assumptions, and derive quantitative predictions matching each of (1)–(6) within current observational uncertainties.
status_search_result: No comprehensive, broadly accepted model has been published that jointly resolves all of the listed QSO anomalies; standard explanations address items individually (e.g. relativistic beaming for superluminal motion, AGN unified models for luminosity, early enrichment scenarios for high-z metallicity), but combined tensions concerning time dilation, DLA host non-detections, and abundance uniformity remain actively discussed.

paper_title: Observational Cosmology: caveats and open questions in the standard model
original_question: How can observations of particles with energies above 60 × 10^18 electron-volts be reconciled with the standard interpretation of the cosmic microwave background radiation, given that interactions with microwave-background photons impose a theoretical propagation limit for particles traveling more than about 20 to 50 megaparsecs?
self_contained_problem:
Cosmic-ray primaries arriving at Earth are observed with energies exceeding $E_{\rm GZK} \approx 6\times 10^{19}$ eV. According to the Greisen–Zatsepin–Kuzmin (GZK) argument, an ultra-high-energy proton (or nucleus) propagating through an isotropic blackbody radiation field at temperature $T \approx 2.725$ K (the cosmic microwave background, CMB) loses energy by photopion production $p + \gamma_{\rm CMB} \to p + \pi^0$ (or $\to n + \pi^+$), and analogous photodisintegration processes for nuclei. The energy-loss length for protons above this threshold is of order $20$–$50$ Mpc, so that any such primary originating at cosmological distances should be degraded below the threshold before reaching Earth.

Assuming
(i) the standard cosmological interpretation of the CMB as a relic blackbody bath filling all of space at $T \approx 2.725$ K,
(ii) standard-model particle physics governing the proton–photon (and nucleus–photon) cross sections, and
(iii) sources of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays distributed predominantly at extragalactic distances $\gg 50$ Mpc,

provide a quantitative, self-consistent mechanism that reconciles the observed flux of cosmic-ray events with energies above $6\times 10^{19}$ eV with the GZK propagation bound. A satisfactory answer should either:
(a) identify and characterize a population of sources within the GZK horizon ($\lesssim 100$ Mpc) capable of producing the observed integral flux, arrival-direction distribution, and mass composition; or
(b) specify modifications of propagation physics (e.g., new particles, Lorentz-invariance violation, or modified dispersion relations) that suppress the energy losses, while remaining consistent with all other CMB-related observations.
category_tag: Ultra-high-energy cosmic rays and the GZK cutoff
status_search_result: The expected flux suppression near the GZK energy has been confirmed at high significance by the Pierre Auger Observatory, HiRes, and Telescope Array, so the existence of events above the threshold is no longer in tension with the CMB interpretation per se. However, whether the observed suppression is fully due to the GZK effect or partly reflects the maximum acceleration energy at sources remains unsettled, and the mass composition reported by Auger (heavier) versus Telescope Array (lighter) is still under active debate. The problem of identifying the nearby sources of trans-GZK events is therefore only partially resolved.

paper_title: Observational Cosmology: caveats and open questions in the standard model
original_question: Can primordial Big Bang nucleosynthesis be tested without circularly choosing inferred primordial abundances and adjustable parameters, and can it consistently account for low reported helium mass fractions, uncertain deuterium evolution and production mechanisms, excessive beryllium abundances, baryon-density requirements, and the preference in some fits for two rather than three neutrino species?
self_contained_problem:
Standard Big Bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) predicts the primordial mass/number abundances of the light elements ⁴He, D, ³He, ⁷Li and ⁹Be as functions of the baryon-to-photon ratio η (equivalently the baryon density parameter Ω_b h²) and the effective number of light neutrino species N_ν, given the standard set of nuclear reaction rates and a Friedmann–Lemaître background.

Address the following methodological and empirical questions about this framework:

1. Can the predictions of standard BBN be confronted with observation in a non-circular way — that is, by genuine a priori predictions of light-element abundances that are tested against measurements, rather than by inferring "primordial" abundances from Population II (and similar) data under the assumption of the model whose parameters are simultaneously being adjusted?

2. Within a single choice of η (consistent with the baryon density determined independently, e.g. from the cosmic microwave background) and a fixed N_ν, can standard BBN simultaneously be made consistent with:
   (a) reports of a ⁴He mass fraction Y_p as low as ≈ 0.21 in very metal-poor galaxies,
   (b) the observed scatter and poorly-understood galactic chemical evolution and possible non-primordial production mechanisms of deuterium,
   (c) observed beryllium (⁹Be) abundances in metal-poor halo stars that appear in excess of standard predictions,
   (d) the baryon density required by CMB and large-scale structure data, and
   (e) the apparent preference of some abundance fits for N_ν ≈ 2 rather than the Standard Model value N_ν = 3?

Either exhibit a single consistent choice of parameters and astrophysical assumptions that reconciles (a)–(e), or prove that no such reconciliation is possible within standard BBN, identifying which item provides the obstruction.
status_search_result: As of 2025, standard BBN predictions for D and ⁴He show excellent agreement with high-precision observations and with the baryon density inferred from the CMB; N_ν = 3 is consistent with current data. The historical concerns about very low Y_p ≈ 0.21 have largely been retracted as observational systematics improved. The lithium-7 problem (and a milder deuterium-lithium tension) remains unresolved, with proposed astrophysical (stellar depletion, mixing) and exotic-physics solutions still under active investigation. Thus the methodological/empirical bundle is partially resolved: most items are settled in favor of standard BBN, while ⁷Li (and the methodological circularity concern in a strict sense) remain open.

paper_title: Observational Cosmology: caveats and open questions in the standard model
original_question: Why does the observable universe appear to be dominated by matter rather than containing equal amounts of matter and antimatter, if protons do not decay and standard physics would otherwise produce matter and antimatter equally, and if experiments have not yet found successful evidence for the required asymmetry while antimatter galaxies would create unseen gamma-ray boundaries?
self_contained_problem:
In the standard model of particle physics and cosmology, baryon number is effectively conserved at low energies (protons do not decay on observed timescales), and elementary interactions produce matter and antimatter in equal proportions. Yet the observable universe is overwhelmingly dominated by matter: distant galaxies cannot consist of antimatter, since a matter–antimatter interface with the intergalactic medium would yield characteristic gamma-ray annihilation signatures that are not observed, and known sources of CP violation are quantitatively insufficient to account for the observed baryon-to-photon ratio.

Problem. Identify a physical mechanism (within or beyond the standard model) that satisfies the three Sakharov conditions — (i) baryon number violation, (ii) C and CP violation, (iii) departure from thermal equilibrium — and which, applied to the early universe, quantitatively reproduces the observed cosmological baryon asymmetry

  η = (n_B − n_{ ar B}) / n_γ ≈ 6 × 10^{-10},

while remaining consistent with: (a) the experimental absence of proton decay, (b) measured magnitudes of CP violation in the quark and lepton sectors, and (c) the non-observation of gamma-ray signatures from large-scale matter–antimatter domain boundaries in the universe.
status_search_result: The origin of the baryon asymmetry of the universe (baryogenesis) remains an open problem in cosmology and particle physics. Standard Model CP violation is known to be insufficient, and proposed mechanisms (electroweak baryogenesis, leptogenesis, Affleck–Dine, GUT baryogenesis) remain unconfirmed experimentally as of 2026.

paper_title: Observational Cosmology: caveats and open questions in the standard model
original_question: Do the oldest Galactic stars truly have ages of 16–19 billion years or more, exceeding the standard cosmological age estimate of about 13.7 billion years, or are the stellar and cosmological age measurements still too inaccurate to establish a real conflict?
self_contained_problem:
Let $t_\star$ denote the age (in years) of the oldest stars in the Milky Way Galaxy, determined from stellar astrophysics (e.g., main-sequence turnoff fitting in globular clusters, white-dwarf cooling sequences, or nucleocosmochronology of metal-poor halo stars). Let $t_U$ denote the age of the Universe (in years), determined from cosmological observations within the standard $\Lambda$CDM framework (e.g., the cosmic microwave background, baryon acoustic oscillations, and Hubble-constant measurements), with a fiducial value near $t_U \approx 1.37 \times 10^{10}$ yr.

Determine which of the following holds:

(a) The oldest Galactic stars genuinely satisfy $t_\star \gtrsim 1.6\text{–}1.9 \times 10^{10}$ yr, so that $t_\star > t_U$ at a statistically significant level, indicating a real tension with the standard cosmological age estimate; or

(b) The current uncertainties in both the stellar age determinations and the cosmological age determination are large enough that the intervals for $t_\star$ and $t_U$ overlap, so that no statistically significant conflict can be established.

In other words, decide whether the inequality $t_\star > t_U$ holds at a meaningful confidence level given the best current observational and modeling uncertainties, or whether the apparent excess of stellar ages over the cosmological age is consistent with measurement and modeling errors.
status_search_result: Subsequent measurements have effectively resolved the apparent conflict. Early Hipparcos-era estimates giving ages of 16–19 Gyr for the oldest halo stars (e.g., HD 140283) have been revised downward with improved parallaxes (HST, Gaia), updated stellar-evolution models, and better treatment of uncertainties. Current best estimates for the oldest Galactic stars are about 13.8 ± 0.4 Gyr, consistent within errors with the Planck cosmological age of 13.787 ± 0.020 Gyr. The consensus is that the stellar and cosmological ages now agree within uncertainties, so no real conflict is established.

paper_title: (Two) Open Questions in Stellar Nuclear Physics
context_brief: S34(0) precision for the 4He(3He,γ)7Be solar-model reaction
original_question: How can the astrophysical cross-section factor S34(0) for the 4He(3He,γ)7Be reaction be measured with the high precision needed for the Standard Solar Model, given that it remains poorly known with a 9% error and must be improved before direct detection of 7Be solar neutrinos and high-precision prediction of all solar neutrino fluxes?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the radiative capture reaction $^{4}\mathrm{He}(^{3}\mathrm{He},\gamma)^{7}\mathrm{Be}$, which is a key branch in the proton–proton chain that fuels stars such as the Sun and produces $^{7}\mathrm{Be}$ (and subsequently $^{8}\mathrm{B}$) solar neutrinos. For a non-resonant charged-particle reaction with center-of-mass energy $E$, cross section $\sigma(E)$, and Sommerfeld parameter $\eta(E)$, the astrophysical S-factor is defined by
$$S(E)=E\,\sigma(E)\,\exp(2\pi\eta(E)),$$
and $S_{34}(0)$ denotes the zero-energy extrapolation of $S(E)$ for the $^{4}\mathrm{He}(^{3}\mathrm{He},\gamma)^{7}\mathrm{Be}$ reaction. The Standard Solar Model requires $S_{34}(0)$ to be known to an accuracy of 5% or better in order to enable precision predictions of the $^{7}\mathrm{Be}$ and $^{8}\mathrm{B}$ solar neutrino fluxes; at the time the question was posed, $S_{34}(0)$ was known only to about 9%, with a long-standing $\sim 3\sigma$ discrepancy between determinations based on prompt $\gamma$-ray detection and those based on $^{7}\mathrm{Be}$ activity measurements.

Problem: Devise an experimental and/or theoretical program that determines $S_{34}(0)$ for the $^{4}\mathrm{He}(^{3}\mathrm{He},\gamma)^{7}\mathrm{Be}$ reaction with a total (statistical plus systematic) uncertainty of 5% or less, and resolves the discrepancy between the prompt-$\gamma$ and activation methods.
status_search_result: Significant progress has been made since the question was posed. LUNA underground measurements (e.g., Confortola et al. 2007) and the ERNA recoil-separator experiments produced new high-precision determinations of S34(0) using both prompt-gamma and activation methods, reconciling the previous discrepancy and yielding values near 0.56 keV·b with ~4–5% total uncertainty. Recent ab initio and effective field theory calculations (2024–2025) further refine the value. Thus the original 9% precision goal has effectively been reached for the 5% target, although community-recommended uncertainty quotations still hover at the 4–6% level and refinements continue.

paper_title: Some Open Problems in Matrix Theory Arising in Linear Systems and Control
context_brief: robust stability certification by a test subset
original_question: Given a collection M of real n x n matrices, determine a subset M_0 subseteq M with the property that if every matrix in M_0 is stable, meaning that all of its eigenvalues have negative real part, then every matrix in M is stable. The source highlights this as a fundamental robust-stability problem for uncertain linear-system models and asks for such certifying subsets beyond the polynomial cases covered by Kharitonov-type results.
self_contained_problem: A real n×n matrix A is called (Hurwitz) stable if every eigenvalue of A has negative real part. Let M be a family (in general infinite) of real n×n matrices. A subset M_0 ⊆ M is called a stability-certifying subset for M if the following implication holds: whenever every matrix in M_0 is stable, every matrix in M is stable.\n\nProblem. Develop a general theory that, for natural classes of matrix families M ⊆ R^{n×n} (for example, families defined by interval, polytopic, affine, or other structured parametric uncertainty), identifies an explicit stability-certifying subset M_0 ⊆ M, preferably finite or of small cardinality. In particular, for classes of matrix families that go beyond those arising from interval polynomials (where Kharitonov-type results provide a four-element certifying set in coefficient space), characterize when such certifying subsets exist and how they may be constructed.
status_search_result: For matrix families this problem remains largely open. While Kharitonov-style results provide finite certifying subsets at the level of interval polynomials, and certain "edge" and "vertex" extreme-point theorems exist for restricted classes (e.g., interval polynomial matrices with structured row/column dependence), counterexamples are known showing that for general interval matrices the four "vertex" or "extreme" matrices do not suffice. No general construction of stability-certifying subsets for arbitrary matrix families is known.

paper_title: Some Open Problems in Matrix Theory Arising in Linear Systems and Control
original_question: Let A and B be square matrices with algebraic entries. If exp(A) exp(B) = exp(A + B), must A and B commute? The source notes that commutativity is known under the stronger hypothesis exp(A) exp(B) = exp(B) exp(A) for algebraic matrices, but states that the case exp(A) exp(B) = exp(A + B) remains open.
self_contained_problem:
Let $A, B \in M_n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ be square matrices of the same size whose entries are algebraic numbers (i.e., roots of nonzero polynomials with rational coefficients). For a square matrix $X$, define the matrix exponential by the convergent series $\exp(X) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{X^k}{k!}$. Suppose that
$$\exp(A)\,\exp(B) \;=\; \exp(A+B).$$
Must it follow that $A$ and $B$ commute, i.e., $AB = BA$?

(For context: it is known that if instead $\exp(A)\exp(B) = \exp(B)\exp(A)$ and the entries of $A, B$ are algebraic, then $AB = BA$. The question above replaces this commutativity-of-exponentials hypothesis by the additivity hypothesis $\exp(A)\exp(B) = \exp(A+B)$.)

The related result that $\exp(A)\exp(B)=\exp(B)\exp(A)$ implies $AB=BA$ for algebraic matrices is established, and de Seguins Pazzis (2012) proved commutativity under the stronger hypothesis that $\exp(A)^k \exp(B)^\ell = \exp(kA+\ell B)$ for all integers $k,\ell$. The single-equation case $\exp(A)\exp(B)=\exp(A+B)$ for algebraic matrices appears to remain open.

paper_title: Some Open Problems in Matrix Theory Arising in Linear Systems and Control
context_brief: deriving exponential inequalities from expansion formulas

self_contained_problem:
Setting. Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A,B\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ with $A,B$ Hermitian (so that $A+B$ and $\exp(A)\exp(B)$ make sense and the relevant traces and eigenvalues are real). For a square matrix $M$, write $\mathrm{tr}(M)$ for its trace, $\lambda_{\max}(M)$ for the largest (real) eigenvalue when it exists, $M^{T}$ for the transpose, and $\exp(M)=\sum_{k\ge 0} M^{k}/k!$ for the matrix exponential.

Three classical structural identities for the matrix exponential of a sum are available:

(F1) The Lie–Trotter product formula:
$$\exp(A+B)=\lim_{m\to\infty}\bigl(\exp(A/m)\exp(B/m)\bigr)^{m}.$$

(F2) The Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff series:
$$\exp(A)\exp(B)=\exp\!\Bigl(A+B+\tfrac12[A,B]+\tfrac1{12}[A,[A,B]]-\tfrac1{12}[B,[A,B]]+\cdots\Bigr),$$
where $[X,Y]=XY-YX$.

(F3) The Feynman/time-ordered "disentangling" identity:
$$\exp(A+B)=\exp(A)\,\mathcal{T}\exp\!\Bigl(\int_{0}^{1}e^{-tA}Be^{tA}\,dt\Bigr),$$
or equivalently
$$\exp(A+B)=\exp(A)+\int_{0}^{1}\exp\!\bigl((1-s)(A+B)\bigr)\,B\,\exp(sA)\,ds.$$

Three inequalities of interest are:

(I1) Golden–Thompson: for all Hermitian $A,B$,
$$\mathrm{tr}\bigl(\exp(A+B)\bigr)\;\le\;\mathrm{tr}\bigl(\exp(A)\exp(B)\bigr).$$

(I2) For every real square matrix $A$,
$$\mathrm{tr}\bigl(\exp(A)\exp(A^{T})\bigr)\;\le\;\mathrm{tr}\bigl(\exp(A+A^{T})\bigr).$$

(I3) For every real square matrix $A$,
$$\lambda_{\max}\bigl(\exp(A)\exp(A^{T})\bigr)\;\le\;\lambda_{\max}\bigl(\exp(A+A^{T})\bigr).$$

Question. Can the three inequalities (I1), (I2), (I3) be derived directly — by purely algebraic/analytic manipulation, without invoking auxiliary tools such as the Lieb concavity theorem, log-majorization, or analytic interpolation arguments — from one of the structural expansion formulas (F1), (F2), or (F3)? In particular, does formula (F3) admit a term-by-term comparison that yields each of (I1)–(I3)?
status_search_result: The Golden–Thompson inequality (I1) has many known proofs (Lie–Trotter plus log-majorization, complex interpolation, pinching, etc.), but the specific question of whether all three inequalities (I1)–(I3) can be obtained as direct consequences of a single structural expansion formula such as Lie–Trotter, Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff, or the Feynman/time-ordered disentangling identity does not appear to have a definitive resolution in the literature. The inequalities (I2)–(I3) involving $A$ and $A^{T}$ are less standard and no derivation explicitly via these expansion formulas was located. Status appears unresolved.

paper_title: Some Open Problems in Matrix Theory Arising in Linear Systems and Control
context_brief: whether the H2 norm is induced
original_question: Do there exist normed spaces D and E for which the H_2 norm of a linear-system transfer function is an induced operator norm? The source asks whether one can realize the H_2 performance measure as a true induced norm between suitable signal spaces rather than only as an energy-like quantity.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G(s)$ be a strictly proper, stable rational matrix-valued transfer function on the open right half-plane, viewed as an element of the Hardy space $H_2$ with norm
$$\|G\|_{H_2} := \left(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \operatorname{tr}\bigl(G(j\omega)^* G(j\omega)\bigr)\,d\omega\right)^{1/2}.$$
Equivalently, if $G$ is the transfer function of a linear time-invariant input/output operator $\mathcal{G}:u\mapsto y$, the $H_2$ norm coincides with the $L_2$ norm of the impulse response.

Question: Do there exist normed signal spaces $(D,\|\cdot\|_D)$ and $(E,\|\cdot\|_E)$, together with a realization of $\mathcal{G}$ as a bounded linear operator $\mathcal{G}:D\to E$, such that
$$\|G\|_{H_2} \;=\; \|\mathcal{G}\|_{D\to E} \;:=\; \sup_{u\in D,\;u\neq 0}\frac{\|\mathcal{G}u\|_E}{\|u\|_D}\,?$$
That is, can the $H_2$ performance measure be expressed as a genuine induced (operator) norm of $\mathcal{G}$ between suitable normed spaces of input and output signals?
category_tag: H2 norm and induced operator norms in control
status_search_result: Standard references state that the $H_\infty$ norm of an LTI system is an induced ($L_2\to L_2$) norm, whereas the $H_2$ norm is usually described only as an "energy" or stochastic measure and not as an induced norm in the classical sense. A targeted web search did not turn up a published result either constructing such normed spaces $D,E$ that induce the $H_2$ norm or proving that no such pair exists, so the status of this specific question is unclear from available sources.

original_question: For matrix norms that satisfy submultiplicativity or mixed submultiplicativity, determine whether such norms must be induced norms or whether some of them cannot be induced. The source explicitly asks for a structural characterization of inducedness within these broader multiplicative classes.

Let $\mathbb{F}\in\{\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}\}$ and, for each pair $(m,n)$ of positive integers, let $\|\cdot\|_{m,n}$ be a norm on the space $\mathbb{F}^{m	imes n}$ of $m	imes n$ matrices. The family $\{\|\cdot\|_{m,n}\}$ is called:

(a) submultiplicative if for all positive integers $m,p,n$ and all $A\in\mathbb{F}^{m	imes p}$, $B\in\mathbb{F}^{p	imes n}$,
$$\|AB\|_{m,n}\le \|A\|_{m,p}\,\|B\|_{p,n};$$

(b) mixed submultiplicative if there exist norms $\|\cdot\|_{m,n}$, $\|\cdot\|'_{m,p}$, $\|\cdot\|''_{p,n}$ (possibly distinct) such that for all compatible $A,B$,
$$\|AB\|_{m,n}\le \|A\|'_{m,p}\,\|B\|''_{p,n}.$$

A family of matrix norms $\{\|\cdot\|_{m,n}\}$ is called induced (operator) if there exist vector norms $
u_k$ on $\mathbb{F}^k$ for every $k\ge 1$ such that
$$\|A\|_{m,n}=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{F}^n\setminus\{0\}} rac{
u_m(Ax)}{
u_n(x)}$$
for every $A\in\mathbb{F}^{m	imes n}$.

Give a structural characterization that determines, for an arbitrary submultiplicative (resp. mixed submultiplicative) family of matrix norms, whether the family must be an induced family or whether it cannot be realized as an induced family. Equivalently, provide necessary and sufficient conditions on the family $\{\|\cdot\|_{m,n}\}$ for the existence (or nonexistence) of vector norms $\{

paper_title: Some Open Problems in Matrix Theory Arising in Linear Systems and Control
original_question: For the decentralized static controller with block-diagonal gains u_i(t) = K_i y_i(t) across r feedback channels, determine when there exist gains K_1, ..., K_r such that the closed-loop matrix A + sum_i B_i K_i C_i is stable. The source frames this as the decentralized analogue of centralized output-feedback stabilization and states that the available theory is incomplete.
self_contained_problem:
Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$, and for $i=1,\dots,r$ let $B_i \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times m_i}$ and $C_i \in \mathbb{R}^{p_i\times n}$ be given matrices. Consider the linear time-invariant system
$$\dot x(t) = A x(t) + \sum_{i=1}^{r} B_i u_i(t), \qquad y_i(t) = C_i x(t), \quad i=1,\dots,r,$$
together with the decentralized static output-feedback control law
$$u_i(t) = K_i\, y_i(t), \qquad K_i \in \mathbb{R}^{m_i \times p_i}, \quad i=1,\dots,r.$$
The resulting closed-loop dynamics matrix is
$$A_{\mathrm{cl}}(K_1,\dots,K_r) \;=\; A + \sum_{i=1}^{r} B_i K_i C_i.$$
A square real matrix is called (Hurwitz) stable if all of its eigenvalues have strictly negative real part.

Problem. Give verifiable necessary and sufficient conditions on the data $(A, B_1,\dots,B_r, C_1,\dots,C_r)$ for the existence of gain matrices $K_1,\dots,K_r$ such that $A_{\mathrm{cl}}(K_1,\dots,K_r)$ is stable. Equivalently, characterize the class of multi-channel triples $\{(A,B_i,C_i)\}_{i=1}^{r}$ that are stabilizable by decentralized static output feedback with block-diagonal gain structure.
status_search_result: Decentralized static output-feedback stabilization remains an open problem in control theory. Even the centralized static output-feedback stabilization problem (r=1) does not have a tractable necessary and sufficient verifiable characterization; only sufficient LMI/BMI conditions, iterative algorithms, and partial characterizations (e.g., via fixed modes for the decentralized case) are known. No general computationally verifiable necessary and sufficient condition has been established.

paper_title: Some Open Problems in Matrix Theory Arising in Linear Systems and Control
original_question: Characterize, and ideally parameterize, the full set of feedback gains that stabilize a given linear system under the output-feedback structures discussed in the source. Such a parameterization should make it possible to optimize additional design criteria once stabilization is achieved.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a finite-dimensional linear time-invariant control system
  x'(t) = A x(t) + B u(t),  y(t) = C x(t),
where A ∈ ℝ^{n×n}, B ∈ ℝ^{n×m}, C ∈ ℝ^{p×n}, and a static output-feedback law u(t) = K y(t) with K ∈ ℝ^{m×p}. The closed-loop system matrix is A + B K C, and the feedback gain K is called stabilizing if every eigenvalue of A + B K C has strictly negative real part. Define the stabilizing set
  𝒮(A,B,C) = { K ∈ ℝ^{m×p} : A + B K C is Hurwitz }.

Problem: Give an explicit characterization, and ideally an explicit parameterization, of the set 𝒮(A,B,C) for general triples (A,B,C). That is, find a (preferably finite-dimensional) parameter space Θ and a map Φ: Θ → ℝ^{m×p} whose image equals 𝒮(A,B,C), and such that Φ is amenable to further optimization (so that, once stabilization is guaranteed, secondary design criteria such as performance, robustness, or minimal gain can be optimized over Θ).

Equivalently, determine necessary and sufficient conditions on a matrix K ∈ ℝ^{m×p} for K ∈ 𝒮(A,B,C), expressed in a form that exposes the geometric/algebraic structure of 𝒮(A,B,C) (e.g., its connected components, its closure, and free vs. dependent parameters).
status_search_result: The problem of characterizing and parameterizing the set of stabilizing static output feedback gains is widely regarded as a long-standing open problem in linear systems and control. It is known to be NP-hard in general, and the feasible set is typically non-convex and can be disconnected. Partial results exist (LMI/Riccati-based sufficient conditions, dissipative-Hamiltonian parameterizations, H∞ state-feedback parameterizations, iterative LMI methods), but no general explicit parameterization of the full stabilizing set is known.

paper_title: Some Open Problems in Matrix Theory Arising in Linear Systems and Control
context_brief: coupled equations for optimal static output feedback
original_question: Understand the existence, uniqueness, and qualitative solution properties of the coupled matrix equations (6.24)-(6.25) that characterize optimal static output feedback when only partial noise-free measurements y(t) = C x(t) are available. Equivalently, solve the underlying optimal static output-feedback problem in a way that clarifies when the coupled equations admit meaningful positive semidefinite solutions.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the linear time-invariant stochastic system
  dx(t)/dt = A x(t) + B u(t) + w(t),  y(t) = C x(t),
where x(t) ∈ ℝⁿ is the state, u(t) ∈ ℝᵐ is the control input, y(t) ∈ ℝᵖ is the measured output (a noise-free partial measurement), and w(t) is zero-mean white noise with intensity V = Vᵀ ≥ 0. Let Q = Qᵀ ≥ 0 and R = Rᵀ > 0 be given weighting matrices, and assume (A,B) is stabilizable and (A,C) is detectable.

Consider the static output feedback control law u(t) = K y(t), K ∈ ℝ^{m×p}, and the associated infinite-horizon quadratic cost
  J(K) = lim_{t→∞} E[ x(t)ᵀ Q x(t) + u(t)ᵀ R u(t) ],
defined whenever A + BKC is Hurwitz.

Standard first-order necessary conditions for K to minimize J over the set of stabilizing static output-feedback gains take the form of the coupled matrix equations
  (E1)  0 = (A + BKC)ᵀ P + P (A + BKC) + Q + Cᵀ Kᵀ R K C,
  (E2)  0 = (A + BKC) S + S (A + BKC)ᵀ + V,
  (E3)  0 = R K C S Cᵀ − Bᵀ P S Cᵀ,
in the unknowns P = Pᵀ ≥ 0, S = Sᵀ ≥ 0, and K ∈ ℝ^{m×p}.

Problem. Establish a complete theory of these coupled equations:
(a) Give verifiable necessary and sufficient conditions on (A, B, C, Q, R, V) under which the system (E1)–(E3) admits a solution (P, S, K) with P, S positive semidefinite and A + BKC Hurwitz.
(b) Characterize uniqueness, multiplicity, and the structure of the solution set, and determine which solutions correspond to the global minimum of J(K).
(c) Equivalently, solve the underlying optimal static output-feedback problem: characterize the existence, uniqueness, and qualitative properties of a globally optimal stabilizing gain K* minimizing J(K), and relate K* to solutions of (E1)–(E3).

status_search_result: The optimal static output feedback problem and the associated coupled Riccati–Lyapunov optimality equations are widely regarded as a long-standing open problem in control theory. paper_title: Some Open Problems in Matrix Theory Arising in Linear Systems and Control
context_brief: indefinite Riccati equations in H-infinity control
original_question: Develop general existence and structural results for the indefinite algebraic Riccati equation A^T P + P A - P Sigma P + gamma^{-2} P V_1 P + R_{1,\infty} = 0 that arises in full-state-feedback H_infinity control. In this equation the quadratic term P (gamma^{-2} V_1 - Sigma) P may be indefinite, and the source notes that, aside from limited prior work, virtually no theory is available for such equations.
self_contained_problem:
Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$, let $\Sigma, V_1, R_{1,\infty} \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be symmetric matrices, and let $\gamma > 0$ be a real parameter. Consider the indefinite continuous-time algebraic Riccati equation
$$A^{T} P + P A - P\,\Sigma\, P + \gamma^{-2} P\, V_1\, P + R_{1,\infty} = 0$$
for a symmetric matrix $P \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$. Equivalently, with $Q := \gamma^{-2} V_1 - \Sigma$, the quadratic term takes the form $P\,Q\,P$, where $Q$ is permitted to be indefinite (i.e., $Q$ need not be positive semidefinite or negative semidefinite).

Develop a general theory for such indefinite algebraic Riccati equations. Specifically:

(a) Give necessary and sufficient conditions on the data $(A, \Sigma, V_1, R_{1,\infty}, \gamma)$ for the existence of a real symmetric solution $P$, and for the existence of a stabilizing solution (one for which $A - \Sigma P + \gamma^{-2} V_1 P$ is Hurwitz).

(b) Describe the structure of the set of all real symmetric solutions, including ordering properties, extremal solutions, and the dependence of solutions on the parameter $\gamma$.

(c) Provide structural characterizations (e.g., via Hamiltonian or symplectic matrices, invariant Lagrangian subspaces, or matrix pencils) that account for the indefiniteness of $Q$.

The objective is a unified existence and structural theory comparable to that available for the classical (definite) algebraic Riccati equation.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made on indefinite algebraic Riccati equations arising in H-infinity control since the problem was posed. Results include existence theorems for positive semidefinite and sign-indefinite stabilizing solutions via Hamiltonian/eigenvalue tests (Scherer; Wimmer), characterizations through invariant Lagrangian subspaces in indefinite inner product spaces (Ran-Rodman and others), and Popov-function factorization approaches. However, a fully general theory comparable to the definite case is not yet complete, and the problem is typically regarded as only partially resolved.

paper_title: Open Problems Related to Algebraic Attacks on Stream Ciphers
original_question: For the same algebraic-attack system built from the equations g∘L^t(x_0)=0 and h∘L^t(x_0)=0 arising from low-degree annihilators of f and 1+f in a stream cipher with linear state transition L and output s_t=f(L^t(x_0)), determine how the rank of that system depends on the choice of the transition map L and the filtering function f.
self_contained_problem:
Let n be a positive integer and let L: F_2^n → F_2^n be an F_2-linear map (the state transition). Let f: F_2^n → F_2 be a Boolean function (the filtering function). For an unknown initial state x_0 ∈ F_2^n, the keystream is defined by s_t = f(L^t(x_0)) for t = 0, 1, 2, ….

For a Boolean function f, define its annihilator set
   AN(f) = { g: F_2^n → F_2 : f·g = 0 identically on F_2^n }.
Fix a positive integer d. Let G_d = {g_1, …, g_r} be a basis of the F_2-vector space of functions of degree at most d in AN(f), and let H_d = {h_1, …, h_s} be a basis of the F_2-vector space of functions of degree at most d in AN(1+f).

Suppose N keystream bits s_0, …, s_{N-1} have been observed. Form the algebraic system in the unknown x_0 ∈ F_2^n consisting of:
   • g_i(L^t(x_0)) = 0    for every t ∈ {0,…,N-1} with s_t = 1 and every g_i ∈ G_d,
   • h_j(L^t(x_0)) = 0    for every t ∈ {0,…,N-1} with s_t = 0 and every h_j ∈ H_d.

After linearization (treating each monomial in x_0 of degree at most d as an independent unknown), this becomes a linear system over F_2 in M = Σ_{k=0}^{d} C(n,k) unknowns.

Problem: Determine the rank of this linearized system as a function of the choice of the linear transition map L and the filtering function f (and, where relevant, of d and N).
status_search_result: The problem of determining the rank of the linearized algebraic-attack system in terms of L and f was posed as an open problem in Canteaut's 2005/2006 survey of open problems in algebraic attacks on stream ciphers. Subsequent literature on algebraic immunity, annihilators, and algebraic attacks (e.g., follow-up works on AI(f) and recent algebraic attacks on nonlinear filter generators) addresses related complexity and immunity questions, but no source found provides a general formula or characterization of the rank as a function of L and f. The problem appears to remain open in general.

original_question: For balanced Boolean functions of n variables, determine what proportion of them attain optimal algebraic immunity, meaning the maximum algebraic immunity allowed for that number of variables.
self_contained_problem:
Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $\mathcal{B}_n$ denote the set of Boolean functions $f:\mathbb{F}_2^n \to \mathbb{F}_2$. For $f \in \mathcal{B}_n$, the algebraic immunity $\mathrm{AI}(f)$ is defined as the smallest positive integer $d$ such that there exists a nonzero function $g \in \mathcal{B}_n$ of algebraic degree at most $d$ with $fg = 0$ or $(f \oplus 1)g = 0$; equivalently, $\mathrm{AI}(f)$ is the minimum degree of a nonzero annihilator of $f$ or of $f \oplus 1$. It is known that $\mathrm{AI}(f) \leq \lceil n/2 \rceil$ for every $f \in \mathcal{B}_n$, and a function attaining this bound is said to have optimal algebraic immunity. A Boolean function $f$ is balanced if $|\{x \in \mathbb{F}_2^n : f(x) = 1\}| = 2^{n-1}$. Let $B_n$ denote the set of balanced Boolean functions of $n$ variables, and let $B_n^* \subseteq B_n$ denote the subset of those that have optimal algebraic immunity. Determine the proportion
$$ \rho(n) \;=\; \frac{|B_n^*|}{|B_n|}, $$
and in particular describe its asymptotic behavior as $n \to \infty$.
status_search_result: A web search reveals extensive literature on constructions of balanced Boolean functions achieving optimal algebraic immunity, but no result giving the exact proportion or its asymptotic value among all balanced n-variable Boolean functions. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open Problems Related to Algebraic Attacks on Stream Ciphers
original_question: For a multi-output Boolean function, and in particular for augmented functions whose Boolean output components are all linearly equivalent, does that linear equivalence among the output components affect the algebraic immunity of the multi-output function?
self_contained_problem:
Let $F:\mathbb{F}_2^n \to \mathbb{F}_2^m$ be a multi-output Boolean function with coordinate functions $f_1,\dots,f_m:\mathbb{F}_2^n\to\mathbb{F}_2$. Two Boolean functions $g,h:\mathbb{F}_2^n\to\mathbb{F}_2$ are called linearly equivalent if there exists an invertible linear map $L\in GL_n(\mathbb{F}_2)$ such that $h(x)=g(Lx)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{F}_2^n$. The algebraic immunity of $F$, denoted $\mathrm{AI}(F)$, is defined as the minimum algebraic degree of a nonzero Boolean function $g:\mathbb{F}_2^{n+m}\to\mathbb{F}_2$ that vanishes on the graph $\{(x,F(x)) : x\in\mathbb{F}_2^n\}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_2^{n+m}$ (equivalently, the minimum degree of any nonzero annihilator of the indicator of the graph of $F$).

A motivating example is the augmented function associated with a stream cipher: if $S:\mathbb{F}_2^n\to\mathbb{F}_2^n$ is the state-update function and $f:\mathbb{F}_2^n\to\mathbb{F}_2$ is the filtering function, the augmented function $F_m(x)=(f(x),f(S(x)),\dots,f(S^{m-1}(x)))$ has all of its output coordinate functions linearly equivalent to one another (when $S$ is linear).

Question: Does the existence of pairwise linear equivalences among all output coordinate functions $f_1,\dots,f_m$ of a multi-output Boolean function $F$ influence (constrain, increase, or decrease) the algebraic immunity $\mathrm{AI}(F)$? More precisely, is there a non-trivial bound or structural property relating $\mathrm{AI}(F)$ to the property that $f_1,\dots,f_m$ are all in the same linear-equivalence class?
status_search_result: Web search turned up follow-up work characterizing algebraic immunity for multi-output Boolean functions (e.g., Armknecht–Krause constructions, IACR ePrint 2012/338) and noting that algebraic immunity is not invariant under affine transformations on the outputs but is invariant under linear transformations on the inputs. However, no source was found that directly resolves whether linear equivalence among all output components of a multi-output function influences its algebraic immunity. The question therefore appears not to have a definitive published resolution.

paper_title: Classification of Finite Groups: Recent Developements and Open Problems
context_brief: orders with at most five prime factors
original_question: Determine, up to isomorphism, the finite groups whose order has at most five prime factors, extending the existing complete classification for the case of at most four prime factors. An especially important part of the problem is whether this extension can be achieved by symbolic computation rather than only by case distinctions and hand calculations, so that the resulting method is more efficient.
self_contained_problem:
For a positive integer n, let Ω(n) denote the number of prime factors of n counted with multiplicity, so that if n = p_1^{a_1} p_2^{a_2} ... p_k^{a_k} is the prime factorization, then Ω(n) = a_1 + a_2 + ... + a_k. A complete classification (up to isomorphism) is known for all finite groups whose order n satisfies Ω(n) ≤ 4; these correspond to the orders of the forms p^4, p^3 q, p^2 q r, p^2 q^2, and p q r s (with p, q, r, s distinct primes), and was obtained through case distinctions and hand calculations.

The problem is the following:

(a) Provide a complete classification, up to isomorphism, of all finite groups whose order n satisfies Ω(n) ≤ 5. Equivalently, classify the finite groups whose order has one of the forms p^5, p^4 q, p^3 q^2, p^3 q r, p^2 q^2 r, p^2 q r s, or p q r s t, where p, q, r, s, t are distinct primes.

(b) Determine whether this classification can be carried out via a symbolic-computation method (yielding an algorithm that, for any allowed factorization type, produces a list of isomorphism class representatives) rather than by ad hoc case distinctions, in such a way that the resulting procedure is more efficient than direct hand analysis.
status_search_result: The classification of finite groups whose order has at most 4 prime factors (counted with multiplicity) is known (work by Dietrich and collaborators). No source found indicating that the analogous classification for at most 5 prime factors has been completed in general; it remains posed as an open problem, including the question of an efficient symbolic-computation approach.

paper_title: Classification of Finite Groups: Recent Developements and Open Problems
original_question: Determine all groups of order p^8, for a prime p, up to isomorphism. The paper describes this as a highly challenging classification problem and indicates that any successful solution should rely on computational methods together with symbolic computation.
self_contained_problem: For a prime number $p$, classify, up to isomorphism, all finite groups of order $p^8$. That is, produce a complete and irredundant list of isomorphism class representatives of groups $G$ with $|G| = p^8$, parametrized by $p$, together with explicit presentations (for example, power–commutator presentations) for each isomorphism type.
status_search_result: The full classification of all groups of order $p^8$ for general primes $p$ remains open. paper_title: Euclidean random matrices: solved and open problems
context_brief: Spontaneous supersymmetry breaking and its physical effects
original_question: Within the same Euclidean random-matrix framework, does there exist a phase in which the BRST-type supersymmetry is spontaneously broken, and if such a phase exists, what physical effects follow from that supersymmetry breaking for the spectrum and related observables of the system?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Euclidean random matrix framework defined as follows. Let $x_1,\dots,x_N$ be i.i.d. random points distributed in a region of $\mathbb{R}^d$ with density $\rho$, and let $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ be a fixed (typically smooth, translation-invariant) function. The associated Euclidean random matrix $M$ is the $N\times N$ symmetric matrix with entries $M_{ij}=f(x_i-x_j)$ (or its translation-invariant variant $M_{ij}=\delta_{ij}\sum_k f(x_i-x_k)-f(x_i-x_j)$). The spectral problem for $M$, after introducing bosonic and fermionic (ghost) replicas or superfield variables, admits a BRST-type global supersymmetry that relates the bosonic and fermionic sectors of the effective field-theoretic representation of the resolvent and density of states.

Questions:
(a) Does there exist a region of parameter space (e.g., values of the density $\rho$, the function $f$, or the dimension $d$) in which this BRST-type supersymmetry is spontaneously broken, in the sense that the ground state of the associated effective action fails to be invariant under the BRST charge while the action itself is?
(b) If such a phase exists, determine the physical consequences of this spontaneous supersymmetry breaking for observable quantities of the random matrix ensemble, including: the spectral density of $M$ (in particular, the appearance or modification of band edges, tails, or Lifshitz-type singularities), the localization/delocalization properties of eigenvectors, the behavior of the resolvent and its analytic structure, and the relations (Ward identities) between bosonic and fermionic correlators that follow from or are violated by the breaking.
status_search_result: A web search returns general references on BRST supersymmetry, supersymmetric methods for random matrices, and spontaneous SUSY breaking in matrix models, but no source was located that decisively settles whether the BRST-type supersymmetry of the Euclidean random matrix framework admits a spontaneously broken phase and characterizes its physical effects. The problem appears to remain open or unresolved in the literature accessible by the search.

paper_title: XXX Spin Chain: from Bethe Solution to Open Problems
original_question: Consider the XXZ spin chain with Hamiltonian H_XXZ in the gapped antiferromagnetic regime Δ < -1. In this regime the entropy S(ρ(n)) of a block of n neighboring spins in the ground state is expected to converge, as n becomes large, to a finite limiting value S(∞). Determine analytically this limiting subsystem entropy S(∞) for the XXZ spin chain when the block size tends to infinity.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the spin-1/2 XXZ Heisenberg chain on the infinite lattice Z with Hamiltonian
  H_{XXZ} = - sum_{j in Z} ( S^x_j S^x_{j+1} + S^y_j S^y_{j+1} + Δ S^z_j S^z_{j+1} ),
where S^x, S^y, S^z = (1/2) σ^{x,y,z} are spin-1/2 operators, and assume the gapped antiferromagnetic regime Δ < -1. Let |GS> be a ground state of H_{XXZ} (in the thermodynamic limit), and for a contiguous block A_n = {1, 2, ..., n} of n neighboring sites let
  ρ(n) = Tr_{Z \ A_n} |GS><GS|
be the reduced density matrix on A_n. Define the von Neumann subsystem entropy
  S(ρ(n)) = - Tr( ρ(n) log ρ(n) ).
Since the model is gapped, S(ρ(n)) tends to a finite limit S(∞) = lim_{n → ∞} S(ρ(n)).

Determine S(∞) analytically as an explicit function of the anisotropy parameter Δ < -1.
category_tag: Entanglement entropy in integrable spin chains
status_search_result: The limiting block entropy of the gapped antiferromagnetic XXZ chain has been computed analytically using the corner transfer matrix method, by relating ρ(n) (in the n → ∞ limit) to the corner transfer matrix of the six/eight-vertex model. The exact expression for S(∞) as a function of Δ < -1 is given in closed form involving the elliptic nome / modular parameter associated with Δ; see Calabrese, Ercolessi, Evangelisti, Ravanini and related work, as well as the corner-transfer-matrix treatment of the XYZ chain whose sine-Gordon / XXZ limit yields the XXZ result.

paper_title: XXX Spin Chain: from Bethe Solution to Open Problems
original_question: For the six-vertex model with domain wall boundary conditions, compute the correlation functions both in the bulk and at the boundary. The difficulty is that this model lacks translation invariance, although some determinant representations and boundary results are already known near the boundary.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the six-vertex model on an N×N square lattice with domain wall boundary conditions (DWBC): on each edge place an arrow so that at every internal vertex the ice rule holds (two arrows in, two arrows out), and on the boundary all horizontal arrows on the left and right sides point inward while all vertical arrows on the top and bottom sides point outward (or equivalently, the standard DWBC configuration). Assign Boltzmann weights a, b, c to the six allowed vertex configurations in the usual symmetric way, so that the partition function Z_N(a,b,c) admits the Izergin–Korepin determinant representation.

Define, for a finite collection of lattice edges or vertices, the corresponding (multi-point) correlation function as the weighted statistical average of the indicators of prescribed local arrow/vertex configurations on those edges/vertices, normalized by Z_N.

Problem: Obtain explicit closed-form expressions (e.g. determinant or multiple-integral representations, and their thermodynamic / scaling limits) for the bulk multi-point correlation functions of the six-vertex model with domain wall boundary conditions, as well as for the boundary multi-point correlation functions beyond the already known one-point boundary results. In particular, derive formulas valid uniformly in the disordered, ferroelectric and antiferroelectric phases, taking into account the lack of translation invariance inherent to the DWBC setup.
category_tag: six-vertex model with domain wall boundary conditions
status_search_result: Significant progress has been made: boundary one-point functions are known as N×N determinants (Bogoliubov–Pronko–Zvonarev), and various nonlocal bulk correlation functions such as the emptiness formation probability and row-configuration probability have been studied by Colomo–Pronko and others, with integral/determinant representations and limit-shape results. However, general bulk and boundary multi-point correlation functions of the DWBC six-vertex model do not have complete closed-form solutions, and the problem is generally considered partially solved / still open.

original_question: For the hard-core lattice gas (independent-set model) on a countably infinite graph G=(V,E) of maximum degree Delta, with vertex fugacities {w_x} and Gibbs measures defined for nonnegative fugacities, is it true that uniqueness of the infinite-volume Gibbs measure holds whenever 0 <= w_x <= (1-epsilon)*(Delta-1)^(Delta-1)/(Delta-2)^Delta for all vertices x and some epsilon>0 (possibly even epsilon=0)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a countably infinite graph of maximum degree $\Delta\ge 3$. The hard-core lattice gas on $G$ with vertex fugacities $\{w_x\}_{x\in V}$, $w_x\ge 0$, is the family of probability measures on $\{0,1\}^V$ (interpreted as independent sets, where $\sigma_x=1$ means $x$ is occupied) defined by the Gibbsian specifications: for each finite $\Lambda\subset V$ and each boundary condition $\eta\in\{0,1\}^{V\setminus\Lambda}$ that is compatible with the hard-core constraint (no two adjacent vertices are both occupied),
$$\mu_\Lambda^\eta(\sigma_\Lambda)=\frac{1}{Z_\Lambda^\eta}\,\mathbf{1}\{\sigma_\Lambda\cup\eta\text{ is an independent set}\}\prod_{x\in\Lambda:\sigma_x=1}w_x.$$
A probability measure $\mu$ on $\{0,1\}^V$ is an (infinite-volume) Gibbs measure if its conditional distributions agree with these specifications. Let
$$\lambda_c(\Delta):=\frac{(\Delta-1)^{\Delta-1}}{(\Delta-2)^\Delta}$$
denote the uniqueness threshold of the hard-core model on the infinite $\Delta$-regular tree.

Prove or disprove: For every countably infinite graph $G$ of maximum degree $\Delta$, the hard-core lattice gas on $G$ has a unique infinite-volume Gibbs measure whenever there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that
$$0\le w_x\le (1-\varepsilon)\,\lambda_c(\Delta)\qquad\text{for all }x\in V.$$
Determine also whether the statement remains true with $\varepsilon=0$.
category_tag: hard-core lattice gas / Gibbs measure uniqueness
status_search_result: The related conjecture of Sokal concerning zero-freeness of the independence polynomial in a complex neighborhood of $[0,\lambda_c(\Delta))$ for all graphs of maximum degree $\Delta$ was resolved by Peters and Regts (2017), yielding deterministic FPTAS up to the tree threshold. However, the question of uniqueness of the infinite-volume Gibbs measure on all countably infinite graphs of maximum degree $\Delta$ up to the tree uniqueness threshold $\lambda_c(\Delta)$ appears to remain open in general; uniqueness up to this threshold is known on the $\Delta$-regular tree and (via correlation decay/strong spatial mixing arguments) implies results for amenable graphs in specific settings, but a full proof for arbitrary infinite graphs of maximum degree $\Delta$ has not been established. Related questions (e.g., whether strong spatial mixing on the tree transfers to all bounded-degree graphs) are explicitly open.

original_question: In the hard-core/repulsive-gas context, Dobrushin's approach proves nonvanishing of the partition function Z first and then analyticity/convergence of log Z. Can this approach be extended so that it works without assuming hard-core self-repulsion?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a lattice (or continuous) gas of polymers with activities $\{z_\gamma\}_{\gamma\in\Gamma}$ and a pairwise interaction encoded by a symmetric "compatibility" relation, with grand-canonical partition function
$$Z(\Lambda;z) \;=\; \sum_{\{\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_n\}\subset\Lambda} \prod_{i=1}^n z_{\gamma_i}\,\prod_{1\le i<j\le n} w(\gamma_i,\gamma_j),$$
where $w(\gamma,\gamma')\in[0,1]$ in the hard-core (purely repulsive) case is the indicator $\mathbf 1[\gamma\sim\gamma']$ of compatibility (so $w=0$ for incompatible polymers and $w=1$ otherwise). Dobrushin's inductive approach establishes, in this hard-core setting, the following two-step result for activities $z$ in an explicit polydisc $\mathcal D$:
(i) $Z(\Lambda;z)\ne 0$ for every finite $\Lambda$ and every $z\in\mathcal D$;
(ii) $\log Z(\Lambda;z)$ is analytic on $\mathcal D$ with absolutely and uniformly convergent cluster expansion.
The argument proceeds by induction on $|\Lambda|$, deriving (i) directly without recourse to power-series/cluster-expansion estimates, and then deducing (ii).

Question. Can Dobrushin's inductive approach be extended so as to prove the analogous nonvanishing and analyticity results for partition functions of polymer/lattice-gas systems whose pair interactions $w(\gamma,\gamma')$ are not assumed to enforce hard-core self-repulsion — for instance, soft-repulsive interactions $0\le w\le 1$, or more general (possibly complex-valued) Boltzmann weights — without assuming the hard-core constraint $w\in\{0,1\}$?
status_search_result: Subsequent work has extended Dobrushin-style inductive arguments beyond the strict hard-core case. Fernández–Procacci (2007) gave new bounds from an old approach for abstract polymer models, and later inductive proofs (e.g., the 2020 simple inductive proof of the Fernández–Procacci criterion) and follow-ups have established zero-freeness/cluster-expansion convergence in settings including soft-repulsive (0 ≤ w ≤ 1) and even complex-valued multi-body interactions. Thus the question is at least partially resolved in the affirmative for various classes beyond hard-core, although a fully general extension matching all features of Dobrushin's original argument is not uniformly stated as completely settled.

context_brief: Claw-free graphs and real negative zeros
original_question: If G is claw-free (has no induced K_{1,3}), must every zero of the hard-core lattice-gas partition function Z(w) be a negative real number?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph. The hard-core lattice-gas partition function (independence polynomial) of $G$ is
$$Z_G(w) \;=\; \sum_{I \subseteq V \text{ independent}} w^{|I|},$$
where the sum is over all independent sets $I$ of $G$ (sets containing no edge of $G$), including the empty set. The graph $K_{1,3}$ (the "claw") is the complete bipartite graph with parts of sizes $1$ and $3$. A graph $G$ is called claw-free if it contains no induced subgraph isomorphic to $K_{1,3}$.

Prove or disprove: for every finite simple claw-free graph $G$, every (complex) zero of $Z_G(w)$ is a negative real number.
status_search_result: The conjecture was proved by Maria Chudnovsky and Paul Seymour in "The roots of the independence polynomial of a clawfree graph" (J. Combin. Theory Ser. B, 2007), establishing that the independence polynomial of every claw-free graph has only real roots; since the coefficients are nonnegative, all roots are negative real numbers.

original_question: For the q-coloring model (zero-temperature antiferromagnetic Potts model), prove uniqueness of the infinite-volume Gibbs measure and exponential decay of correlations in specific unresolved cases, including q=3 on the hexagonal lattice and q=4,5,6 on the square lattice.
self_contained_problem:
Let $L$ be either the hexagonal lattice $H$ or the square lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$, and fix an integer $q\ge 3$. A proper $q$-coloring of $L$ is a function $\sigma:V(L)\to\{1,2,\dots,q\}$ such that $\sigma(x)\neq \sigma(y)$ whenever $x$ and $y$ are adjacent vertices in $L$. The $q$-coloring model on $L$ is the zero-temperature antiferromagnetic $q$-state Potts model: a probability measure $\mu$ on colorings of $V(L)$ is called an infinite-volume Gibbs measure if for every finite subset $\Lambda\subset V(L)$, the conditional distribution of $\sigma\!\restriction_\Lambda$ given $\sigma\!\restriction_{V(L)\setminus\Lambda}$ is, $\mu$-almost surely, uniform over the proper $q$-colorings of $\Lambda$ that agree with the boundary configuration on the outer boundary of $\Lambda$.

Prove the following statements in each of the indicated cases:

(a) There exists a unique infinite-volume Gibbs measure $\mu$ for the $q$-coloring model on $L$.

(b) Correlations decay exponentially under $\mu$: there exist constants $C,c>0$ such that for any local events $A,B$ supported on finite sets $S_A,S_B\subset V(L)$,
$$\bigl|\mu(A\cap B)-\mu(A)\mu(B)\bigr|\;\le\; C\,\|\mathbf 1_A\|_\infty\,\|\mathbf 1_B\|_\infty\,e^{-c\,\mathrm{dist}(S_A,S_B)}.$$

The cases to be resolved are:
- $L=H$ (hexagonal lattice) with $q=3$;
- $L=\mathbb{Z}^2$ (square lattice) with $q\in\{4,5,6\}$.
category_tag: antiferromagnetic Potts / proper colorings of lattices
status_search_result: The cases listed remain open in their full strength. Uniqueness with exponential decay for proper $q$-colorings on $\mathbb Z^2$ is known via Dobrushin-type arguments only for $q$ sufficiently large (e.g., $q>2r$ where $r$ is the maximum coordination), covering $q\ge 7$ on $\mathbb Z^2$ but not $q=4,5,6$. For the 3-coloring on the hexagonal lattice, only Monte Carlo evidence of disorder at all temperatures is available, with no rigorous proof of uniqueness and exponential decay. Recent rigorous progress on antiferromagnetic Potts models has focused on trees and on power-law (critical) decay rather than these specific planar cases.

original_question: For chromatic-polynomial zeros of graphs with maximum degree Delta, what is the optimal sharp bound C_opt(Delta) on their modulus, and what can be proved about zero-free or root-location regions in the complex q-plane beyond discs centered at q=0?
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a finite simple graph with maximum degree Δ, and let P(G,q) denote its chromatic polynomial, i.e. the unique polynomial in q whose value at every positive integer k equals the number of proper k-colorings of G. It is known that there exists an absolute constant C(Δ), depending only on Δ, such that every complex root q of P(G,q) satisfies |q| ≤ C(Δ)·... more precisely, results of Sokal and others establish that |q| ≤ C·Δ for some absolute constant C (with current upper bounds C ≤ 6.91, and lower bounds of the form C ≥ some value > 1) for every graph of maximum degree Δ.

Define
   C_opt(Δ) = sup { |q| : q ∈ ℂ is a root of P(G,q) for some graph G with maximum degree at most Δ }.

(a) Determine the exact value of C_opt(Δ) for each integer Δ ≥ 2. In particular:
   (i) Is it true that C_opt(Δ) ≤ 2Δ for all Δ?
   (ii) Is C_opt(3) = 3?

(b) Beyond closed discs {q ∈ ℂ : |q| ≤ R} centered at q = 0, characterize the regions of the complex q-plane that are zero-free for the chromatic polynomials of all graphs of maximum degree at most Δ. That is, determine (or describe meaningfully) the complement in ℂ of the closure of the set of chromatic roots of all such graphs.
status_search_result: The sharp constant in the bound |q| ≤ C·Δ for chromatic roots of graphs of maximum degree Δ remains open. Sokal originally proved C ≤ 7.963907; this was successively improved (Borgs; Fernández–Procacci to C ≤ 6.91; Jackson–Procacci–Sokal and later work giving further refinements), and for real roots Dong–Koh obtained C ≤ 5.67. No matching lower bound is known, so neither the conjectures C_opt(Δ) ≤ 2Δ nor C_opt(3) = 3 have been resolved. The characterization of zero-free regions beyond discs centered at 0 also remains an active research area.
