paper_title: Some Open Problems in Random Matrix Theory and the Theory of Integrable Systems. II
original_question: Can one prove an analog of the Toda stopping-time universality theorem for the full deflation time T_{ε,n,A,E} of some eigenvalue algorithm A, where deflation requires control of more of the eigenvector structure and not only the top eigen-gap?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $E$ be an ensemble of $n\times n$ real symmetric or complex Hermitian random matrices (for example a Wigner ensemble with i.i.d. entries of mean zero and finite variance). Let $A$ be a deterministic eigenvalue algorithm acting on Hermitian matrices that produces, starting from $M_0=M$ drawn from $E$, a sequence of isospectral iterates $M_0,M_1,M_2,\dots$ converging to a diagonal matrix (e.g. the Toda flow sampled at integer times, the QR algorithm, or the QR algorithm with shifts).

Halting (top‑gap) time. For $\varepsilon>0$, define the top‑gap halting time
$$\tau_{\varepsilon,n,A,E}(M)=\min\Bigl\{k\ge 0\ :\ \bigl|(M_k)_{n,n-1}\bigr|<\varepsilon\Bigr\},$$
which measures the first time the off‑diagonal entry coupling the last eigenvalue to the rest of the spectrum has dropped below $\varepsilon$.

Deflation time. Define the full deflation time
$$T_{\varepsilon,n,A,E}(M)=\min\Bigl\{k\ge 0\ :\ \max_{1\le j\le n-1}\bigl|(M_k)_{j+1,j}\bigr|<\varepsilon\Bigr\},$$
that is, the first iteration at which every sub‑diagonal entry of $M_k$ is smaller than $\varepsilon$, so that all eigenvalues have been numerically separated.

Known result (top‑gap universality). For $A$ equal to the Toda algorithm, there exist scaling constants $a_n=a_n(\varepsilon,A,E)$, $b_n=b_n(\varepsilon,A,E)$ and a distribution function $F_A$, independent of the choice of $E$ within a wide universality class, such that
$$\frac{\tau_{\varepsilon,n,A,E}-a_n}{b_n}\ \Longrightarrow\ F_A\qquad(n\to\infty).$$

Problem. Prove (or disprove) the analogous universality statement for the full deflation time: namely, exhibit an eigenvalue algorithm $A$ (e.g. Toda, QR, or QR with shifts), scaling constants $\widetilde a_n,\widetilde b_n$, and a distribution function $G_A$ such that
$$\frac{T_{\varepsilon,n,A,E}-\widetilde a_n}{\widetilde b_n}\ \Longrightarrow\ G_A\qquad(n\to\infty)$$
holds with $G_A$ independent of $E$ across an appropriate universality class (e.g. Wigner ensembles with sufficient moments). Unlike the top‑gap case, a proof must control not only the topmost spectral gap but also the joint behavior of all sub‑diagonal entries, equivalently the localization/delocalization and rigidity properties of the entire eigenvector basis throughout the iteration.
status_search_result: Rigorous universality has been established (Deift–Trogdon, 2016, and subsequent works including the recent monograph on the Toda lattice and universality) for the halting time associated with computing the largest eigenvalue (top eigen-gap) via the Toda algorithm, and analogous results for sample covariance matrices. However, the analog for the full deflation time—where all sub-diagonal entries must drop below ε and finer control of the full eigenvector basis is required—does not appear to have been proved for any eigenvalue algorithm; it remains a stated central open problem in this line of work.

paper_title: Some Open Problems in Random Matrix Theory and the Theory of Integrable Systems. II
original_question: Can the high-accuracy orthogonal-polynomial-based sampling method for invariant unitary ensembles be extended to orthogonal and symplectic invariant ensembles?
self_contained_problem:
Background. For a unitary-invariant matrix ensemble on N×N Hermitian matrices with joint eigenvalue density proportional to
   ∏_{i<j}(x_i−x_j)^2 · ∏_i w(x_i),
the eigenvalues form a determinantal point process whose correlation kernel is
   K_N(x,y) = √{w(x)w(y)} · Σ_{k=0}^{N−1} p_k(x) p_k(y),
where {p_k} are the orthonormal polynomials associated with the weight w. Using this representation, exact sampling of the eigenvalues can be performed to high accuracy via the algorithm: draw x_1 from the marginal density K_N(x,x)/N, then sequentially draw x_{j+1} from the conditional density obtained by Schur-complementing the kernel against the previously sampled points. This requires only the ability to compute the orthonormal polynomials p_k for the weight w with sufficient accuracy.

The orthogonal (β=1) and symplectic (β=4) invariant ensembles have joint eigenvalue densities proportional to
   ∏_{i<j}|x_i−x_j|^β · ∏_i w(x_i),  β ∈ {1,4},
and form Pfaffian point processes with 2×2 matrix-valued skew-symmetric correlation kernels expressible in terms of the skew-orthogonal polynomials associated with w.

Problem. Develop an exact, high-accuracy sampling algorithm for the eigenvalues of the orthogonal (β=1) and symplectic (β=4) invariant ensembles with a general weight function w, analogous to the orthogonal-polynomial-based algorithm available for the unitary (β=2) case. In particular, provide (i) an effective numerical method for computing the skew-orthogonal polynomials associated with w, and (ii) a sequential conditional-sampling procedure based on the resulting 2×2 matrix-valued Pfaffian kernel, that produces samples from the joint eigenvalue distribution to a prescribed accuracy.
status_search_result: A recent preprint, "Sampling Pfaffian point processes and the symplectic Arnoldi method" (arXiv:2605.01202), presents an exact sampling algorithm for Pfaffian point processes—based on a skew-symmetric analogue of Cholesky factorization—together with a symplectic Arnoldi method for computing the skew-orthogonal polynomials needed to build the 2×2 matrix-valued kernels of β=1,4 ensembles. Numerical examples include the finite-N Gaussian orthogonal and symplectic ensembles and the β=1,4 Airy/Tracy–Widom distributions, indicating that the extension of the orthogonal-polynomial-based sampling method to orthogonal and symplectic invariant ensembles has been carried out.

paper_title: Some Open Problems in Random Matrix Theory and the Theory of Integrable Systems. II
original_question: Can the Bikbaev–Tarasov Bäcklund-transform method be used to solve the initial-boundary value problem for the defocusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation on the half-line with Robin boundary conditions at x=0, while controlling the singularities introduced by the extension to x<0?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the defocusing nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation
  i u_t = u_{xx} - 2|u|^2 u,   x > 0, t > 0,
posed on the half-line, with initial data u(x,0) = u_0(x), x ≥ 0, and homogeneous Robin boundary condition at the origin,
  u_x(0,t) + α u(0,t) = 0,   t > 0,   α ∈ ℝ.

The Bikbaev–Tarasov method consists of using a Bäcklund (auto-)transformation of NLS, compatible with the Robin boundary condition, to extend the half-line solution u(x,t) to a function ũ(x,t) defined for all x ∈ ℝ that solves the defocusing NLS equation on the full line; one then attempts to apply the inverse scattering transform / Riemann–Hilbert machinery to ũ. A central difficulty is that the Bäcklund extension may introduce singularities in ũ for x < 0 that must be controlled.

Problem. Develop the Bikbaev–Tarasov Bäcklund-extension approach for the defocusing NLS with Robin boundary conditions on the half-line: produce a well-defined extension ũ(x,t) of u(x,t) to all x ∈ ℝ which solves defocusing NLS, give a rigorous control of the singularities of ũ on x < 0 (e.g. their location, finiteness, and integrability properties), and use this construction to solve the initial–boundary value problem above, including a description of the solution and its long-time asymptotics for general α ∈ ℝ and suitable classes of initial data u_0.

Soc., 2023), who established long-time asymptotics and stability of stationary solitons. paper_title: Some Open Problems in Random Matrix Theory and the Theory of Integrable Systems. II
original_question: For focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equations in the small-dispersion regime ε=ℏ→0 and general smooth initial data, can one solve the non-self-adjoint forward scattering problem and then implement the associated Riemann–Hilbert method to compute the Cauchy problem asymptotically?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation in one space dimension with a small dispersion parameter ε > 0:

    i ε ∂_t ψ + (ε²/2) ∂_x² ψ + |ψ|² ψ = 0,    x ∈ ℝ, t > 0,
    ψ(x, 0; ε) = ψ_0(x),

where ψ_0 ∈ C^∞(ℝ) is a general smooth (e.g., Schwartz-class) initial datum, independent of ε. The associated Zakharov–Shabat spectral problem for focusing NLS is non-self-adjoint, so the eigenvalues of the forward scattering problem may be distributed throughout the complex plane and standard self-adjoint techniques do not apply.

Develop a rigorous method that:

(1) Solves the forward (direct) scattering problem for the non-self-adjoint Zakharov–Shabat operator with potential ψ_0, including a description of the limiting distribution (as ε ↓ 0) of discrete eigenvalues and norming constants together with the continuous-spectrum reflection coefficient, for general smooth ψ_0; and

(2) Uses the resulting scattering data to formulate and asymptotically analyze, via the Riemann–Hilbert/steepest-descent (nonlinear steepest descent or ∂̄) method, the inverse scattering Riemann–Hilbert problem, so as to compute the leading-order asymptotic behavior of ψ(x, t; ε) as ε ↓ 0 for (x, t) in the relevant regions of the (x, t)-plane (including pre- and post-caustic regimes).

In short: solve the non-self-adjoint forward scattering problem for general smooth initial data and implement the Riemann–Hilbert methodology to obtain the small-dispersion (semiclassical) asymptotics of the Cauchy problem for the focusing NLS equation.
category_tag: semiclassical focusing NLS and Riemann–Hilbert analysis
status_search_result: The semiclassical limit of focusing NLS via Riemann–Hilbert methods has been carried out rigorously only for special classes of initial data (analytic data via the Kamvissis–McLaughlin–Miller semiclassical soliton ensemble construction; specific families such as square-barrier data; certain analytic real data by Tovbis–Venakides–Bertola and others). For general smooth, non-analytic initial data, the non-self-adjoint forward scattering problem is not understood (eigenvalues are not confined to a curve and WKB-type analyses break down), and a complete RHP-based asymptotic solution of the Cauchy problem remains an outstanding open problem in the field.

paper_title: Some Open Problems in Random Matrix Theory and the Theory of Integrable Systems. II
original_question: For perturbations of the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation of the form i u_t + u_xx + 2|u|²u + ε|u|^ℓ u = 0 with decaying initial data, especially when the unperturbed initial data produces a two-soliton solution, what is the long-time behavior of the perturbed solution?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the perturbed focusing nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation on the real line:
$$ i\,u_t + u_{xx} + 2|u|^2 u + \varepsilon\,|u|^{\ell} u = 0, \qquad x\in\mathbb{R},\ t>0, $$
where $\varepsilon>0$ is a small parameter and $\ell>0$ with $\ell\neq 2$ (so the extra term is a genuine non-integrable perturbation of cubic focusing NLS). The initial data $u(x,0)=f(x)$ is assumed to be smooth and decaying at infinity (e.g. in Schwartz class).

Describe rigorously the long-time asymptotic behavior as $t\to\infty$ of the solution $u(x,t)$ to the Cauchy problem above, for general decaying initial data $f$, and in particular in the distinguished case where $f$ is the initial datum of a two-soliton solution of the unperturbed focusing cubic NLS equation
$$ i\,u_t + u_{xx} + 2|u|^2 u = 0. $$
The goal is to determine, in each space-time cone $x/t = \xi$ fixed, the leading-order asymptotics of $u(x,t)$ (including the modulation of soliton parameters such as amplitudes, velocities, positions, and phases, together with the radiation component) induced by the perturbation $\varepsilon|u|^\ell u$.
status_search_result: Long-time asymptotics for the unperturbed focusing cubic NLS have been substantially advanced (e.g., Borghese–Jenkins–McLaughlin and follow-ups using ∂̄-steepest descent yield soliton resolution in each space-time cone). However, the corresponding rigorous long-time asymptotic analysis for genuinely non-integrable perturbations of the form ε|u|^ℓ u with decaying data — particularly when the unperturbed datum produces a two-soliton — does not appear to have been carried out. Formal/integrable perturbation theory exists, but a rigorous treatment remains open.

paper_title: Some Open Problems in Random Matrix Theory and the Theory of Integrable Systems. II
original_question: If the exponential Toda interaction e^x is replaced by a general force law F(x) that is a sufficiently small perturbation of e^x and admits a suitable 2-periodic solution, does the corresponding shock problem still have the same long-time asymptotic behavior as the Toda shock problem, and how can that behavior be analyzed rigorously?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a one-dimensional infinite chain of unit-mass particles with positions $q_n(t)$, $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, governed by the Newtonian equations of motion
$$\ddot q_n(t)=F\bigl(q_{n+1}(t)-q_n(t)\bigr)-F\bigl(q_n(t)-q_{n-1}(t)\bigr),\qquad n\in\mathbb{Z},\ t>0,$$
with shock-type initial data consisting of two semi-infinite lattices in equilibrium, moving toward each other so that asymptotically as $n\to -\infty$ the particles travel with velocity $2c>0$ and as $n\to +\infty$ with velocity $0$ (or equivalent step-like Flaschka variables for the relative displacements). 

The classical Toda case corresponds to the exponential force law $F(x)=e^x$, in which case the system is completely integrable and the long-time behavior of $q_{n+1}(t)-q_n(t)$ and $\dot q_n(t)$ is known: for $n/t$ in a finite interval the lattice converges to a modulated $2$-periodic (genus-one) finite-gap Toda solution, while outside this interval it converges to the two constant equilibria; the modulation parameters and the wedge of oscillation are explicitly computable from the integrable structure.

Now suppose $F:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is a smooth function that is a sufficiently small perturbation of $e^x$ (in a suitable norm) and that the perturbed lattice still admits a $2$-periodic traveling-wave solution analogous to the Toda $2$-periodic solution used in the integrable analysis. 

Prove or disprove: the corresponding shock problem for the perturbed force law $F$ exhibits the same long-time asymptotic behavior as the Toda shock problem, namely convergence (in an appropriate sense, locally uniformly on rays $n/t=\xi$) to the two constant states outside a wedge and to a modulated $2$-periodic profile inside the wedge, with the wedge boundaries and the modulation determined by the perturbed $2$-periodic solution. Provide a rigorous analytic framework (necessarily non-integrable, since $F\ne e^x$) for establishing this asymptotic description.
category_tag: Toda shock and nonintegrable lattice perturbations
status_search_result: Recent rigorous results (e.g., Egorova–Michor–Teschl and collaborators, 2020s) have justified the long-time asymptotics of the integrable Toda shock problem via nonlinear steepest descent, confirming the Venakides–Deift–Oba conjecture in the exponential case. However, no published work appears to extend this asymptotic analysis to general non-integrable small perturbations $F(x)$ of $e^x$, which would require non-integrable techniques. The problem of analyzing the shock problem for perturbed force laws thus appears to remain open.

paper_title: Developments and open problems on chiral polytopes
original_question: Which finite simple groups occur as automorphism groups of chiral d-polytopes, where a chiral d-polytope is an abstract rank-d polytope whose automorphism group has exactly two flag-orbits and adjacent flags lie in different orbits?
self_contained_problem:
An abstract polytope of rank d (or d-polytope) is a partially ordered set P with a unique minimum element and a unique maximum element, in which every maximal chain (flag) has exactly d+2 elements, and which satisfies the usual diamond condition and strong flag-connectivity. Two flags are called adjacent if they differ in exactly one element. An automorphism of P is an order-preserving bijection P → P; the automorphism group Γ(P) acts on the set of flags.

The polytope P is called chiral if Γ(P) has exactly two orbits on the flags of P and any two adjacent flags lie in different orbits.

Problem. Determine precisely which finite non-abelian simple groups G arise as the automorphism group Γ(P) of some chiral d-polytope P, for some integer d ≥ 3.
status_search_result: The problem is partially solved. For rank d = 3 (chiral polyhedra), Leemans and Liebeck showed that every finite non-abelian simple group is the automorphism group of a chiral polyhedron, with the exceptions of PSL_2(q), PSL_3(q), PSU_3(q), and A_7. Subsequent work has addressed specific families (e.g., PSL(3,q), almost simple groups with socle PSL(2,q), and chiral 5-polytopes from alternating groups A_n by Conder–Hubard–O'Reilly Regueiro). The general classification across all ranks d remains an active area, with several recent papers (2022–2025), so the overall problem is not fully resolved.

paper_title: Developments and open problems on chiral polytopes
original_question: Does there exist a chiral polytope whose monodromy group on flags, generated by the involutions r_i that send a flag to its i-adjacent flag, is not a string C-group?
self_contained_problem:
An abstract polytope of rank n is a partially ordered set P with a unique minimum element and unique maximum element, in which every maximal totally ordered subset (flag) has exactly n+2 elements (so elements naturally receive ranks 0,1,...,n-1 between the minimum and maximum), every flag has, for each i in {0,1,...,n-1}, a unique i-adjacent flag differing from it only in its rank-i element, P is strongly flag-connected, and P satisfies the diamond condition. The polytope is called chiral if its automorphism group has exactly two orbits on flags such that adjacent flags lie in different orbits.

For each i in {0,1,...,n-1}, let r_i be the permutation of the set of flags of P that sends every flag to its i-adjacent flag. Each r_i is an involution. The monodromy group (also called the connection group) of P is the subgroup Mon(P) = ⟨r_0, r_1, ..., r_{n-1}⟩ of the symmetric group on the flags.

A string C-group of rank n is a pair (G, {s_0,...,s_{n-1}}) where G is a group generated by involutions s_0,...,s_{n-1} satisfying:
 (1) (s_i s_j)^2 = 1 whenever |i-j| ≥ 2 (the string condition), and
 (2) the intersection property: for all subsets I, J ⊆ {0,...,n-1}, ⟨s_i : i ∈ I⟩ ∩ ⟨s_j : j ∈ J⟩ = ⟨s_k : k ∈ I ∩ J⟩.

Question: Does there exist a chiral abstract polytope P such that the monodromy group Mon(P), with its distinguished generating set {r_0, r_1, ..., r_{n-1}}, is not a string C-group?
status_search_result: Searches on the monodromy/connection group of chiral polytopes and the string C-group property did not surface a definitive resolution. It is known that the monodromy group of any abstract polyhedron (rank 3) is a string C-group (Hartley–Hubard–Pellicer–type results), and there is recent work constructing 4-polytopes whose connection groups fail to be string C-groups in the non-chiral setting, but no clear evidence that the question has been settled specifically for chiral polytopes was found.

paper_title: Developments and open problems on chiral polytopes
original_question: Develop a theory of chiral covers of polytopes: define the right notion of quotient and cover in the chiral setting, and formulate the analogue of the regular-cover theory for chiral polytopes.
self_contained_problem:
An abstract polytope of rank $n$ is a partially ordered set $\mathcal{P}$, with a strictly monotone rank function onto $\{-1,0,1,\dots,n\}$, satisfying: (i) $\mathcal{P}$ has a unique minimum face (of rank $-1$) and a unique maximum face (of rank $n$); (ii) every maximal chain (flag) has exactly $n+2$ elements; (iii) $\mathcal{P}$ is strongly flag-connected; and (iv) the diamond condition: whenever $F < G$ with $\mathrm{rank}(G)-\mathrm{rank}(F)=2$, there are exactly two faces strictly between $F$ and $G$. An automorphism of $\mathcal{P}$ is an order-preserving bijection. The polytope $\mathcal{P}$ is called regular if its automorphism group acts transitively on flags, and chiral if its automorphism group has exactly two orbits on flags such that adjacent flags lie in different orbits.

Given two abstract polytopes $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{Q}$ of the same rank, $\mathcal{P}$ is said to cover $\mathcal{Q}$ if there exists a surjection $\mathcal{P} \to \mathcal{Q}$ which preserves rank, incidence, and adjacency of flags; one then says $\mathcal{Q}$ is a quotient of $\mathcal{P}$. For regular polytopes, there is a well-developed theory in which quotients correspond to certain normal subgroups of the automorphism group of the universal regular polytope of a given Schläfli type.

Develop the analogous theory of covers and quotients in the chiral setting. Specifically:
(a) Formulate the appropriate notions of "chiral cover" and "chiral quotient" between chiral polytopes (and possibly between chiral and regular polytopes), accounting for the role of the two flag orbits and the handedness (mirror image) of chiral polytopes.
(b) Give a group-theoretic characterization of chiral covers in terms of the rotation subgroups (or their analogues) of the automorphism groups, identifying which subgroups give rise to chiral quotients that are again polytopes.
(c) Establish the analogue, in the chiral setting, of the regular-cover theory: in particular, describe a universal chiral polytope of a prescribed Schläfli type from which all chiral polytopes of that type arise as quotients, and characterize the corresponding covering relations.
status_search_result: Partial progress has been made on aspects of chiral covers since the problem was posed. Notable contributions include work on abelian covers of chiral polytopes (Cunningham–Pellicer, J. Algebra 2017), chiral extensions of chiral polytopes (Cunningham–Pellicer), and the study of chiral polytopes whose smallest regular cover is itself a polytope (J. Combin. Theory Ser. A, 2024). However, a complete general theory of chiral covers and quotients fully analogous to the regular-cover theory does not appear to have been established in the literature, so the program as a whole remains open.

paper_title: Developments and open problems on chiral polytopes
original_question: Determine conditions under which the Petrie scheme of a chiral polytope is acoptic, meaning that each proper face is contained in at most one flag of the Petrie scheme.
self_contained_problem:
An (abstract) polytope of rank $n$ is a partially ordered set $\mathcal{P}$ with a least face $F_{-1}$ and a greatest face $F_n$, in which every maximal chain (called a flag) has exactly $n+2$ elements, which is strongly flag-connected, and which satisfies the diamond condition: whenever $F < G$ with $\operatorname{rank}(G)-\operatorname{rank}(F)=2$, there are exactly two faces $H$ with $F<H<G$. Two flags are $i$-adjacent ($0\le i\le n-1$) if they differ exactly in their face of rank $i$; the unique flag $i$-adjacent to a flag $\Phi$ is denoted $\Phi^i$.

The polytope $\mathcal{P}$ is called chiral if its automorphism group has exactly two orbits on flags, with adjacent flags lying in different orbits.

The Petrie scheme through a base flag $\Phi_0$ is the sequence of flags
$$\Phi_0,\ \Phi_1,\ \Phi_2,\ \dots$$
defined recursively by
$$\Phi_{k+1} = \Phi_k^{\,i_k}, \qquad \text{where } i_k \equiv k \pmod{n},$$
that is, one applies the adjacencies $0,1,2,\dots,n-1,0,1,\dots$ cyclically until the sequence closes up to $\Phi_0$. The Petrie scheme is called acoptic if every proper face of $\mathcal{P}$ is contained in at most one flag of the scheme (so the scheme does not "self-intersect" through any proper face).

Problem. Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on a chiral abstract polytope $\mathcal{P}$ under which its Petrie scheme is acoptic.
status_search_result: Web search did not surface a paper resolving the question of when the Petrie scheme of a chiral polytope is acoptic. The notion of acoptic Petrie scheme appears in Williams' 2005 paper on Petrie schemes and is referenced in subsequent work on chiral polyhedra and Petrie–Coxeter constructions, but no source explicitly characterizing acopticity for chiral polytopes was found.

paper_title: Developments and open problems on chiral polytopes
original_question: Does there exist a chiral polytope whose left Petrie paths are polygons but whose right Petrie paths are not polygons?
self_contained_problem:
An abstract polytope is a partially ordered set whose elements (called faces) are ranked, satisfying the standard axioms generalising the face lattice of a convex polytope: it has a least face and a greatest face, every maximal chain (flag) has the same length, it satisfies the diamond condition (between any face of rank i−1 and any face of rank i+1 incident with it there are exactly two faces of rank i), and it is strongly flag-connected. The automorphism group of an abstract polytope P acts freely on the set of flags. P is called regular if this action is transitive, and chiral if it has exactly two flag-orbits under the automorphism group such that adjacent flags always lie in different orbits.

For a chiral polytope P of rank n, fix a base flag Φ and let σ_1, …, σ_{n−1} be the distinguished generators of Aut(P) that map Φ to its i-adjacent flag's orbit representative (so σ_i changes only the face of rank i). The left Petrie motion is the automorphism σ_1 σ_2 ⋯ σ_{n−1}, and the right Petrie motion is σ_1 σ_2^{−1} σ_3 σ_4^{−1} ⋯ (alternating). The orbits of the edges of P under the cyclic group generated by the left (respectively right) Petrie motion, traversed by following the action on edges, are called the left Petrie paths (respectively right Petrie paths) of P. Such a path is said to be a polygon when it closes up into a finite cycle without self-intersection in the appropriate combinatorial sense (i.e. it is a genuine finite polygonal closed path rather than an unbounded or improperly-closing walk).

Question: Does there exist a chiral polytope P such that every left Petrie path of P is a polygon while at least one right Petrie path of P is not a polygon?
status_search_result: A web search located surveys and constructions on chiral polytopes and on left/right Petrie polygons (e.g. Coxeter's chiral 4-polytopes obtained by making left and right Petrie motions have different lengths), but no source was found explicitly resolving whether a chiral polytope can have all left Petrie paths closed as polygons while some right Petrie path fails to close as a polygon. The status appears unresolved based on available sources.

paper_title: Developments and open problems on chiral polytopes
original_question: Determine the pairs of positive integers (m, n) for which there exists a chiral 4-polytope whose right Petrie paths have length m and whose left Petrie paths have length n.
self_contained_problem:
An abstract polytope of rank $n$ is a partially ordered set $\mathcal{P}$ (with elements called faces, ranked from $-1$ to $n$) satisfying the standard axioms: it has a unique minimum face $F_{-1}$ and unique maximum face $F_n$; every maximal chain (flag) contains exactly $n+2$ faces; $\mathcal{P}$ is strongly flag-connected; and it satisfies the diamond condition (whenever $F<G$ with $\mathrm{rank}(G)-\mathrm{rank}(F)=2$, there are exactly two faces strictly between $F$ and $G$).

The automorphism group $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ acts freely on the set of flags. The polytope $\mathcal{P}$ is called chiral if $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ has exactly two orbits on the flags, and adjacent flags (differing in exactly one face) lie in distinct orbits. For a chiral $4$-polytope, define the right Petrie element $\rho_R = \sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_3$ and the left Petrie element $\rho_L = \sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1}\sigma_3$. The orbits of edges (or equivalently, the closed zig-zag paths through the $1$-skeleton that turn alternately right/left at successive faces) under $\langle\rho_R\rangle$ and $\langle\rho_L\rangle$ are called the right Petrie paths and left Petrie paths, and their common lengths are the orders of $\rho_R$ and $\rho_L$ respectively.

paper_title: Developments and open problems on chiral polytopes
original_question: Do there exist chiral tessellations of spherical space-forms?
self_contained_problem:
A spherical space-form is a quotient manifold of the form $S^n/\Gamma$, where $S^n$ is the unit $n$-sphere (with $n \geq 2$) equipped with its standard round metric and $\Gamma$ is a finite group of isometries of $S^n$ acting freely on $S^n$.

An abstract polytope of rank $n+1$ is a partially ordered set $\mathcal{P}$ with a strictly monotone rank function whose elements (called faces) have ranks in $\{-1, 0, 1, \dots, n+1\}$, satisfying: (i) there is a unique least face (rank $-1$) and a unique greatest face (rank $n+1$); (ii) every maximal chain (flag) has exactly $n+3$ elements; (iii) $\mathcal{P}$ is strongly flag-connected; and (iv) the diamond condition holds, namely for any two faces $F<G$ with $\mathrm{rank}(G)-\mathrm{rank}(F)=2$ there are exactly two faces strictly between $F$ and $G$. A tessellation of a spherical space-form $S^n/\Gamma$ is a face-to-face decomposition of $S^n/\Gamma$ into closed convex spherical cells that realises geometrically an abstract polytope of rank $n+1$.

Two flags of $\mathcal{P}$ are $i$-adjacent if they differ exactly in their rank-$i$ face. The automorphism group $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ of an abstract polytope acts freely on flags. A polytope (or tessellation) is called regular if $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ acts transitively on the flags, and chiral if $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ has exactly two orbits on the flags such that adjacent flags lie in distinct orbits. Equivalently, a chiral tessellation has maximal rotational symmetry but no symmetry that reverses orientation/flag-orbit.

Question: Does there exist an integer $n \geq 2$, a finite fixed-point-free group $\Gamma$ of isometries of $S^n$, and a chiral tessellation of the spherical space-form $S^n/\Gamma$?

original_question: Determine all pairs of spherical or toroidal (d−1)-polytopes K1 and K2 such that at least one of K1 or K2 is chiral and there exists a chiral d-polytope whose facets are isomorphic to K1 and whose vertex-figures are isomorphic to K2.
self_contained_problem:
An abstract d-polytope is a ranked partially ordered set (with rank function taking values −1, 0, 1, …, d) satisfying the standard combinatorial axioms of abstract polytopes: it has a unique minimum face and a unique maximum face, every maximal chain (flag) has exactly d+2 elements, it is strongly flag-connected, and it satisfies the diamond condition (for any two faces F < G with rank(G) − rank(F) = 2 there are exactly two faces H with F < H < G). The facets of a d-polytope are its faces of rank d−1, and the vertex-figure at a vertex v is the section consisting of all faces strictly between v and the maximum face; both are themselves abstract (d−1)-polytopes.

An automorphism of an abstract polytope is an order-preserving bijection of its face lattice. A d-polytope P is called regular if its automorphism group acts transitively on the flags, and chiral if the automorphism group has exactly two orbits on flags such that adjacent flags lie in different orbits (so P admits all "rotational" symmetry but no reflections).

A (d−1)-polytope is called spherical if it is isomorphic to the face lattice of a convex (d−1)-polytope (equivalently, its order complex is a (d−2)-sphere), and toroidal if its underlying topological space is a (d−2)-torus (the standard locally toroidal case studied for d = 4, 5, 6).

Problem. Determine all pairs (K₁, K₂) of spherical or toroidal (d−1)-polytopes, with at least one of K₁ or K₂ being chiral, such that there exists a chiral abstract d-polytope whose facets are all isomorphic to K₁ and whose vertex-figures are all isomorphic to K₂.

paper_title: Developments and open problems on chiral polytopes
original_question: Determine all positive integers g for which there exist chiral maps, equivalently chiral polyhedra, on orientable surfaces of genus g.
self_contained_problem:
A map on a surface is an embedding of a connected graph (or multigraph) into a closed surface such that each connected component of the complement of the embedded graph (a face) is homeomorphic to an open disk. An automorphism of the map is a permutation of its flags (incident vertex–edge–face triples) induced by a self-homeomorphism of the surface preserving the embedded graph. The automorphism group of a map on an orientable surface acts semi-regularly on the set of flags; the map is called orientably regular if its orientation-preserving automorphism group acts transitively (hence regularly) on the set of arcs (directed edges). Such a map is called reflexible if it additionally admits an orientation-reversing automorphism, and chiral if it does not (so the map and its mirror image are distinct but isomorphic as abstract structures, with two orbits of flags under the full automorphism group). Equivalently, a chiral polyhedron in this combinatorial sense is a chiral orientably regular map.

Determine the set of all positive integers g such that there exists a chiral map on the closed orientable surface of genus g.
status_search_result: The complete characterization of genera supporting chiral maps remains open. Partial results are known: Garbe (1969) showed there are no chiral maps for genus 2–6; Conder and Dobcsányi (2001) enumerated chiral maps for genus 7–15; and Conder has extended computational classifications up to genus 301. Infinitely many gaps in the genus spectrum of chiral maps are known to exist, but a full description of which positive integers g arise is not available.

paper_title: Developments and open problems on chiral polytopes
original_question: Does every chiral polytope K with regular facets admit a chiral extension whose Schläfli symbol has any prescribed last entry?
self_contained_problem:
An abstract polytope of rank $n$ is a ranked partially ordered set (with faces of ranks $-1, 0, 1, \dots, n$, including a unique minimum face of rank $-1$ and a unique maximum face of rank $n$) satisfying the standard diamond, flag-connectivity, and strong flag-connectivity axioms; its facets are the faces of rank $n-1$. The Schläfli symbol of such a polytope (when it is well-defined) is the tuple $\{p_1, p_2, \dots, p_{n-1}\}$, where $p_i$ is the number of $i$-faces in any section of rank $2$ formed by an $(i-2)$-face and an $(i+1)$-face. A polytope is called regular if its automorphism group acts transitively on its flags. It is called chiral if its automorphism group has exactly two orbits on flags, with adjacent flags lying in different orbits (so the polytope has full rotational symmetry but admits no reflection-like symmetry). 

Given an abstract polytope $\mathcal{K}$ of rank $n-1$, a polytope $\mathcal{P}$ of rank $n$ is called an extension of $\mathcal{K}$ if every facet of $\mathcal{P}$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal{K}$. It is known that if $\mathcal{K}$ is chiral with regular facets and has Schläfli symbol $\{p_1, \dots, p_{n-2}\}$, then any chiral extension $\mathcal{P}$ of $\mathcal{K}$ has Schläfli symbol of the form $\{p_1, \dots, p_{n-2}, q\}$ for some integer $q \geq 3$.

Problem. Does every chiral polytope $\mathcal{K}$ with regular facets admit, for every prescribed integer $q \geq 3$ (or more generally, for every admissible value $q$), a chiral extension whose Schläfli symbol has last entry equal to $q$?
status_search_result: The question has been partially addressed. Constructions exist showing that certain chiral polytopes with regular facets admit chiral extensions whose Schläfli symbol has arbitrarily large last entry (e.g., extensions where the last entry is lcm(2s, q) for a parameter s, and constructions for chiral toroids). However, the general statement—that every chiral polytope with regular facets admits a chiral extension with any prescribed last entry of the Schläfli symbol—does not appear to be fully established.

self_contained_problem:
An abstract d-polytope is a ranked partially ordered set whose elements (called faces) have ranks in {-1, 0, 1, ..., d}, with a unique minimum face of rank -1 and a unique maximum face of rank d, satisfying the diamond condition (every flag, i.e. every maximal chain, can be uniquely modified at any intermediate rank) and a strong connectivity condition on flags. paper_title: Dima Khavinson’s 60th: a summary of open problems in analysis and mathematical physics
original_question: Let Γ be a real-analytic nonsingular hypersurface in R^n, and let u_Γ be its modified Schwarz potential, meaning a local solution of Δu_Γ = 1 with u_Γ = 0 and ∇u_Γ = 0 on Γ. If the only singularities of u_Γ in R^n are isolated polar singularities x_0 with local behavior u_Γ(x) = O(|x-x_0|^{-m}) for some m > 0, must Γ necessarily be a sphere?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ ($n \geq 2$) be a real-analytic, nonsingular hypersurface. The modified Schwarz potential of $\Gamma$ is defined as a function $u_\Gamma$, defined in a neighborhood of $\Gamma$, satisfying
$$\Delta u_\Gamma = 1, \qquad u_\Gamma\big|_{\Gamma} = 0, \qquad \nabla u_\Gamma\big|_{\Gamma} = 0.$$
By the Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem, such a $u_\Gamma$ exists and is unique in some neighborhood of $\Gamma$, and it admits a (possibly multi-valued) analytic continuation to $\mathbb{R}^n$ outside its singular set.

Suppose that the only singularities of (the analytic continuation of) $u_\Gamma$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ are isolated polar singularities, i.e., there exist finitely many points $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that, near each such $x_0$,
$$u_\Gamma(x) = O\!\left(|x - x_0|^{-m}\right)$$
for some $m > 0$, and $u_\Gamma$ extends real-analytically to $\mathbb{R}^n$ minus this finite set of points.

Prove or disprove: under these hypotheses, $\Gamma$ must be a sphere.
status_search_result: The question is part of a circle of conjectures around the Khavinson–Shapiro program on singularities of the Schwarz potential and characterizations of spheres/ellipsoids. Surveys and recent literature (e.g., Lundberg's work on Laplacian/elliptic growth, the AMS Surveys volume 232 by Ebenfelt–Khavinson–Shapiro, and the Notices article "A Tale of Ellipsoids in Potential Theory") discuss this and related conjectures as outstanding problems. No published proof or counterexample establishing that isolated polar singularities of the modified Schwarz potential force $\Gamma$ to be a sphere has been located, so the problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Call a domain Ω ⊂ C an arclength null-quadrature domain if ∫_{∂Ω} g(z) ds(z) = 0 for every function g in the Smirnov space E^1(Ω). Which planar domains Ω satisfy this condition; equivalently, how can all arclength null-quadrature domains be classified?

   sup_n ∫_{Γ_n} |g(z)| |dz| < ∞.

Call Ω an arclength null-quadrature domain (ALNQD) if

   ∫_{∂Ω} g(z) ds(z) = 0

for every g ∈ E^1(Ω) (the boundary integral being understood via nontangential boundary values, which exist a.e. for functions in E^1(Ω)).

original_question: Suppose Ω ⊂ C satisfies the arclength null-quadrature identity ∫_{∂Ω} g(z) ds(z) = 0 for every g in E^1(Ω). Does this condition force the unit tangent vector on ∂Ω to admit an analytic continuation throughout Ω?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}$ be a domain with rectifiable boundary $\partial\Omega$, and let $ds$ denote arclength measure on $\partial\Omega$. Recall that the Smirnov class $E^1(\Omega)$ consists of those holomorphic functions $g$ on $\Omega$ for which there exists a sequence of rectifiable Jordan curves $\{\Gamma_n\}$ exhausting $\Omega$ such that $\sup_n \int_{\Gamma_n} |g(z)|\, |dz| < \infty$; equivalently, $g$ has nontangential boundary values in $L^1(\partial\Omega, ds)$ and is recovered by the Cauchy integral of these boundary values.

Call $\Omega$ an arclength null-quadrature domain (ALNQD) if
$$\int_{\partial\Omega} g(z)\, ds(z) = 0 \quad \text{for every } g \in E^1(\Omega).$$

Let $T(z)$ denote the unit tangent vector to $\partial\Omega$ (defined a.e. on the rectifiable boundary), viewed as a complex-valued function on $\partial\Omega$.

Question: Does the ALNQD condition above force $T$ to extend from $\partial\Omega$ to an analytic function on all of $\Omega$? That is, does there exist a function $h$ holomorphic in $\Omega$ whose nontangential boundary values agree a.e. on $\partial\Omega$ with the unit tangent vector $T$?

original_question: In cases where the nonlinear evolution ∂_t f(z,t) = z f′(z,t) ∫_T ((z+ζ)/(z-ζ)) |dζ| / |f′(ζ,t)|^α is well posed, what geometric information can be proved about the resulting hulls K(t)? In particular, do their boundaries have any regularity, and is the evolution stable under perturbations of the initial conformal map φ?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disk and $\mathbb{T}=\partial\mathbb{D}$ the unit circle. Fix a parameter $\alpha>0$, and let $\varphi:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ be a univalent (conformal) map with $\varphi(0)=0$ and $\varphi'(0)>0$. Consider the family of univalent maps $f(\cdot,t):\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}\setminus K(t)$ (with $f(\cdot,0)=\varphi$) governed by the nonlinear Loewner-type evolution
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(z,t)\;=\;z\,f'(z,t)\int_{\mathbb{T}}\frac{z+\zeta}{z-\zeta}\,\frac{|d\zeta|}{|f'(\zeta,t)|^{\alpha}},\qquad z\in\mathbb{D},$$
where $f'$ denotes the derivative in $z$ and the boundary values $f'(\zeta,t)$ are understood in a suitable (e.g., nontangential) sense. The increasing family of compact "hulls" is $K(t)=\mathbb{C}\setminus f(\mathbb{D},t)$.

In any regime in which this evolution is well posed (existence and uniqueness of $f(\cdot,t)$ on some time interval $[0,T)$), establish geometric properties of the hulls $K(t)$. Specifically:

(a) Prove or disprove that for $t\in(0,T)$ the boundary $\partial K(t)$ enjoys some degree of regularity (for example, that it is a Jordan curve, locally connected, Hölder, or smoother), and identify the optimal regularity as a function of $\alpha$ and of the regularity of $\varphi$.

(b) Prove or disprove stability of the evolution with respect to the initial datum: if $\varphi_n\to\varphi$ in a suitable topology of conformal maps on $\mathbb{D}$, do the corresponding solutions $f_n(\cdot,t)$ converge to $f(\cdot,t)$ (equivalently, do the hulls $K_n(t)$ converge to $K(t)$, e.g., in the Carathéodory or Hausdorff sense) on the common interval of existence?
status_search_result: The specific nonlinear Loewner-type evolution with the $|f'(\zeta,t)|^{-\alpha}$ weight (a continuum analogue of Hastings–Levitov HL($\alpha$)) is studied actively, and partial results exist on related regularized models (scaling limits to Loewner–Kufarev equations, Hölder regularity of hull complements, stability in subcritical regimes). However, regularity and stability for this exact unregularized continuum equation, in the generality posed, do not appear to have been resolved.

paper_title: Dima Khavinson’s 60th: a summary of open problems in analysis and mathematical physics
original_question: The case α = 2 of the nonlinear Loewner-type growth equation has been studied extensively. What special behavior occurs at α = 1, where the boundary’s normal velocity is heuristically constant and the evolution is compared with the α = 1 Hastings-Levitov/Eden-type regime?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the following family of nonlinear Loewner-type planar growth processes. Let $K_0 = \overline{\mathbb{D}}^c \cup \{\infty\}$ be the exterior of the closed unit disk, and consider a growing family of compact hulls $K_t \supset K_0$, $t \ge 0$, in the Riemann sphere whose complements are simply connected. For each $t$, let $g_t : \mathbb{C} \setminus K_t \to \{|z|>1\}$ be the unique conformal map fixing $\infty$ with $g_t'(\infty)>0$. Given a parameter $\alpha > 0$ and a probability measure $\mu_t$ on the unit circle, the family $(g_t)$ is required to satisfy the weighted Loewner-Kufarev equation
$$\partial_t g_t(z) = g_t(z) \int_{|\zeta|=1} \frac{g_t(z)+\zeta}{g_t(z)-\zeta} \, |g_t'(z)|^{-\alpha}\bigg|_{\text{boundary push-forward}} \, d\mu_t(\zeta),$$
so that, heuristically, the inward normal velocity of the boundary $\partial K_t$ at a point $w \in \partial K_t$ is proportional to $|g_t'(w)|^{\alpha-1}$ times a local driving density. The case $\alpha = 2$ corresponds to Hele–Shaw / Laplacian growth and has been studied extensively (Carleson–Makarov and others), where one obtains existence, scaling limits, and information on the limit shapes.

Investigate the case $\alpha = 1$, in which the normal velocity of the boundary is (formally) a constant independent of conformal distortion, so that the evolution is heuristically an Eden-type isotropic growth and is conjecturally related to the $\alpha = 1$ Hastings–Levitov regime $\mathrm{HL}(1)$. Specifically: establish existence and uniqueness of solutions $K_t$ for natural classes of driving measures $\mu_t$; describe the scaling limit and the regularity (e.g. smoothness or roughness) of $\partial K_t$; and determine whether the limit shapes coincide with, or qualitatively differ from, those produced by random $\mathrm{HL}(1)$ / Eden aggregation in an appropriate scaling limit.
status_search_result: The α = 1 case of nonlinear Loewner-driven planar aggregation (and the related Hastings–Levitov HL(1) model) is widely identified as a critical and subtle regime. While the α = 2 (Hele–Shaw/Laplacian) case is well developed via Carleson–Makarov and successors, no complete description of existence, scaling limits, and limit shapes for the α = 1 deterministic Loewner growth or rigorous matching with HL(1) appears in the literature as of 2026; partial results exist for anisotropic/regularized Hastings–Levitov families and related stationary HL(0) models, but the α = 1 case remains open.

original_question: Let f(z) = exp(-(1+z)/(1-z)). Can one prove that f is an inner function in H^2 using only H^2 information encoded by its Taylor series, without appealing to boundary-value characterizations of inner functions on the unit circle?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ denote the open unit disk, and let $H^2 = H^2(\mathbb{D})$ be the Hardy space consisting of all holomorphic functions $g(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n z^n$ on $\mathbb{D}$ such that
$$\|g\|_{H^2}^2 := \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} |a_n|^2 < \infty.$$
A function $g \in H^2$ is called inner if its non-tangential boundary values satisfy $|g(e^{i\theta})| = 1$ for almost every $\theta \in [0, 2\pi)$.

Consider the function
$$f(z) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{1+z}{1-z}\right), \qquad z \in \mathbb{D}.$$

original_question: Given an infinite discrete collection of positive point masses a_k located at x_k in R^n, assume the gravitational force field F(x) = Σ_{k=0}^∞ a_k (x_k - x) / |x - x_k|^n converges under the summability condition Σ a_k / |x_k|^{n-1} < ∞. Must this force field always vanish at some point; equivalently, must the associated logarithmic or Newtonian potential always have a critical point?
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \geq 2$ and let $\{x_k\}_{k=0}^{\infty} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be an infinite discrete set of points (with no finite accumulation point), and let $\{a_k\}_{k=0}^{\infty}$ be a sequence of positive real numbers ("masses") satisfying the convergence condition
$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{a_k}{|x_k|^{n-1}} < \infty.$$
Define the associated gravitational force field on $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{x_k : k \geq 0\}$ by
$$F(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \, \frac{x_k - x}{|x - x_k|^n}.$$
Equivalently, $F = -\nabla U$, where $U$ is the corresponding logarithmic ($n=2$) or Newtonian ($n \geq 3$) potential generated by the masses $a_k$ at the points $x_k$.

Question: Must there always exist a point $x^* \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{x_k\}$ with $F(x^*) = 0$? Equivalently, must $U$ always possess at least one critical point?
status_search_result: The question is the Clunie–Eremenko–Rossi conjecture, posed in their 1993 paper "On equilibrium points of logarithmic and Newtonian potentials" (J. London Math. Soc.). Subsequent work by Eremenko, Langley, Rossi and others has obtained partial results and an "operator version," but the original conjecture concerning the existence of equilibrium points of potentials of infinite discrete positive mass distributions appears to remain open.

paper_title: Fair Division under Joint Ownership: Recent Results and Open Problems
context_brief: Manna division with fairness and monotonicity constraints
original_question: In the manna-division problem, where a fixed stock of unproduced goods is divided among agents with arbitrary convex and monotonic preferences, does there exist a Pareto optimal mechanism that satisfies Population Monotonicity and No Domination, where Population Monotonicity means that when an additional agent joins the population sharing the same cake no pre-existing agent benefits, and No Domination means that no agent ever receives a strictly bigger share of every good than another agent? If such a mechanism exists, can one also require Equal Split Guarantee, meaning that each agent's welfare is at least as high as the welfare of that agent's per-capita share of the resources?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the manna-division problem: a fixed bundle of perfectly divisible, unproduced goods (a "cake") is to be divided among a finite set of agents. Each agent has an arbitrary preference relation over their share that is convex and monotonic (more of every good is weakly better, and preferences have convex upper-contour sets). A mechanism associates to every population (finite set of agents) and every profile of such preferences an allocation of the entire cake among the agents.

Define the following properties of a mechanism:

1. Pareto Optimality: at every profile, the allocation chosen is not Pareto-dominated by any other feasible allocation of the cake.

2. Population Monotonicity: if a new agent joins the population sharing the same cake (so the cake is now split among more agents), then no pre-existing agent strictly prefers the new allocation to the old one — equivalently, every pre-existing agent weakly loses.

3. No Domination: at every profile, the chosen allocation never assigns to any agent a bundle that is strictly larger in every coordinate (every good) than the bundle assigned to some other agent.

4. Equal Split Guarantee: at every profile, every agent weakly prefers their assigned bundle to receiving the equal-split bundle (the per-capita share 1/n of the cake, where n is the number of agents).

Question (a): Does there exist a mechanism on this domain (arbitrary convex monotonic preferences over a divisible heterogeneous manna) that simultaneously satisfies Pareto Optimality, Population Monotonicity, and No Domination?

Question (b): If such a mechanism exists, can one in addition require it to satisfy Equal Split Guarantee?
status_search_result: A web search did not surface a published resolution of this combined axiomatic question for manna division with arbitrary convex monotonic preferences. Related literature (e.g., the competitive/Nash rule for mixed manna by Bogomolnaia–Moulin–Sandomirskiy–Yanovskaya, and work on population/resource monotonicity in cake-cutting) establishes monotonicity properties of specific Pareto-optimal rules in restricted domains, but does not appear to settle the existence of a Pareto-optimal mechanism satisfying both Population Monotonicity and No Domination (and additionally Equal Split Guarantee) on the general convex monotonic domain. Status appears to remain open.

original_question: Let O(n, n, q) be a pseudo-oval, meaning a set of q^n + 1 mutually constrained (n − 1)-dimensional subspaces in PG(3n − 1, q) as defined in the paper. Is every such pseudo-oval regular, in the sense of arising from the paper’s field-extension construction of a regular pseudo-oval?
self_contained_problem:
Work in the finite projective space $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$ over the field $\mathbb{F}_q$, where $n\geq 1$ and $q$ is a prime power. A pseudo-oval (also called a generalized oval, or $[n-1]$-oval) is a set
$$\mathcal{O} = \{\pi_0, \pi_1, \ldots, \pi_{q^n}\}$$
of $q^n+1$ pairwise disjoint $(n-1)$-dimensional subspaces of $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$ satisfying the tangent-space condition: every three distinct elements of $\mathcal{O}$ span a $(3n-1)$-dimensional subspace (equivalently, they are in general position), and for each $\pi_i\in\mathcal{O}$ there exists a $(2n-1)$-dimensional subspace $T_i$ (the tangent space at $\pi_i$) containing $\pi_i$ and meeting every $\pi_j$, $j\neq i$, trivially.

The standard field-extension construction produces a so-called regular pseudo-oval as follows. Let $\mathcal{O}'$ be an oval (a set of $q^n+1$ points, no three collinear) in $\mathrm{PG}(2,q^n)$. Viewing $\mathrm{PG}(2,q^n)$ as $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$ by restriction of scalars from $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ to $\mathbb{F}_q$, each point of $\mathcal{O}'$ becomes an $(n-1)$-dimensional $\mathbb{F}_q$-subspace, and the resulting collection is a pseudo-oval in $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$. A pseudo-oval is called regular if it is projectively equivalent to one obtained in this way.

Question: Is every pseudo-oval in $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$ regular?
status_search_result: The general regularity question for pseudo-ovals appears still open. Recent classification work (2024) addresses only small parameters: all pseudo-ovals in $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,2)$ for $n=3,4$, and in $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$ for $n=5,6$ under a Desarguesian-plane hypothesis, have been classified, and all known pseudo-ovals are regular, but no general proof or counterexample is reported.

original_question: For a pseudo-oval O(n, n, q) in odd characteristic, is O always isomorphic to its translation dual O∗(n, n, q), where O∗ is the pseudo-oval formed by the tangent spaces of O in the dual projective space?
self_contained_problem:
Let $q$ be an odd prime power and let $n$ be a positive integer. A pseudo-oval (or generalized oval) $O = O(n,n,q)$ in the projective space $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1, q)$ is a set of $q^n + 1$ pairwise disjoint $(n-1)$-dimensional subspaces $\pi_0, \pi_1, \dots, \pi_{q^n}$ with the property that any three of them span a $(3n-1)$-dimensional subspace (equivalently, they span the whole space). For each element $\pi_i \in O$ there is a unique $(2n-1)$-dimensional subspace $\tau_i$ of $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$, called the tangent space of $O$ at $\pi_i$, that contains $\pi_i$ and is disjoint from every other element of $O$. In the dual projective space $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)^*$, the $q^n + 1$ tangent spaces $\tau_0, \tau_1, \dots, \tau_{q^n}$ (viewed as points of the appropriate Grassmannian via duality) themselves form a pseudo-oval, denoted $O^* = O^*(n,n,q)$, and called the translation dual of $O$.

Question: For every odd prime power $q$ and every positive integer $n$, is every pseudo-oval $O(n,n,q)$ projectively isomorphic to its translation dual $O^*(n,n,q)$?
status_search_result: Recent literature (e.g., classification results for translation generalized quadrangles of small order published in 2024) treats this as an active question and does not announce a general answer. No proof or counterexample for arbitrary odd $q$ and $n$ appears to be known; the question remains open.

original_question: Let O(n, n, q) = {π_0, …, π_{q^n}} be a pseudo-oval in PG(3n − 1, q). For fixed i, the paper defines an (n − 1)-spread S_i of a skew PG(2n − 1, q) using the tangent space τ_i and the intersections <π_i, π_j> ∩ PG(2n − 1, q). In the even-q case, it also defines an (n − 1)-spread S using the nucleus η and the intersections PG(2n − 1, q) ∩ <η, π_j>. What structural consequences follow when, in the situation described by the source, the spread S, respectively S_i, is regular?
self_contained_problem:
Let q be a prime power and n a positive integer. A pseudo-oval of PG(3n−1, q) is a set
  O(n, n, q) = {π_0, π_1, …, π_{q^n}}
of q^n + 1 mutually disjoint (n−1)-dimensional subspaces of PG(3n−1, q) such that any three of them span PG(3n−1, q). For each i there is a unique (3n−1−n)=(2n−1)-dimensional subspace τ_i, called the tangent space at π_i, that contains π_i and meets every other π_j (j ≠ i) trivially in the sense required by the pseudo-oval (equivalently, the unique (2n−1)-space through π_i skew to all π_j for j ≠ i in the appropriate dual sense). When q is even, the tangent spaces τ_0, …, τ_{q^n} all share a common (n−1)-dimensional subspace η, called the nucleus of O(n, n, q).

Fix a (2n−1)-dimensional subspace PG(2n−1, q) of PG(3n−1, q) that is skew to π_i (resp. skew to η). Define
  S_i = {ξ_i, ξ_0, ξ_1, …, ξ_{q^n}} \ {ξ_i-duplicate},
where ξ_i = τ_i ∩ PG(2n−1, q) and ξ_j = ⟨π_i, π_j⟩ ∩ PG(2n−1, q) for j ≠ i; this is an (n−1)-spread of PG(2n−1, q).
When q is even, define analogously
  S = {ζ_0, ζ_1, …, ζ_{q^n}}, where ζ_j = PG(2n−1, q) ∩ ⟨η, π_j⟩;
this is also an (n−1)-spread of PG(2n−1, q).

Recall that an (n−1)-spread of PG(2n−1, q) is called regular (Desarguesian) if for any three of its elements the unique regulus they determine is contained in the spread; equivalently, the spread arises from the field-reduction of a 1-spread of PG(1, q^n).

Problem. Assume q is even. Determine the structural consequences for the pseudo-oval O(n, n, q) (and for the associated translation generalized quadrangle T(O)) under each of the following hypotheses:
 (a) the (n−1)-spread S defined via the nucleus η is regular;
 (b) for some (equivalently, every) i, the (n−1)-spread S_i defined via the tangent space τ_i is regular.
In particular, does regularity of S (resp. S_i) force O(n, n, q) to be a pseudo-conic (i.e., to arise from field reduction of a conic in PG(2, q^n)), and consequently force T(O) to be isomorphic to the classical generalized quadrangle Q(4, q^n)?

original_question: For pseudo-ovals O(n, n, q) with q even, Theorem 5.7 assumes 2-transitivity in order to characterize classicality. How far can that hypothesis be weakened—for example, would transitivity alone already force the pseudo-oval to be classical?
self_contained_problem:
Let $q$ be an even prime power and let $n\ge 1$ be an integer. A pseudo-oval $\mathcal{O}=\mathcal{O}(n,n,q)$ in $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$ is a set of $q^n+1$ pairwise disjoint $(n-1)$-dimensional subspaces of $\mathrm{PG}(3n-1,q)$ such that any three of them span the whole space. The pseudo-oval $\mathcal{O}$ is called classical (or elementary, arising from a conic) if there exists a conic $C$ in $\mathrm{PG}(2,q^n)$ such that, after applying field reduction from $\mathrm{GF}(q^n)$ to $\mathrm{GF}(q)$, the points of $C$ become precisely the elements of $\mathcal{O}$.

The collineation stabiliser $G\le \mathrm{P}\Gamma\mathrm{L}(3n,q)$ of $\mathcal{O}$ is said to act $2$-transitively on $\mathcal{O}$ if for any two ordered pairs of distinct elements of $\mathcal{O}$ there is an element of $G$ sending the first pair to the second; it acts transitively on $\mathcal{O}$ if any single element of $\mathcal{O}$ can be mapped to any other.

It is known that, for $q$ even, $\mathcal{O}(n,n,q)$ is classical if and only if it admits a $2$-transitive collineation group.

Question: Can the hypothesis of $2$-transitivity be weakened to mere transitivity? That is, is every pseudo-oval $\mathcal{O}(n,n,q)$ with $q$ even that admits a transitive collineation group necessarily classical?
status_search_result: Significant partial progress has been made. Bamberg–Penttila ("Transitive eggs", 2006) and subsequent work by Bamberg, Glasby, Popiel and Praeger (2016) showed that a pseudo-oval (not an oval) admitting an insoluble transitive collineation group is elementary, arising via field reduction from a conic, an elliptic quadric, or a Suzuki–Tits ovoid. Rottey and Van de Voorde (arXiv:1701.09126) classified regular pseudo-ovals in even characteristic for prime $n$. However, the full question—whether transitivity alone (without insolubility or regularity hypotheses) forces classicality of $\mathcal{O}(n,n,q)$ in even characteristic—does not appear to have been settled in full generality.

original_question: If O(n, 2n, q) is an egg in even characteristic, is it always regular, in the sense of the paper’s notion of a regular pseudo-ovoid?
self_contained_problem:
Let $q$ be a prime power and let $n\ge 1$ be an integer. In the finite projective space $\mathrm{PG}(4n-1,q)$, an egg (also called a pseudo-ovoid, generalized ovoid, or $[n-1]$-ovoid), denoted $O(n,2n,q)$, is a family $\mathcal{E}$ of $q^{2n}+1$ pairwise disjoint $(n-1)$-dimensional subspaces such that:

(i) any three distinct elements of $\mathcal{E}$ span a $(3n-1)$-dimensional subspace; and
(ii) at every element $E\in\mathcal{E}$ there exists a unique $(3n-1)$-dimensional subspace $T_E$ (the tangent space at $E$) which contains $E$ and is disjoint from every other element of $\mathcal{E}$.

Such an egg is called regular (a regular pseudo-ovoid) if the $q^{2n}+1$ tangent spaces $\{T_E : E\in\mathcal{E}\}$ form the dual of an egg in $\mathrm{PG}(4n-1,q)$; equivalently, every hyperplane of $\mathrm{PG}(4n-1,q)$ either contains exactly one tangent space or contains exactly $q^n+1$ tangent spaces.

Question: Suppose $q$ is even. Is every egg $O(n,2n,q)$ in $\mathrm{PG}(4n-1,q)$ necessarily regular?
status_search_result: The question of whether every egg O(n,2n,q) in even characteristic is regular is a well-known open problem in finite geometry. Recent partial results (e.g., classifications of eggs containing a pseudo-conic, characterizations of classical eggs, and progress on translation generalized ovals in even characteristic) address special cases but do not resolve the general question. No source found that fully settles it.

original_question: For an egg O(n, 2n, q) in even characteristic, is O always isomorphic to its translation dual O∗(n, 2n, q), where O∗ is the dual egg formed by the tangent spaces of O?

(i) any three distinct egg elements span a (3n-1)-dimensional subspace, and

original_question: For every egg O(n, 2n, q), is there always a pseudo-oval lying on O itself or on its translation dual O∗(n, 2n, q)?
self_contained_problem:
Work in the projective space PG(2n+m-1, q) over the finite field of order q. An egg O(n, m, q) is a set of q^m + 1 mutually disjoint (n-1)-dimensional subspaces of PG(2n+m-1, q) such that:
(i) any three of them span a (3n-1)-dimensional subspace, and
(ii) each element E of the egg is contained in a unique (n+m-1)-dimensional subspace T_E (the tangent space at E) that meets the egg only in E.

When n = m, an egg O(n, n, q) is called a pseudo-oval (or generalized oval) in PG(3n-1, q): it consists of q^n + 1 pairwise disjoint (n-1)-spaces in PG(3n-1, q), every three of which span the whole space.

For an egg O = O(n, m, q), the q^m + 1 tangent spaces T_E form an egg O*(n, m, q) in the dual space of PG(2n+m-1, q), called the translation dual of O.

Now specialize to the case m = 2n, so that O = O(n, 2n, q) lives in PG(4n-1, q) and consists of q^{2n} + 1 mutually disjoint (n-1)-spaces, while its translation dual O* = O*(n, 2n, q) also lives in (a) PG(4n-1, q).

Question: Does every egg O(n, 2n, q) contain a pseudo-oval, in the sense that either O itself or its translation dual O*(n, 2n, q) contains a subset of q^n + 1 of its elements forming a pseudo-oval in some (3n-1)-dimensional subspace?

The status of this specific question appears unresolved.

paper_title: Finite translation generalized quadrangles: old results, new results, open problems
original_question: Suppose an egg O(n, 2n, q) contains a sub pseudo-conic, where the paper uses “pseudo-conic” for a regular pseudo-oval arising from a conic. Must the egg then be good?
self_contained_problem:
Let q be a prime power and n a positive integer. An egg O(n, 2n, q) is a set E of q^{2n}+1 mutually disjoint (n−1)-dimensional subspaces of PG(4n−1, q) such that:
(i) any three of them span a (3n−1)-dimensional subspace, and
(ii) every element π ∈ E is contained in a unique (3n−1)-dimensional subspace τ(π), called the tangent space of E at π, that is disjoint from all other elements of E.

Such an egg E is said to be good at an element π ∈ E if for every two distinct elements π′, π″ of E ∖ {π}, the (3n−1)-dimensional space ⟨π, π′, π″⟩ contains exactly q^n + 1 elements of E; the egg E is called good if it is good at some element.

A pseudo-oval in PG(3n−1, q) is a set of q^n + 1 mutually disjoint (n−1)-dimensional subspaces, every three of which span PG(3n−1, q). A pseudo-oval is called regular if it arises by field reduction from an oval O₁ in PG(2, q^n); when O₁ can be taken to be a (nondegenerate) conic, the regular pseudo-oval is called a pseudo-conic.

A sub pseudo-conic of an egg O(n, 2n, q) is a subset of q^n + 1 of its elements that all lie in a common (3n−1)-dimensional subspace and form a pseudo-conic there.

Question: Must every egg O(n, 2n, q) that contains a sub pseudo-conic be good?
status_search_result: For q even, results of Brown and Lavrauw show that an egg O(n,2n,q) containing a pseudo-conic is classical (arising from an elliptic quadric), and classical eggs are good at every element; thus the answer is affirmative in even characteristic. For q odd, no general resolution of the question appears in the literature found, so the problem appears to remain open in the odd case.
